title: Digital Financial Literacy as a Catalyst for Inclusive International Business Expansion: Lessons from Malaysian Gen Z B40 Households and Implications for Emerging Market Strategies

detail.title: Digital Financial Literacy as a Catalyst for Inclusive International Business Expansion: Lessons from Malaysian Gen Z B40 Households and Implications for Emerging Market Strategies
detail.abstract: Digital financial literacy (DFL) has emerged as a critical capability in the rapidly digitising global economy, particularly for underserved populations in emerging markets where digital financial services are expanding faster than user competencies (Jose & Ghosh, 2025; Klapper et al., 2025). Drawing on insights from a Malaysian study of Generation Z households in the Bottom 40% (B40) income group, this article examines DFL's role in household wealth management and extends the analysis to international business (IB) contexts. Using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) as a foundational lens, the discussion explores how performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions shape the adoption of digital financial services among digitally native yet financially vulnerable youth (Sabri et al., 2026). The analysis further investigates how DFL influences financial inclusion, cross-border financial behaviours such as remittances and digital trade payments, and the strategic opportunities available to multinational enterprises (MNEs), fintech providers and policymakers. Findings synthesised from recent empirical work indicate that higher DFL correlates with improved savings behaviour, better risk management and greater participation in formal digital financial services (Dandi, 2026; Sarlawa, 2025). These individual-level gains in turn support SME internationalisation, remittance efficiency and more resilient global value chains by expanding the pool of capable local suppliers and customers (OECD, 2026). The article proposes an extended conceptual model that links individual-level DFL to firm-level IB outcomes, positioning literacy as both a market-readiness factor and a moderator of technology acceptance in emerging economies. Practical recommendations are offered for MNE market-entry strategies that embed financial education, capacity-building partnerships with local institutions, and regulatory harmonisation across ASEAN and other emerging regions. Implications are drawn for achieving Sustainable Development Goals related to poverty reduction and inclusive growth, underscoring that DFL is no longer solely a domestic policy concern but a strategic enabler of inclusive international business expansion.

title: Beyond Five Stars: What Drives Exceptional Hospitality? A Topic Modelling Analysis of Hotel Reviews from Shanghai

detail.title: Beyond Five Stars: What Drives Exceptional Hospitality? A Topic Modelling Analysis of Hotel Reviews from Shanghai

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it used publicly available secondary data and did not involve human participants or direct interaction with respondents.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The rapid growth of online travel platforms has transformed customer reviews into a valuable source of information for understanding guest experiences in the hospitality industry. Unlike traditional survey methods, online reviews provide rich and unsolicited narratives that capture diverse aspects of hotel stays. However, the large volume of user-generated content makes manual analysis impractical, necessitating the use of advanced text analytics techniques. This study aims to identify the latent dimensions that drive exceptional hospitality by analysing 415,504 hotel reviews collected from TripAdvisor for hotels in Shanghai, China. A Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline was implemented to preprocess the review texts, followed by Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for topic modelling. The optimal number of topics was determined using coherence score analysis, resulting in an 11-topic model with a coherence score of 0.5257. The findings reveal that customer experiences are primarily shaped by themes related to overall service quality, room comfort, breakfast quality, location and accessibility, front desk operations, personalised hospitality, room maintenance, recreational amenities, transportation, and food and beverage services. Among these, overall guest satisfaction and service excellence emerged as the most dominant topic, accounting for 28.04% of all reviews, followed by general travel experience (25.57%) and room comfort with value for money (20.59%). The study demonstrates the effectiveness of topic modelling in uncovering hidden patterns within large-scale hospitality datasets and provides actionable managerial insights for improving customer experience. By analysing one of the largest hotel review datasets in the literature, this research contributes to the growing application of Natural Language Processing in hospitality management and offers practical implications for service improvement and strategic decision-making.

title: A Free AI-assisted Keyword Intelligence Framework for e-commerce SMEs in Bangladesh: Effects on Conversion Performance

detail.title: A Free AI-assisted Keyword Intelligence Framework for e-commerce SMEs in Bangladesh: Effects on Conversion Performance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that this study was conducted with honesty, transparency, and adherence to accepted standards of academic research. All primary data reported in this paper were collected directly through a structured online survey of 212 Bangladeshi e-commerce SME owners and operators in April 2026; no data were fabricated, falsified, or manipulated. Where limitations exist in the data — including below-threshold reliability for the Free AI Tool Usage scale (Cronbach's α = 0.579) and the use of a non-probability convenience/snowball sample — these are explicitly disclosed in the Limitations section rather than concealed. The author declares no conflict of interest, financial or otherwise, that could have influenced the design, analysis, or reporting of this research. All secondary sources cited have been credited according to APA 7th edition referencing standards. Generative AI tools were used to assist with drafting, statistical scripting, and formatting, as disclosed in the AI Disclosure Statement; all interpretations, conclusions, and academic judgements remain the author's own.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not undergo formal review by an institutional ethics review board, as it was conducted as an undergraduate project report under the academic supervision of Muhammad Ataur Rahman, Senior Lecturer, Department of Business Administration, East West University. Participation in the survey was voluntary, and respondents were informed of the purpose of the study prior to completing the questionnaire. No personally identifying information was collected from respondents, and all responses were treated as confidential and reported only in aggregate, anonymised form.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or funding from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted independently by the author as part of an undergraduate project report (Course Code: BUS 498) submitted to the Department of Business Administration, East West University.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of using a structured Keyword Intelligence Framework (KIF) on conversion performance among Bangladeshi e-commerce SMEs. Small sellers have access to free tools such as Google Trends, Google Search Console, ChatGPT, and Claude to research their keywords, yet most continue to work with keywords in a disorganised, intuitive manner. To bridge this gap, the study proposes and tests a five-step KIF-Discovery, Intent Mapping, Implementation, Monitoring, and Refinement-as a low-cost alternative to the expensive paid SEO plans that many SMEs cannot afford. A structured online survey was used to gather primary data from 212 owners of Bangladeshi e-commerce SMEs, analysed descriptively and with the help of Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, hierarchical regression, and one-way ANOVA. KIF adoption positively and significantly predicts conversion performance, explaining an additional 55 percent of variance after controlling for firm size, experience, and revenue. SMEs that follow the framework are more likely to report increased organic traffic, higher online sales, and greater satisfaction, showing that the disciplined application of free AI tools can translate into real commercial benefits for small online businesses.

title: The Authored Brake: Delegating the Right of Refusal to AI Agents in Consumer Finance

detail.title: The Authored Brake: Delegating the Right of Refusal to AI Agents in Consumer Finance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a practitioner in the wealth-management technology industry. This research is independent and was not commissioned, reviewed, or approved by any employer or commercial party. The author has no financial interest in any product, framework, or firm named in the paper. The fictional platform used in the study materials is not modelled on any real firm. Statements about legal and regulatory requirements are descriptive summaries of publicly available sources, conditional on facts not established in the paper, and are not legal advice.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No external ethics committee reviewed this study. The author holds no institutional affiliation, so no committee has jurisdiction over it and none was engaged. Self-assessment is not equivalent to approval, and the paper states this in Section 8.2 rather than leaving it to be inferred. The paper reports no hypothesis test. The partial data collection it describes (Study 1b; 90 participants; anonymous online vignette administered via Prolific; August 2026) ran under a documented self-assessment against the British Psychological Society Code of Human Research Ethics, completed on 9 August 2026 before any data were collected. Participants are told on the consent screen, before agreeing, that no external committee reviewed the study. Risk is minimal and proportionate: a fictional platform, no real money, no account access, no transaction, and no disclosure of the participant's own financial circumstances. Consent is informed. There is one incomplete disclosure by design, in that participants are not told in advance that the description they read is one of two versions, because telling them would destroy the measurement; nothing false is stated at any point and every participant is debriefed in full on the final screen before receiving a completion code. No name, email address, postal address, date of birth, IP address, device fingerprint, or financial detail is collected. The only identifier is the pseudonymous ID supplied by the recruitment platform, retained solely to honour withdrawal requests and to detect duplicate submissions, and removed before any public release. The legal basis for processing is consent under UK GDPR Article 6(1)(a). Withdrawal is available for 14 days via the anonymous ID, as stated on the consent screen. One participant declined data use and is excluded from the dataset and from every figure reported. The self-assessment and the full protocol are available from the author on request. Institutional oversight adequate to the programme's scale is treated as a precondition of completing the study to its pre-registered target.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research is independent and unfunded. Participant payments for the partial Study 1b data collection were met by the author personally.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence in consumer finance is moving from advising to acting. When an agent can execute a transaction, the consumer's decision is no longer whether to believe a recommendation but which decision rights to transfer, and on what terms. This paper takes up one such right for which existing frameworks have no category: the veto, an agent's authority to refuse a transaction its principal has instructed. Permission taxonomies and autonomy ladders scale how much an agent does relative to its user; none of them contains the case of an agent doing less than the user asked. We define delegated financial authority as the standing set of conditions under which a consumer transfers to an automated agent one or more of three separable rights over transactions in the consumer's own resources: the right to initiate a transaction the consumer has not instructed, the right to veto one the consumer has instructed, and the right to defer one pending the consumer's confirmation. A grant may transfer any subset of the three, and each exercise is classified by who initiated and who held terminal disposition; the rights are not points on an autonomy scale. Crossing them with the provenance of the governing rule, as the consumer experiences it, yields six regimes, of which one is this paper's focus: the Authored Brake, where an agent refuses its principal on a rule the principal composed. The central claim is that in domains where consumers anticipate acting against their own interest, they are more willing to transfer the veto right than the initiation right, and that this advantage is amplified when they experience the governing rule as their own. We advance three numbered propositions: that the veto right is transferred more readily than the initiation right, that its experienced provenance moves that transfer, and that neither result survives if the agent is presented as a mechanism rather than as a judgement-exercising mind. We argue that the third should be tested first, because its failure would collapse the other two into the study of commitment products generally. We are explicit that machine enforcement, deferral, the composed-versus-inferred contrast, and provenance effects at constant enforcement are all prior art, and narrow the claim accordingly: what is untested is the veto right's joint structure with experienced provenance under an agent treated as a judgement-exercising mind, an attribution we state as a falsifiable proposition rather than assume.

title:
Metaphors before Features 
Diagnosing Category Meaning in the Indian Electric-SUV Market

detail.title:
Metaphors before Features 
Diagnosing Category Meaning in the Indian Electric-SUV Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author’s employment at MSIL is not only a conflict to disclose at the end of a paper. It is a methodological condition that influences research access, question selection, interpretation and the reception of findings. Wilson, Janes, and Williams (2022) describe positionality and reflexivity as relevant throughout the research process, not merely at the point of ethics disclosure. They also reject a simple binary between insider and outsider: researchers can occupy different positions across organisational, professional, demographic and epistemic dimensions. Insider proximity can improve the practical relevance of this work. It may sharpen awareness of dealer realities, product-development timelines, infrastructure constraints and the risks of simplistic competitor commentary. It may also increase the likelihood that findings can be translated into action. The risks are equally substantial: loyalty can create interpretive charity, commercially familiar language can be mistaken for consumer language, and participants may perceive a study as an indirect sales or performance-evaluation exercise. The paper therefore treats reflexivity as a design practice. Four safeguards follow. First, the study avoids confidential sales, customer or internal strategy data; all company and competitor claims are based on public sources or the author’s transparent brochure corpus. Second, recruitment, interviewing and primary coding should be conducted or audited by researchers who are not in the author’s reporting line and, where feasible, not employed by MSIL. Third, the protocol includes rival hypotheses—notably that supply allocation, not brand meaning, explains domestic volume—and preserves cases that favour competitor or e-VITARA interpretations equally. Fourth, the author should keep a positionality memo documenting decisions about the corpus, city frame, interview prompts, surprise findings and changes to interpretation. The resulting stance is neither defensive nor promotional. It recognises the author as an insider with bounded access and commitments, whose research quality depends on making those commitments inspectable. This is especially appropriate for a practitioner working paper intended as the seed of doctoral research rather than an official corporate document.
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: No one funded the research; it was self-motivated and self-funded.

detail.abstract:
The first electric sport-utility vehicle (SUV) from Maruti Suzuki entered India under conditions that make a simple launch-success narrative untenable. The e-VITARA began nationwide deliveries on 17 February 2026, with an introductory battery-as-a-service (BaaS) entry price of ₹10.99 lakh plus ₹3.99 per kilometre for the battery (Maruti Suzuki India Limited, 2026). Domestic retail volumes were modest in the initial ramp, but that fact must be interpreted against a deliberately export-led allocation: by May 2026, more than 35,000 e-VITARAs had been exported to 46 countries, compared with 7,097 domestic sales, while domestic monthly allocation had reportedly been capped at about 2,000 units because production was prioritised for exports (Autocar Professional, 2026b; Financial Express, 2026). The managerial and scholarly question is therefore not whether the model has “failed.” It is whether domestic pull is weaker than the category opportunity would suggest, and whether that pattern is a supply-side outcome, a meaning-side outcome, or both.

This paper develops a two-study architecture for that question.

Study 1 is an original, systematic semiotic content analysis of six Indian electric-SUV brochures, coded against the seven deep metaphors proposed by Zaltman and Zaltman (2008): Balance, Transformation, Journey, Container, Connection, Resource and Control. Competitors cluster around Control—Tata Sierra.ev (11 primary-coded units), MG ZS EV (8), and Mahindra BE 6 (7)—whereas e-VITARA’s message is dispersed across Transformation (5), Container (4), and Connection, Resource and Control (3 each). The paper calls this sender-side diagnosis metaphoric diffuseness: a firm-controlled communication system without a clearly governing human drama.

Study 2, proposed rather than reported, is a condensed but rigorously specified Zaltman Metaphor Elicitation Technique (ZMET) field protocol with first-time EV considerers in Tier-2 cities. It tests whether intended positioning is received as such, and whether a resource-and-reassurance heritage can be translated into category-appropriate confidence and progress.

The paper contributes a replicable method for connecting brochure-level category signals to consumer meaning, a falsifiable field protocol, and a defensible practitioner research agenda for incumbent EV entry. It also sets narrow, evidence-based boundaries on generative AI: it can assist transparent first-pass coding but should not substitute for Indian respondents, especially where a new product category is concerned.

title: Which Way Should the Car Face?: Consumer Preferences Regarding Direction from a Mental Simulation Perspective
affiliations: Meiji University

detail.title: Which Way Should the Car Face?: Consumer Preferences Regarding Direction from a Mental Simulation Perspective
detail.abstract: People who are the subjects of photographs tend to want to show the left side of their face, which is more likely to show emotions. Furthermore, viewers also tend to perceive left-facing faces as more typical and are more likely to rate them highly, exhibiting a left-cheek preference bias. Looking at cars, the headlights are likened to eyes, the grille to a mouth, and the front mask to a human or animal face. Therefore, considering the left-cheek preference bias and the tendency to perceive cars as faces, it can be inferred that left-facing car advertisements are desirable. However, this lacks a mental simulation perspective. According to this theory, consumers imagine themselves using the product and the value they derive from it when they see an advertisement. Therefore, this study conducted an RCT in an online survey environment targeting 1,225 car users aged 20-60 in Japan. The results showed that, in Japan, where right-hand drive cars are common, passengers significantly higher rated the product value in advertisements where the car was facing left. Conversely, although no statistically significant difference was detected, drivers tended to higher rate the product value in advertisements where the car was facing right. Therefore, if car manufacturers want to convey the appeal of their product to drivers, they should position their products facing right. On the other hand, if the goal is to appeal to passengers with the interior space, as in a minivan, it is preferable to use the opposite side, the left side.

title: When the Room Authenticates: Status, Context, and the Psychology of Conditional Authenticity

detail.title: When the Room Authenticates: Status, Context, and the Psychology of Conditional Authenticity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No specific funding was received for this working paper.

detail.abstract: This note examines a recent conversation in which a high-net-worth individual openly wore a high-quality replica luxury watch and explained that his established status rendered material authenticity largely irrelevant. Treated strictly as an illustration, the case is used to sharpen an existing insight in the psychology of status and consumption: the perceived authenticity of a status signal is not determined solely by the material properties of the object. It is co-produced by the social context in which the object appears. When an individual’s status is already high and legible, observers default to assuming authenticity. The social setting itself authenticates the signal. Drawing on costly signaling theory, countersignaling, research on class asymmetries in counterfeit perception, and work on social-adjustive motives, the note analyses how context modulates authenticity judgments while maintaining the analytical tension between signaling efficiency and the residual value of material authenticity.

title: AI-Empowered Customers and the Erosion of Brand Power
affiliations: Peking University and National University of Singapore

detail.title: AI-Empowered Customers and the Erosion of Brand Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: IRB protocol: #2026-11 (Peking University)
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the 2025 NSFC Pilot Program of Research Fund for Excellent International PhD Students (RFEIPS Project No. 8200909920)

detail.abstract: How does consumer access to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reshape brand-based competitive advantage? We argue that LLM-based assistants reduce consumers' productevaluation costs, enabling greater reliance on product attributes and less reliance on brand reputation. We test this argument in a randomized online experiment in which 350 participants made 1,750 incentivized choices across five product categories, with or without an embedded GenAI assistant. Participants with assistant access were significantly less likely to choose the more reputable brand when it was weaker on the prespecified attributes displayed in the comparison. They also reported lower mental effort, greater reliance on technical specifications, and less reliance on brand names. These findings identify reduced consumer informationprocessing costs as a demand-side mechanism through which GenAI may erode established brands' competitive advantage. Managerial Summary Generative AI assistants can change how customers compare products. In our experiment, customers who could use an AI assistant were less likely to choose a familiar brand when that option was weaker on the product attributes displayed in the comparison. They also found the task less mentally demanding and relied more on technical specifications. These findings suggest that established brands may receive less benefit from name recognition when AI makes detailed comparisons easier. Lesser-known firms can benefit by presenting clear, verifiable product information that AI tools can interpret. Managers should therefore treat the accessibility and structure of product information as an increasingly important part of competitive strategy.

title: Bridging Digital Marketing and Financial Inclusion: Leveraging Targeted Digital Strategies to Elevate Digital Financial Literacy Among Malaysian Gen Z B40 Households

detail.title: Bridging Digital Marketing and Financial Inclusion: Leveraging Targeted Digital Strategies to Elevate Digital Financial Literacy Among Malaysian Gen Z B40 Households
detail.abstract: Malaysia's rapid digital transformation has positioned digital marketing as a critical enabler of financial inclusion, particularly for Generation Z (Gen Z) within the Bottom 40% (B40) income group. Drawing on the original thesis focus on digital financial literacy (DFL) and its demonstrated links to household wealth among financially disadvantaged Malaysians, this article examines how carefully designed digital marketing strategies can systematically enhance DFL. The study is grounded in an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT/UTAUT2) framework, which is adapted to incorporate marketing stimuli as antecedents of technology acceptance. The paper synthesises recent empirical evidence from 2025-2026 on Gen Z payment behaviours, fintech adoption patterns, socialmedia-based financial education, and digital engagement among B40 households. Findings indicate that performance expectancy, hedonic motivation, social influence channelled through influencers and short-form video platforms, and facilitating conditions, when mediated by elevated levels of DFL, strongly shape actual usage of digital financial services. The analysis further reveals that while Gen Z B40 individuals exhibit high digital fluency, gaps in risk awareness, consumer rights knowledge, and long-term financial planning persist, creating both opportunities and vulnerabilities within the digital marketing ecosystem. Practical implications are offered for marketers, digital banks, policymakers, and educators seeking to close the literacy-usage gap and support sustainable wealth creation among underserved youth. The article contributes a marketing-centric conceptual model that positions DFL as both an intentional outcome of campaign design and a critical mediator between behavioural intention and effective digital financial service utilisation in the Malaysian context. By aligning commercial digital marketing practices with national financial literacy objectives under the National Strategy for Financial Literacy 2026-2030, the proposed framework advances a more inclusive and resilient digital economy.

title: Navigating the Algorithmic Paradox: Determinants of Consumer Trust and Distrust in AI-Powered Predictive Marketing Frameworks

detail.abstract: Today's Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the world of predictive marketing and is empowering companies to serve personalised products and customer experiences to consumers. This study looks at key criteria for influencing consumer trust and distrust of predictive marketing systems driven by AI tools such as algorithmic transparency or explainability, ethics of data-handling practices, and privacy concerns/surveillance. This research method is interpretivist, using an inductive approach, the philosophy applied, and a qualitative literature review method, with secondary data obtained from academic journals, books, and industry reports. The findings suggest that improvements in transparency, personalisation, and trust in ethical governance are positive correlates of trust, whereas privacy and ethical surveillance concerns are negative correlates of trust. The study reveals the conflict between personalisation and privacy, as well as the need to implement AI-marketing-oriented strategies that are transparent, consumer-centric, and ethically responsible to ensure consumer acceptance of the algorithms.

title: Using Large Language Models to Discover and Disentangle Mechanisms from Participant Explanations
affiliations: University of Southern California, Marshall School of Business

detail.title: Using Large Language Models to Discover and Disentangle Mechanisms from Participant Explanations
detail.abstract: Explaining why an effect occurs is a central goal of consumer research, and for decades its tool has been mediation analysis.  That design has a blind spot: it credits only measured constructs and picks the winner by significance, so it can miss a driver no one measured or credit a near-synonym scales cannot separate from the real cause.  We develop and validate a way to let participants’ own words nominate the mechanism.  A large language model (LLM) pipeline, blind to the hypothesis and the outcome, reads each open-ended explanation and scores every participant on competing constructs.  Treated as a measurement instrument, it passes a full reliability and validity battery, and rival mechanisms are compared by directly testing the difference between their indirect effects.  Across four preregistered studies ((three of them replications of published effects) it recovers a planted attribute where scales cannot, rediscovers a mediator established by prior work, separates constructs described with the same words, and surfaces drivers no questionnaire included.  We release it as a tool that runs on any experiment with an outcome, a condition, and an open-ended explanation.  Because explanations are read alongside the outcome, the method nominates mechanisms for confirmatory test rather than proving them.

title: Digital Procedural Engineering: A New Paradigm of Evidence in Bribery Investigations

detail.title: Digital Procedural Engineering: A New Paradigm of Evidence in Bribery Investigations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that this research was conducted in an academic capacity as part of post-graduate studies at Kazan Federal University, and there are no financial or personal conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved only anonymized judicial statistics and an anonymous survey of legal professionals for purely academic purposes. No confidential personal data or human patient trials were involved, and no ethics approval was required under institutional guidelines.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The rapid digitalization of economic and administrative relations has transformed bribery from traditional cash-for-favors transactions into sophisticated schemes involving cryptocurrencies, smart contracts, and algorithmic manipulation. Based on an empirical study of 450 criminal cases (2022-2025) and a survey of 13 legal practitioners, this article demonstrates that conventional reactive evidentiary models have become functionally obsolete. The author introduces the paradigm of "Digital Procedural Engineering"-a proactive and predictive approach that integrates data from disparate sources through a centralized Procedural Evidence Hub, applies graph theory for network analysis, and utilizes algorithmic expertise to uncover latent manipulations. The article proposes specific legislative amendments to the Russian Criminal Procedure Code, including the legal recognition of digital evidence, the introduction of algorithmic forensic examinations, and the mechanism of "procedural antifragility"-whereby attempts to obstruct investigation generate independent evidence of guilt. The findings suggest that the future of criminal procedure lies not in reacting to digital crime but in engineering evidentiary environments where corruption inevitably leaves a verifiable digital trace.

title: The Effect of Regularization Policies for Migrants on the Labor Market

detail.title: The Effect of Regularization Policies for Migrants on the Labor Market
detail.abstract: This study reviews the labor-market effects of policies aimed at regularizing irregular migrants, with particular emphasis on amnesty programs and access to legal employment. Drawing on the existing literature and country experiences, it examines the mechanisms through which regularization may affect migrants, local workers, employers, and the broader economy. The analysis highlights that the effects of regularization depend strongly on host-country characteristics, including the size of the informal economy, labor-market structure, welfare arrangements, inspection capacity, and geographical conditions, as well as on migrants’ demographic and skill profiles and their degree of substitutability or complementarity with the local workforce. The study also discusses the potential effects of regularization on wages, employment, productivity, tax revenues, occupational mobility, and migrants’ integration into the formal economy. Evidence from different country experiences suggests that regularization does not produce uniform outcomes and that granting legal status alone is insufficient to ensure successful labor-market integration. The paper concludes that regularization policies are more likely to generate positive outcomes when accompanied by effective labor-market enforcement, access to appropriate employment opportunities, and complementary integration policies tailored to the specific conditions of the host country and migrant population.

title: Generative Social Simulation Needs a Hybrid Validity Standard
affiliations: Queen's University Belfast

detail.title: Generative Social Simulation Needs a Hybrid Validity Standard
detail.abstract:
Current research on generative social simulations can be divided into two tendencies which largely do not engage with one another or consider each other’s strengths. One explicitly sticks with the traditional approach and assesses them against standards inherited from formal and mechanism-oriented Agent-Based Modelling, including explicit behavioural rules, inspectable parameters, and traceable micro-level assumptions—and finds generative simulations genuinely deficient. The other takes a pragmatic stance, emphasising what theoretically informed simulations can reveal or predict (“the proof of the pudding is in the eating” (1)). Additionally, the latter leans on empirical criteria—such as robustness checks and external validity—without integrating them into an explicit account of validity. How do the two accounts connect, and how should we approach the validity challenge?

Generative simulation, especially its confirmatory version—used to make or evaluate theoretically interpretable claims about human behaviour—should be evaluated as a scientific instrument whose credibility depends on an externally acquired data corpus and researcher-specified theory. It is a theory-driven empirical instrument that requires two distinct and complementary methodological components: substrate validity—whether the model’s learned behavioural representations derived from and shaped by data credibly encode the behavioural domain, and instrument validity—whether the architecture of instructions theoretically grounds the simulation. It is not just a formal requirement: recent experimental work suggests that theory-grounded simulations can generalise to novel settings more successfully than theoretically unstructured alternatives (2), which is an empirical, not a formal property. As a result, validation must be hybrid. While this opinion focuses on simulation, the same logic plausibly extends to many other forms of AI-generated research.

title:
Cross-domain Constraint in Physics and Mathematics 
Six Constraints, Four Kinds of Evidence, and the Mapping that has not been Written

detail.title:
Cross-domain Constraint in Physics and Mathematics 
Six Constraints, Four Kinds of Evidence, and the Mapping that has not been Written

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: A widely held intuition holds that constraint accumulates: each precise measurement narrows the space of possible fundamental theories, and enough measurements will narrow it decisively. Within a single domain the intuition is correct. This essay examines what happens across domains that share no parameter space. Six deliberately heterogeneous constraints — drawn from quark mixing, Higgs production, solar neutrinos, the cosmic microwave background, the reflexive polytopes, and a quantum error-correcting code — were each implemented under a stated validation contract, executed, and reported as a constraint record. A seven-level Convergence Ladder is proposed for stating how any two constraints relate. All fifteen pairs reach Level 3, constraint reducibility, and none higher: the lower levels are reachable by curation, the upper require a theoretical statement that no quantity of data supplies. Execution produced findings reasoning alone would not have: the CMS measurement is theory-dominated, and a retrieval error passed every internal consistency check available, failing only against a value published outside the calculation; an exact identity settled the semantics of a published field that its own documentation described incorrectly; and one well-defined, correctly computed statistic was deleted because its value inverted with the mode in which its source file was read. The essay concludes that a discipline for the secondary use of published results must require external anchoring as a condition of reporting, and states one.

title: Ethical Interface Design: A Theory and Framework for Navigating Ethical Tensions in Interface Behavior

detail.title: Ethical Interface Design: A Theory and Framework for Navigating Ethical Tensions in Interface Behavior
detail.abstract: Digital interfaces have become infrastructural technologies that shape cognition, behavior, and everyday life, while ethical responsibility has become increasingly diffuse across teams, tools, and automated processes. Yet guidance for ethical interface design remains fragmented, normatively contested, and difficult to apply when designers face concrete value tradeoffs. This paper introduces Ethical Interface Design (EID), a theory of interface ethics that explains how moral commitments become operationalized through interface design. Grounded in moral and political philosophy, EID organizes recurring ethical conflicts around two foundational dimensions: Protection-Autonomy and Equality-Utility. Rather than defining ethical design by the presence of predetermined features or universal rules, EID examines how interface decisions prioritize some commitments while constraining others. Building on this theoretical foundation, the paper presents the EID Analysis Framework, a structured method for identifying ethical tensions, tracing how competing commitments are expressed through interface mechanisms, evaluating their consequences, and requiring explicit justification for design priorities. Rather than prescribing a single correct outcome, the framework makes ethical reasoning more transparent, comparable, and defensible, providing designers with a repeatable approach for analyzing interface decisions across diverse technologies, contexts, and moral perspectives.

title: Speed, Fraud, and Bank Liquidity: The Operational Architecture of Real-Time Payment Systems

detail.title: Speed, Fraud, and Bank Liquidity: The Operational Architecture of Real-Time Payment Systems
detail.abstract: A real-time payment system settles each payment within seconds, around the clock, with finality. The defining design choice is to drive the settlement window to zero. This paper shows that the zero window shuts off two stabilizers at once. A universal settlement delay buys time to screen fraud before settlement, and it restores the netting that real-time settlement takes away from banks, so one design primitive acts on a fraud channel and a bank-liquidity channel together and the welfare-optimal architecture must weigh it against both. The fraud side adds two suspension tools, targeted and system-wide, by analogy to speed bumps and circuit breakers in equity markets; the liquidity side adds the precautionary-buffer and risk-taking channel documented for Brazil's Pix. The optimal delay is strictly positive and strictly larger than fraud alone would justify, it rises with deposit runnability, the two suspension tools partition rather than reinforce, the system-wide threshold loosens with concentration, and the pure realtime corner is dominated through two independent channels at once. A calibration disciplined by the instant-payments literature shows the optimal delay is measured in seconds and is roughly twice what fraud alone would justify, and the result is an instance of stability-induced fragility.

detail.abstract: Identity Constructed Communication Architecture (ICCA) is a general trust architecture designed to remove customer identity from interactions while preserving accountability, compliance and operational integrity. eCommerce is a native operational domain within ICCA. This paper provides a sector specific explanation of how ICCA enables anonymous commercial transactions, item bound accountability and blind physical delivery without modifying the underlying architecture. ICCA replaces identity centric commerce with item centric accountability. Buyers approve payments through bank verified peer to peer mechanisms, ensuring regulatory compliance while preventing identity leakage into the commerce system. Sellers receive settlement and a non correlatable payment token, enabling provider blind operation. Each purchased item is represented by an autonomous identity container that carries warranty rights, subscription contracts, lifecycle rules and dissolvable accountability. No customer accounts, profiles, or purchase histories are created. Physical delivery is achieved through blind delivery endpoints treated as logistical coordinates rather than identity attributes. Delivery is externalised from seller back-office systems and executed by blind delivery subsystems such as third-party agents or locker networks. Delivery confirmation activates the identity container, ensuring accountability begins only when the item is in the buyer’s possession. ICCA provides structural benefits across the commerce chain: sellers eliminate identity liability and card network fees; delivery services operate without identity exposure; buyers gain anonymity, full post purchase rights and complete control over lifecycle and dissolution. This paper describes how eCommerce companies can operate within ICCA’s trustless, provider blind model using mechanisms already present in the architecture.

title:
Delegated Authority Without Accountability:
The Governance Discontinuity Created by Agentic AI

detail.title:
Delegated Authority Without Accountability:
The Governance Discontinuity Created by Agentic AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial, commercial, institutional, or personal conflicts of interest that influenced the design, analysis, interpretation, or preparation of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required. This work is a conceptual and governance research paper and did not involve human participants, human data, animal subjects, or experimental interventions requiring institutional ethics review.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was independently conceived, developed, and prepared by the author.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly moving beyond prediction, recommendation, and content generation into the initiation and execution of consequential action. Systems capable of selecting tasks, sequencing workflows, using external tools, adapting to changing conditions, and acting without continuous human direction occupy a different functional position from conventional software tools. This paper argues that such systems should be treated as non-human operational actors for governance purposes, without implying consciousness, legal personhood, moral agency, or independent authority. The paper distinguishes technical capability, system permission, and institutional authority, showing how capability combined with access can produce effective operational power without an equivalent act of legitimate delegation. It defines the resulting governance discontinuity as the structural gap between autonomous operational capability and the authority, constraint, interruption, provenance, and accountability arrangements required to govern its exercise. From this discontinuity arise recurring structural failure modes, including authority drift, silent execution, escalation failure, responsibility diffusion, contextual misalignment, compositional overreach, cumulative drift, coordination failure, provenance collapse, and decay of meaningful human oversight. The paper argues that incremental additions to model governance, access control, monitoring, policy, lifecycle assurance, and human-in-the-loop review remain necessary but may be insufficient because they preserve governance assumptions centred on tools and human-initiated action. It identifies minimum requirements for governable agency: declared purpose, explicit delegation, bounded and context-sensitive autonomy, risk-sensitive operation, mandatory interruption and escalation, governance provenance, cumulative and compositional awareness, governance across coordination pathways, institutional control of governance constraints, and accountable human anchoring. The paper concludes that as consequential action becomes increasingly executed by non-human operational actors, governance must remain continuously coupled to both the delegation of authority and the execution of action.

title: Beyond HITL: Continuation Readiness as a Governance Requirement for Enterprise AI Workflows A Role State
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Beyond HITL: Continuation Readiness as a Governance Requirement for Enterprise AI Workflows A Role State

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it is a conceptual and structural research paper and does not involve human participants, patients, personal data collection, experiments, surveys, interviews, or case-study subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) is widely treated as the default mechanism for satisfying AI governance
requirements: when an AI system reaches a checkpoint it cannot resolve, a human is asked to
intervene. This paper argues that intervention is not sufficient. Enterprise AI governance requires
continuability — the ability of a receiving human or machine actor to act on transferred work without
reconstructing it — and continuability is a property of the relationship between what is transferred and
who receives it, not a property of the transferred content alone. We show that checkpoint-scoped
HITL, by construction, cannot observe this relational property: it evaluates only whether AI output is
evidentially complete and whether authority is clearly bounded, both of which are visible from the
delivering side. A third, independent condition — Receiving Capacity — determines whether the
receiving actor can actually act on the work, and this condition is invisible to any evaluation surface
that inspects only the delivered content. We formalize Enterprise AI Workflow as the unit of
governance analysis (rather than the individual AI system or the individual agentic pipeline), and
introduce three model objects — Role State, Work Junction, and Continuation Package — together
with a Role Requirement Feedback Loop that operationalizes the co-design of human roles and AI
delivery formats. We identify six classes of governance failure that checkpoint-scoped HITL cannot
detect — including one on the delegation (H2A) side, where an underspecified transfer causes the
receiving AI to silently infer scope it was never given — the most consequential of which — Capacity-
blind transfer — occurs when every indicator visible to the delivering side is satisfied while the
receiving side is structurally unable to continue the work: a governance failure disguised as a
completed junction closure. We situate this model against Joint Cognitive Systems theory, recent
formal HITL governance frameworks (HAIG; Chiodo et al.), AI-in-the-Loop scholarship, process-
notation extensions (BPMN, Agentic BPMS), and human-robot handover research, and argue that the
reviewed work does not treat continuation as a jointly determined, receiving-side-verified condition of
enterprise work transfer.

title:
The Control-Latency Ratio 
A Measurement Instrument for the Temporal Feasibility of Human Oversight in Automated Decision Systems

detail.title:
The Control-Latency Ratio 
A Measurement Instrument for the Temporal Feasibility of Human Oversight in Automated Decision Systems

detail.abstract:
This paper defines and operationalizes a single measurable quantity for the oversight of autonomous and semi-autonomous systems: the Control-Latency Ratio, S = H / T_c, the ratio of a decision class's reversibility horizon H to the wall-clock time T_c required for a human-governed correction to take effect. The paper makes no predictive or existential claim. Its purpose is narrow and practical: to give operators, risk officers, and auditors a precise, computable indicator of whether meaningful human intervention in a given automated decision is temporally possible, and to specify exactly how each term is measured, what the ratio does and does not establish, and how it should be interpreted.
We define the control-loop time T_c as a sum of independently measurable latencies (detection, judgment, actuation, and signal propagation), define the reversibility horizon H as the time at which the cost of reversing an errant action exceeds the value recoverable by reversing it, and define S as their ratio. We state the operational meaning of S > 1, S ≈ 1, and S < 1; specify measurement procedures and data requirements for each term; give worked measurement examples across several operational domains; and state precisely the boundary of what the metric certifies — namely, that a positive ratio establishes the temporal possibility of human correction, not its sufficiency or correctness. The contribution is a measurement instrument and an interpretation discipline, not a theorem and not a forecast. It is intended to be adoptable by a risk function without specialized training and auditable by a third party.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionized competitive forces in various industries by enabling organizations to achieve differentiation, cost leadership, and improved decision-making. The present study conducts a strategic appraisal of AI implementation, analyzing its contribution to competitive advantage in manufacturing, healthcare, retail, and financial sectors. With automation, predictive information, and personalized customer experiences, AI fuels operational efficiency and innovation. Nonetheless, high cost of implementation, ethical issues, and gaps in skills are some of the barriers to adoption. The research utilizes case studies, facts, and strategic tools to identify the transformational ability of AI. Results indicate that companies using AI strategically are able to maintain long-term competitive advantages, as long as they address adoption challenges successfully.

title: Empowering B40 Generation Z Through Digital Financial Literacy: Catalyzing Inclusive E-Commerce Participation and Household Wealth Accumulation in Malaysia

detail.title: Empowering B40 Generation Z Through Digital Financial Literacy: Catalyzing Inclusive E-Commerce Participation and Household Wealth Accumulation in Malaysia
detail.abstract: Malaysia’s e-commerce sector has expanded rapidly in recent years, generating substantial revenue and embedding digital payments, buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) schemes, and social commerce into everyday consumption patterns (Department of Statistics Malaysia, 2025; Asian Banking & Finance, 2026). Digital wallets now account for a leading share of online transaction value, while BNPL transaction volumes and active accounts have surged, particularly among younger users (I3investor, 2026; Fintech News Malaysia, 2025). Yet financially disadvantaged households, particularly those in the Bottom 40% (B40) income group and Generation Z, remain vulnerable to impulsive spending, online scams, and suboptimal wealth outcomes despite near-universal digital access and high smartphone penetration (Bank Negara Malaysia, 2025; Monash University Malaysia, Versa & AHAM Asset Management, 2026). Drawing on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT/UTAUT2) and accumulating evidence from digital financial literacy (DFL) research, this conceptual article synthesises how DFL, encompassing knowledge of digital products and services, awareness of digital financial risks, risk-control competencies, and understanding of consumer rights and redress procedures, shapes behavioural intention and actual engagement with ecommerce platforms (Sabri et al., 2026; Jahanzeb, Xin & Ali, 2026). It argues that elevated DFL among B40 Gen Z enhances performance expectancy and facilitating conditions while mitigating perceived risks, thereby supporting more responsible platform use, safer credit decisions, and progressive household wealth accumulation (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 2026; Ananta & Juita, 2026). The paper integrates recent empirical findings from Malaysia and comparable emerging economies, proposes an extended conceptual model that positions DFL as both a direct antecedent and a moderator linking UTAUT constructs to e-commerce adoption and wealth outcomes, and outlines policy and platform-level interventions aligned with Malaysia’s National Strategy for Financial Literacy 2026–2030 (NS2.0) (Securities Commission Malaysia, 2025; OECD, 2026). Implications for inclusive growth, strengthened consumer protection, and future empirical testing of the proposed pathways are discussed.

title: When Does Enterprise AI Pay? Threshold Conditions and Qualitative Regimes in a Deterministic Firm-Level Scenario Model

detail.title: When Does Enterprise AI Pay? Threshold Conditions and Qualitative Regimes in a Deterministic Firm-Level Scenario Model

detail.abstract: Enterprise adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is widespread, yet most firms report no measurable profit-and-loss (P&L) impact, and large laboratory productivity gains attenuate to near-zero field effects. We analyze the calculation engine of a deterministic, opensource firm-level scenario calculator of the author's own design, which nets a one-sided quality discount and review, rework, and AI-operations overheads from task-level speed gains, caps monetization at validated demand, and adds cash timing and a workforce-attribution solver. All capability inputs act through one sufficient statistic, the time-release rate τ = xa(γ-H), partitioning the uplift-overhead plane into regimes bounded by vertical translates of a saturating Amdahl-type hyperbola: a viability threshold s * = H/(1-H), an economic break-even s * * , a demand-cap kink τ * with exactly zero marginal return to capability above it, and a capability ceiling τ max that model upgrades alone cannot move. Closed forms extend to the first-year cash shortfall-unrealized first-year value plus unamortized transformation cost-with its three-regime J-curve classification, a minimum efficient scale, and the workforce solver's exact affine geometry, in which AI relieves target-margin pressure only if its profit delta exceeds the target margin levied on its own revenue: a strictly stronger requirement than profitability, so profitable but margin-dilutive AI rationally increases required cuts. All twelve results (one lemma and eleven propositions) are machine-verified at machine precision against the MIT-licensed implementation, and calibration exercises show the identity can inhabit the lab-to-field attenuation range and-under a documented two-component demand-evidence mixture with unimodal capability inputs-the skewed practitioner outcome split. The framework is normative-diagnostic rather than causal: it orders managerial levers-demand evidence before capability spending, overhead reduction over model upgrades at rate (1 + s) 2-and separates AI-justified from margin-driven restructuring.

title: From Forensics to Ecosystems: Rethinking Watermarks for Generative AI Oversight
affiliations: Cornell University, Cornell University and Harvard University - Department of the History of Science

detail.title: From Forensics to Ecosystems: Rethinking Watermarks for Generative AI Oversight

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in the Proceedings of the 2026 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Soceity (AIES)

detail.abstract: The arrival of generative AI as a cheap, widely accessible commercial service, and the tidal wave of AI-generated synthetic content it has unleashed, have provoked deep epistemic and social anxieties and raised difficult governance questions that policymakers are struggling to address. One approach that has attracted both enthusiasm from regulators and skepticism from researchers is digital watermarking. Signals embedded in a synthetically-generated piece of content indicating that it was AI-generated-possibly even identifying the specific systems that generated it-appear to offer a path toward mitigating risks of genAI that avoids the downsides of more interventionist strategies. But critics warn that watermarks may prove technically brittle, epistemically ambiguous, and politically ineffectual tools. In this paper, we explore the challenges and opportunities of using digital watermarking for AI governance, paying special attention to the specific problem of watermarking AI-generated text. We argue that such critiques often treat the problem of identifying synthetic content as an isolated forensic question. Instead, we propose reconceptualizing digital watermarks as tools for understanding the impacts of synthetic content on media ecosystems, rather than reliably identifying individual pieces of synthetic content. Such an "ecosystems approach" more effectively utilizes the features of watermarks. And while this approach raises its own governance challenges, we argue that they are more tractable than the challenges of using watermarks for digital forensics.

title:
Why can Sameness become Difference? 
Branching, Differentiation, and the Problem of a Differentiation-permitting Universe

detail.title:
Why can Sameness become Difference? 
Branching, Differentiation, and the Problem of a Differentiation-permitting Universe

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This essay argues that modern science explains many ways in which differences grow, organize, and sometimes branch, but does not explain why reality is capable of becoming different at all. A universe can be conceived that changes uniformly through time while remaining identical from place to place; ours is not such a world. The essay begins with branching, which makes differentiation visible, then moves beneath it to difference itself. Its thesis is that instability, symmetry breaking, quantum fluctuation, natural selection, and cosmological perturbation explain what happens once a differentiation-permitting framework is in place, and therefore leave unanswered the prior question of why reality has laws, states, and boundary conditions under which sameness can become difference. Two objections are met directly: that the question is one more instance of why the laws are as they are, and that the homogeneous-universe counterfactual is incoherent. If the question is ever resolved, the resolution most likely lies in the direction of necessity. The essay claims no new physical law and no demonstrated cosmic purpose. Its contribution is a bounded reframing that separates mechanisms of differentiation from the condition that differentiation be possible, and asks where competing explanations terminate.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a formal systems science framework, Holographic Anti-Entropy Theory (HAET), that bridges the gap between systems physics (Prigogine's dissipative structures, Friston's variational free energy principle) and digital value chain management. We outline the eight fundamental laws of systems engineering, formalize the prior boundary projection operator and second-order metacognitive operator , and demonstrate how distributed systems collapse factorial complexity into computable, low-entropy steady states. We highlight the empirical validation in Lenovo's proprietary manufacturing networks, achieving automated decision-making.

detail.title: Perception of Lecturers on the Core Curriculum Minimum Academic Standard (CCMAS) at Tai Solarin Federal University of Education

publicationDetails.detailsText: Osiyemi, E. S., Imoh, S. I., Olusanya, K. J., Adebayo, O. R., & Agbajeola, R. O. (2026). Lecturers’ perception on the core curriculum minimum academic standard (CCMAS) at Tai Solarin Federal University of Education. International Journal on Education Insight, 7(2), 189-198.

detail.abstract: The Core Curriculum Minimum Academic Standard (CCMAS) is a framework introduced by the Nigerian National Universities Commision in which 30% of the curriculum content can be defined by universities. The framework has attracted the attention of lecturers on whether a 30% flexibility can be really practicable within universities. This study examined the perception of lecturers on the CCMAS at Tai Solarin Federal University of Education using a descriptive survey research design. The study population comprised all lecturers at Tai Solarin Federal University of Education (NUC) with a sample of 61 lecturers. The data were collected using Lecturers’ Perception of CCMAS Questionnaire (LP-CQ) with a reliability coefficient of 0.75. The results indicated that the level of lecturers’ awareness and understanding was high (mean = 3.12), perceptions of academic autonomy and curriculum flexibility was moderate (mean = 2.78), perceived benefits of implementing CCMAS was moderate (mean = 2.80), and perceived challenges of implementing CCMAS was moderate (mean = 2.89). The study concluded that the effective implementation of CCMAS is not the sole issue related to the policy design, but also to sustain professional growth, sufficient institutional commitment, and real flexibility of the curriculum that enables the universities to innovate within their unique environments. It was recommended, among others, that NUC should increase institutional contribution beyond 30 percent whereas universities must make use of its contribution to the maximum to demonstrate local realities, industry demands and new global tendencies.

detail.abstract: Working paper-SCREEN-01, version 1.5 • August 8, 2026 Preliminary draft; comments welcome. This version supersedes internal drafts 1.0-1.4. License: CC BY 4.0 Abstract. Counterparty screening programs in export control, sanctions, and defense supply-chain compliance are validated almost exclusively by process metrics-alert volume, clearance rate, list-coverage currency, screening latency. None of these measure whether the program detects the conduct it exists to detect. This paper identifies three structural defects common to these programs and specifies a validation framework that corrects them. The defects are: (1) endogenous label generation, in which outcome data is observable only for counterparties the program already flagged, making measured performance a function of the screening policy rather than of the threat; (2) entity resolution as the unmeasured binding constraint, in which screening accuracy is capped by the ability to recognize that nominally distinct counterparties are one operation, a capability no program reports on; and (3) adversary-controlled attribute dependence, in which screening weight concentrates on attributes the screened party can change at negligible cost while structurally costly attributes go unused. The framework specifies an exogenous sampling requirement, an entity-resolution maturity measure, an attribute-cost tiering scheme, and an evaluation battery that produces defensible estimates of screening effectiveness. It applies the result to reasonable-care determinations under EAR §732, to sanctions-compliance testing under OFAC's Framework, and to scienter and materiality analysis under the False Claims Act, including cybersecurity certification under the Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative, where recent settlements supply worked illustrations of each failure mode.

title: Determinants of Mobile Travel Application Adoption - A Causal Examination of Technology Acceptance Factors Among Diverse Consumer Segments

detail.title: Determinants of Mobile Travel Application Adoption - A Causal Examination of Technology Acceptance Factors Among Diverse Consumer Segments
detail.abstract: Aim : This research aims to identify, examine, and establish causal relationships between various technology acceptance factors and the adoption of mobile travel applications across different consumer segments. The study seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of how perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, trust, perceived risk, social influence, and other relevant factors differentially impact adoption decisions among diverse user groups. Methodology : This study employed a quantitative research design using primary data collected through pre-structured questionnaires from 209 multi-occupational participants via random sampling. The research instrument utilized multiple scale types including dichotomous questions, frequency-based and behavior-based Likert scales, ordinal scales, and rank-order questions covering four critical domains: factors influencing adoption decisions, features encouraging use, trust-related factors, and technology-related factors affecting continued usage. Demographic data including age, gender, and profession enabled segmentation analysis. Data analysis techniques combined descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, variance) and single-factor ANOVA to examine relationships between variables and identify patterns across segments. Key Findings : Results revealed that the sample was gender-balanced (50.2% female) with majority (50.2%) aged 18-24, predominantly students (56.9%). Near-universal internet access (100%) and mobile app awareness (97.6%) were observed, with 85.6% preferring mobile travel apps over traditional agents. Perceived ease of use received highest positive response (122 "Always"), while trust showed more conservative patterns (103 "Always"). Ease of use garnered most first-rank selections (92), followed by accuracy of travel information (67). Online booking convenience overwhelmingly dominated feature preferences (100 first ranks), while secure payment gateway led trust factors (85 first ranks). App reliability emerged as critical for continued usage (87 first ranks). High within-group variance (4,972-7,582) indicated diverse opinions even within segments. Younger users prioritized social influence and perceived usefulness, while trust and security showed increasing importance with age. Implications : The research establishes that no single determinant universally drives adoption; different factor combinations create sufficient conditions within specific segments. For developers, findings indicate core functionality priorities (booking convenience, app reliability) while revealing segment-specific opportunities: social features for younger users, simplified interfaces for less tech-savvy segments. Trust-building requires comprehensive approaches addressing payment security, pricing transparency, data privacy, and support availability. Marketers should leverage social influence through reviews and user-generated content, while employing segment-tailored messaging. The 14.4% preferring traditional agents represent an addressable segment requiring hybrid models and educational interventions. These insights enable practitioners to develop targeted strategies addressing segment-specific barriers and motivators, while advancing theoretical understanding of technology acceptance in high-involvement mobile commerce contexts.

title: Research State: A Candidate Semantic Abstraction for Knowledge Continuity in AI-Native Research Operating Systems
affiliations: and

detail.title: Research State: A Candidate Semantic Abstraction for Knowledge Continuity in AI-Native Research Operating Systems
detail.abstract:
The increasing use of large language models, research agents, scientific knowledge graphs, and workflow automation is transforming how scientific investigations are conducted. These technologies provide capable mechanisms for memory, provenance, knowledge representation, workflow execution, and agent interaction. Yet these mechanisms remain distributed across different system abstractions. Persistent agent-state research addresses durable operational state and governance (Ding et al., 2026); workflow-provenance systems represent execution and data lineage (Souza et al., 2025); scientific knowledge-orchestration systems represent entities, claims, evidence, methodological relations, and increasingly, research-agent workflows and executable tool interfaces (Cao et al., 2026); and knowledge-continuity frameworks address the preservation of actionable knowledge across organizational transitions (Türüc, 2026). What remains insufficiently specified is a common abstraction for the evolving semantic condition of a scientific investigation itself-an abstraction that explicitly integrates the multiple dimensions of research continuity within a single, model-agnostic construct.
This paper proposes Research State as a candidate semantic abstraction for AI-native Research Operating Systems. Drawing on design theory (Gregor & Jones, 2007; Walls et al., 1992), Research State is defined as a persistent, research-semantic, and model-agnostic representation of the evolving condition of a scientific investigation. The construct explicitly integrates eight dimensions—identity, knowledge, evidence, governance, workflow, execution, interaction, and recovery—within a single abstraction designed to preserve coherence across the entire research lifecycle. Following the principle of separation of concerns (Dijkstra, 1982) and the tradition of abstract data types (Liskov & Zilles, 1974), we distinguish Research State as a conceptual construct from Research State Object (RSO) as one possible concrete representation.
The construct is developed through a targeted construct-boundary mapping across four adjacent domains. The resulting analysis identifies integration, purpose, semantic, explicitness, and independence gaps within the reviewed corpus. We formulate three candidate system-level properties—cross-dimensional consistency, model-agnostic resumability, and research-lifecycle coherence—as testable design propositions rather than empirical findings. Two analytical walkthroughs, following the analytical evaluation tradition in design science (Hevner et al., 2004), illustrate how these propositions can be evaluated after implementation. 
 The contribution of this paper is a design-theoretical proposal. Within the reviewed corpus, we did not identify a construct that explicitly defines all eight dimensions as an integrated, research-semantic state abstraction whose persistent unit is the scientific investigation and whose semantic interpretation is intended to remain independent of a particular reasoning model. This work builds on two prior contributions: KAMDOL Academic OS (Sutrisno & Lastriyanto, 2026a), which validated a research risk intelligence capability, and KamiOS (Sutrisno & Lastriyanto, 2026b), which proposed the Research Operating System architecture. The present paper formalizes the candidate semantic state abstraction that such a Research Operating System manages—a contribution that is conceptual and definitional rather than architectural or capability-specific.

title: PALISADE: A Passive-Acoustic Silent Wall for Low-Cost, Rapidly-Fieldable Counter-UAS Defence of Critical Infrastructure on NATO's Eastern Flank

detail.abstract: Small, low-flying, low-observable uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) are penetrating the airspace of NATO's eastern flank and reaching critical energy and transport infrastructure while remaining undetected by conventional, radar-centric integrated air and missile defence (IAMD). The economics compound the problem: intercepting a drone that costs hundreds to tens of thousands of euros with a surface-to-air missile that costs a seven-figure sum is not sustainable at scale, and adversaries exploit precisely this cost asymmetry. This study proposes PALISADE, a passive-acoustic-led, multi-sensor, layered and highly automated counter-UAS (C-UAS) architecture designed for the affordable, rapid protection of fixed critical infrastructure and border sectors. The core detection layer is passive: distributed acoustic sensor arrays perform wide-area cueing without emitting, making them resilient to electronic warfare and to anti-radiation targeting; acoustic cues are fused with radio-frequency, passive-radar and electro-optical/infrared sensing and classified by an on-edge and central artificial-intelligence layer. Engagement is human-on-the-loop and doctrinally confined to pre-designated neutralisation zones to eliminate risk to population and infrastructure. The paper argues that such a system is deployable within approximately twenty-four months at a small fraction of the capital cost of missile-based coverage, and positions PALISADE not as a substitute for the EU's Readiness 2030 / SAFE and European Drone Defence Initiative trajectory or NATO IAMD, but as a fast, low-cost national accelerator that de-risks and complements them. Selected technical specifications are restricted and available to vetted partners on request.

title: Blockchain-Enabled Audit Infrastructure and the Feasibility of Restaurant-Level Public Listing: A Conceptual Framework and Research Agenda
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Blockchain-Enabled Audit Infrastructure and the Feasibility of Restaurant-Level Public Listing: A Conceptual Framework and Research Agenda
detail.abstract: Single-unit restaurants are among the most operationally tight retail supply chains in the economy, yet they almost never reach public-market scale as standalone entities. The conventional explanation is cost: the fixed costs of going public are high, and restaurants' historical reliance on cash and paper-based settlement makes financial-statement audit disproportionately expensive relative to firm size. Two developments motivate a reconsideration of this constraint: the near-complete digitization of restaurant point-of-sale payments, and the emergence of blockchain-based distributed ledgers, which proponents argue can lower the marginal cost of audit verification by design. This paper synthesizes three literatures that bear on this question but have not previously been connectedblockchain/triple-entry accounting research, the economics of going public, and behavioral finance research on local investor bias and dynamic market formation-and evaluates them specifically against the operational and financial characteristics of the restaurant industry. It proposes a five-layer reference architecture for restaurant-scale ledger infrastructure, derives four testable propositions, and positions the argument relative to adjacent 2025-2026 developments in SME asset tokenization and institutional tokenized-IPO infrastructure. The paper's central claim is that a purely static cost-benefit framing-the dominant mode in both the accounting and corporate-finance literatures-is insufficient to evaluate this question, because investor demand for restaurant equity is plausibly governed by dynamic, expectation-driven, and locally-biased behavior that a fixed-parameter cost model cannot capture.
