title: Viksit Bharat 2047: Why Investment, Not Ambition, Is the Binding Constraint
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Viksit Bharat 2047: Why Investment, Not Ambition, Is the Binding Constraint

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: No one

detail.abstract: India's Viksit Bharat 2047 ambition is to reach high-income status by its centenary of independence. This paper asks whether, and when, that is achievable, benchmarking India against the historical experience of every economy that has made the climb since 1950. Using the World Bank's Atlas-GNI income classification, it triangulates across several methods: a persistence-adjusted classification of transitions, censoring-corrected survival analysis, a discrete-time hazard model with investment and labor force participation as time-varying covariates, a gap-to-threshold growth calculation, and a recent-decade baserate comparison. The methods converge. Reaching high income by 2047 requires dollar GNI-per-capita growth of about 9.84 percent a year for two decades—roughly double India's 5 percent pace over 2012–2025. No economy above three million population sustained that pace over the post-crisis decade; over any 22-year window since 1990, only China and Vietnam did so through organic, non-transition growth. The hazard model places India's probability of success at about 5 percent. The implied required investment share, about 57 percent of GDP against an actual 30, exceeds any sustained historical precedent—but this is the price of the 2047 date specifically: under a realistic convergence path, India reaches high income around 2067 with an ordinary rise in investment to about 33 percent. Labor force participation, including female participation, is found to be a consequence of growth, not an independent cause, and so is not the missing lever. The binding constraint is investment and the investment climate: a decade-long collapse in foreign direct investment, and the absence of a comprehensive trade agreement with the United States. India would do better to talk less about the 2047 slogan and more about the concrete reforms that raise the trend path of growth.

title: Mountain Agro-Pomological Parks: A Conceptual Framework
affiliations: and CBM International University

detail.title: Mountain Agro-Pomological Parks: A Conceptual Framework
detail.abstract: This study focuses on developing a conceptual framework for establishing mountain public agro-pomological parks (public orchards) through planting or replanting, as an alternative to afforestation or reforestation, with the aim of utilizing degraded lands-particularly abandoned pastures and hayfields. These public orchards should consist of fruit trees and shrubs that require minimal maintenance, considering the limited availability of personnel in Romania for such activities. Harvesting can involve public participation, transforming the orchards into a form of agrotourism, with the possibility of charging a minimal entrance fee. The research is grounded in several key aspects specific to contemporary mountain areas, forming the foundation of the conceptual framework proposed. These include a significant reduction in cattle and sheep populations, a decline in transhumance practices, and a decrease in organic natural fertilizers derived from animal resources, all of which contribute to the degradation of natural vegetation on pastures and hayfields. In this context, soil impoverishment and degradation occur, marked by a decline in organic matter content, reduced microbial biodiversity, and lower soil fertility. The depopulation of mountain areas leads to the neglect of lands-both publicly and privately owned-especially pastures and hayfields, exacerbating existing ecological and economic problems. Within this context, the study proposes a paradigm shift from traditional afforestation/reforestation practices to the planting or replanting of fruit trees and shrubs as a sustainable solution for mountain areas affected by the abandonment of these landscapes. The study also examines the bio-ecological benefits of replanting, including carbon capture and biodiversity restoration, along with agro-economic advantages such as the creation clustering models based on shared characteristics or added-value chains. The article presents research from various regions around the world, demonstrating the positive impact of reforestation and replanting in terms of carbon storage, food security enhancement, and the reshaping of the rural mountain landscape. In terms of practical implementation, the study proposes an agro-economic model for the value chain associated with planting/replanting, including financial/material flows, strategic and operational planning, and the management of the production and distribution of saplings, seeds, and fruits. Furthermore, the research presents specific planting/replanting solutions for fruit trees and shrubs, including species such as berries and medicinal herbs, which can be cultivated at high altitudes-thus contributing to the sustainable development and utilization of high mountain regions.

title: Moat Architecture: The Structural Determinants of Competitive-Advantage Durability

detail.title: Moat Architecture: The Structural Determinants of Competitive-Advantage Durability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Competitive-advantage analysis scores defensibility by counting a firm's moats and rating their strength. This paper introduces moat architecture-the structural arrangement of a firm's competitive advantages-and argues that arrangement, not count, governs how erosion travels: whether a failure stays contained and how many independent engines survive-which, with the durability of the individual moats, determines how long the defense holds. The framework classifies a firm's moat structure into one of five architecture types, each carrying a hypothesized cascade rule for how erosion in one moat transmits to the rest, and extends the reading across firms through signed dependency arrows: directional relationships in which one competitive event strengthens one firm's moats while weakening another's. The method is applied in full to one anchor firm in the artificial intelligence infrastructure stack, whose vertically integrated moat stack-the deepest examined-reads as the least contained architecture, the most exposed if its foundational layer erodes, because vertical reinforcement transmits shocks that lateral and cross-domain arrangements absorb. One realized event, scored retrospectively under a stated rule, matched the mapped arrows in sign: structurally opposed firms moved against each other even as sector-wide correlation dominated daily co-movement. The framework is an analytical lens for competitive assessment and for correlated structural risk in portfolios diversified by firm but not by structure. It is qualitative by design, characterizing architectures by containment and redundancy and leaving calibrated magnitudes to future work. It is not a valuation model, a forecast, or an investment recommendation.

title: Do Female Directors Face Larger Career Consequences After Financial Distress?
affiliations: Oklahoma State University - Stillwater - Department of Finance, Miami University and State University of New York, SUNY at Stony Brook University, College of Business

detail.title: Do Female Directors Face Larger Career Consequences After Financial Distress?
detail.abstract: High-visibility labor markets predict larger career penalties for women after negative performance shocks. We test this among bank directors using the 2007-2009 financial crisis and post-crisis failures from 2012-2019, comparing female and male co-directors of the same distressed bank. Difference-indifferences and triple-difference estimates find no gender-asymmetric decline in appointments, appointment quality, committee assignments, or exits; Bayes factors and equivalence tests confirm the null. Failed banks recruit their first female director 1.5 years faster than non-failed peers. One exception is that female directors from poorly performing banks are less likely to gain seats on boards with multiple incumbent women.

title: Who Gains from Regional Integration? Digital Growth, Spatial Convergence, and Spillovers from the Yangtze River Delta Enlargement
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Who Gains from Regional Integration? Digital Growth, Spatial Convergence, and Spillovers from the Yangtze River Delta Enlargement
detail.abstract: A critical question in evaluating urban agglomeration policies is whether regional integration translates core-city digital dominance into broad-based growth and regional convergence. Using the successive enlargement s of the Yangtze River Delta (YRD) as a quasi-natural experiment, this paper employs a balanced panel of 284 Chinese cities (2003-2022) to estimate these effects. Through comprehensive difference-indifferences , event study, mechanism analysis, and spatial models, we demonstrate that YRD enlargement significantly elevates the urban digital-economy index (UDEI) and reduces the relative digital-economy gap (UDEG), a conclusion supported by extensive robustness checks. The dividends of enlargement are particularly salient in cities characterized by stronger entrepreneurial vitality, more polycentric structures, higher digital-economy attention, and earlier accession cohorts. Furthermore, causal mediation analysis reveals that the of knowledge breadth reorganization and new-technology space reorganization drives this digital catch-up. Moderation analyses reveal that local absorptive capacity-specifically, superior talent-capital matching and technological proximity-amplifies the digital dividends of YRD enlargement. Spatial analysis reveals that YRD enlargement generates a short-range local-shadow effect on UDEI, whereas its effect on neighboring UDEG is only directional. By contrast, digital institutional proximity produces significant convergence-oriented spillovers in UDEG. Ultimately, this study advances the literature by shifting the focus from average growth outcomes to the nuanced distributional, competitive, and spatial dynamics of urban digital transformation

title: Inflation and Unemployment in the 21st Century Nigeria: Does the Phillips Curve Still Hold?

detail.title: Inflation and Unemployment in the 21st Century Nigeria: Does the Phillips Curve Still Hold?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not Applicable for this study
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable for this study - all the data used were sourced from a secondary international organisation's database
declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable for this study

detail.abstract: Nigeria's inflation has remained persistently elevated in recent times, especially throughout the 21st century, prompting sustained monetary tightening by the Central Bank of Nigeria. This policy brief asks whether the theoretical foundation most commonly used to guide that response, the Phillips Curve inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment, is empirically valid in the Nigerian context. Drawing on annual data from 2000 to 2024 sourced from the World Bank World Development Indicators and Global Inflation Database, the brief finds that the Phillips Curve does not hold in Nigeria. The correlation between headline inflation and unemployment is only-0.235, while food inflation returns a near-zero correlation of-0.116 with unemployment. A five-year rolling correlation analysis reveals that the inflation-unemployment relationship fluctuates sharply and unpredictably across the study period, turning strongly positive during the 2016 recession and the 2017 to 2018 window, before reversing again. The trend line does slope the way the Phillips Curve predicts, but weak. It explains only 5.5 percent of the change in inflation (R² = 0.0552). Some years, like 2016 and 2020, show high inflation and high unemployment happening together. Which should not happen if the Phillips Curve is true. The data points are also spread out across all four zones instead of clustering in the pattern the theory predicts. This spread more than the number of stagflation points, shows that there is no reliable trade-off between inflation and unemployment in Nigeria.

title: The Interplay Between Organization and Organizing in Educational and Cultural Dynamics: A Review. Insights from European Countries
affiliations: and CBM International University

detail.title: The Interplay Between Organization and Organizing in Educational and Cultural Dynamics: A Review. Insights from European Countries
detail.abstract: This article revisits the foundational principles behind the concepts of organization and structure. Defining "organization" is particularly challenging, as existing terminology often fails to fully capture its complexity. Words like "organization" can be interchangeable with terms such as entity, connection, mechanism, social complex, and mode of administration, among others. However, relying solely on synonyms is insufficient, often leading to a cycle of circular definitions. Many interpretations tend to lean toward synonymous or circular explanations. As a result, it is essential to deepen our understanding of key concepts in contemporary society-organization and structure-to ensure conceptual clarity. By exploring these ideas, the article moves beyond mere linguistic equivalents, aiming to provide a comprehensive understanding of their multifaceted nature. The paper also examines the cultural dynamics within European countries and presents several organizational models.

title: Innovation Pathways for Modernizing Arctic Oil Pipeline Infrastructure in Russia
affiliations: MGIMO University

detail.title: Innovation Pathways for Modernizing Arctic Oil Pipeline Infrastructure in Russia
detail.abstract: Oil transportation infrastructure in the Russian Arctic operates under some of the harshest environmental and logistical conditions in the world, making technological renewal a strategic priority for the sector. Drawing on a review of domestic and international engineering practice, this paper examines five interconnected directions for innovation-led modernization: predictive analytics built on digital twin models, advanced pipe materials, robotic inspection and in-situ repair, environmentally protective monitoring systems, and cybersecurity for digital pipeline control. The analysis argues that achieving technological self-sufficiency and long-term operational resilience in the Arctic oil transport system requires not only the adoption of new engineering solutions but also parallel reform of regulatory, financial, and workforce development mechanisms.

title: Designing Agentic AI Workflow Portfolios under Selector Confusion and Compute Cost
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Designing Agentic AI Workflow Portfolios under Selector Confusion and Compute Cost
detail.abstract: Agentic AI systems can often approach the same task through several workflows that differ in reasoning strategy, verification structure, and compute cost. A natural deployment policy is to identify the workflow with the highest average performance across task instances and use it alone. This policy may be suboptimal, however, because different workflows may succeed on different instances. We therefore study a portfolio and selector paradigm in which a firm runs multiple workflow executions and chooses the final answer after observing their outputs. Additional executions may reveal a correct answer that the best average performing workflow would miss, but they also consume compute and introduce plausible distractors that make final selection more difficult. We formulate this tradeoff as a workflow portfolio problem in which the firm jointly chooses the run size and the allocation of execution slots across workflow types. We summarize selector quality through an odds lift index and derive sharp bounds on the value of workflow variety. For finite workflow pools, we develop exact formulations, linear programming relaxations, randomized rounding procedures, and computable performance certificates. For a large implicit workflow class, we derive a finite dimensional dual and an ellipsoid method that uses a pricing oracle to search for workflows with high weighted accuracy net of recurring compute cost. Under a weak global pricing condition, the method obtains an $\varepsilon$ optimal solution to the full linear programming relaxation using a polynomial number of oracle calls. The analysis shows that effective deployment requires joint management of workflow generation, run size, selector strength, and compute expenditure.

title: Mountain Precision Agriculture Index: a Review
affiliations: CBM International University,  and Universitatea din Oradea

detail.title: Mountain Precision Agriculture Index: a Review
detail.abstract: The paper develops the Mountain Precision Agriculture Index realized in 2020 at Oradea University-Doctoral School, Agronomy Specialization (Covaci-Sterpu, 2020). The article points the importance of entrepreneurship development, focusing on precision agriculture index in the mountain area. The reviewed papers show that the implementation of precision farming within an IoT framework in highland regions (ζ9) must be developed with attention to various essential aspects, precisely the elevation of the mountain (ζ1), the gradient of the terrain (ζ2), the mean local altitude (ζ3), signal degradation due to the mountainous topography (ζ4), access to internet connectivity (ζ6), the level of smart technology utilization (ζ7), and the concentration of active ICT businesses in the region (ζ8). The current paper show that ζ9 is dependent of other indices too, respectively the interaction with the intensity of geomagnetic storms or weather shortcomings (ζ5). The paper presents a specific map of the mountain peaks from the European area, highlighting the importance of the altitude in applying the precision agriculture index.

title: The Nash & Cibinic Report
affiliations: George Washington University -Law School

detail.title: The Nash & Cibinic Report
detail.abstract:
In the first half of 2026, two separate Government contract tribunals rejected Government requests to withhold the tribunals' opinions from public release. Presumably, the agencies sought to avoid the precedential impact of public decisions and had no qualms with the idea that a Government tribunal would decide cases in secrecy. Each tribunal expressed clear surprise that the Government would even make such a request, and each proceeded to publish its opinions for the public record.

The first opinion came from a bid protest before the Federal Aviation Administration’s Office of Dispute Resolution for Acquisition, Protest of Cavan Solutions, No. 24-ODRA-00966, 2026 WL 1284037 (Jan. 1, 2026). The most recent came from a Contract Disputes Act appeal before the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals, KiewitPhelps, ASBCA 61184, 2026 WL 2101313 (June 25, 2026).

title: How Do Time, Infrastructure, and Environmental Factors Influence Severe Traffic Accidents? An Exploratory Statistical Analysis of U.S. Traffic Accidents (2016-2023)

detail.title: How Do Time, Infrastructure, and Environmental Factors Influence Severe Traffic Accidents? An Exploratory Statistical Analysis of U.S. Traffic Accidents (2016-2023)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it involved the analysis of an existing, publicly available dataset and did not involve human participants, patients, or the collection of personally identifiable data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Traffic accidents remain a major public safety concern worldwide, yet the factors associated with accident severity are often examined in isolation or within limited temporal scopes. This study presents an exploratory statistical analysis of severe traffic accidents in the United States using the US Accidents (2016–2023) dataset, which contains millions of real-world traffic incident records collected from multiple heterogeneous sources. The analysis focuses on the relationship between accident severity and non-medical contextual factors, including temporal patterns (hour of day, day of week, seasonality, and long-term trends), environmental conditions (visibility and weather categories), infrastructural features (traffic signals and junctions), and spatial context (urban versus non-urban areas). Severe accidents are defined as events with a severity level of three or higher, reflecting substantial traffic impact. A combination of descriptive statistics, visualization techniques, and non-parametric statistical tests is employed, including chi-square tests for categorical associations and Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous variables. The results reveal pronounced temporal regularities, with higher probabilities of severe accidents during night-time hours and weekends, as well as clear seasonal and interannual variations. Reduced visibility and specific weather conditions are associated with significantly higher accident severity, while infrastructural and spatial factors further differentiate risk patterns. Additionally, accident duration is examined as a proxy measure of traffic disruption severity. All findings are interpreted as observational associations rather than causal relationships. The study emphasizes transparency regarding data limitations, reporting biases, and potential confounding factors. By providing a comprehensive, reproducible, and statistically grounded overview of severe traffic accident risk patterns, this work aims to contribute to exploratory research in traffic safety analysis and to support further hypothesis-driven investigations.

title: Real-Time Distributional Regime Monitoring: Online Wasserstein Detection of Market Stress
affiliations: and

detail.title: Real-Time Distributional Regime Monitoring: Online Wasserstein Detection of Market Stress
detail.abstract: This paper develops a real-time market-stress monitor based on the geometry of rolling empirical return distributions. A strictly prior-information W1 score compares each current distribution with recursively updated low-and high-stress barycenters; thresholds are calibrated before 2007 and then frozen. Across four equity indices from 2000 through June 2026, raw DRP remains strongly scale-linked, while shapeonly DRP is much less correlated with realized volatility. In an extended seven-episode evaluation, raw DRP detects 21 of 28 market-event cases, compared with 15 for 22-day realized volatility, 14 for EWMA(0.94), and 13 for a pre-2007 fixed-parameter GARCH(1,1), while mean off-window alarm shares remain similar at 3.1%-3.5%. The paired detection advantage does not survive Holm correction, so it is interpreted as systematic but not decisive. Controlled experiments show why the distinction matters: realized volatility identifies scale shifts but is near chance for a variance-matched shape shift, whereas raw and shape-only DRP attain AUCs of 0.84 and 0.85. Predictive gains for future volatility remain limited. The evidence supports DRP as a complementary distribution-sensitive monitoring coordinate rather than a universal forecasting factor.

title: Speed of Intervention in Algorithmic Markets: Controlling Collusion and Stability
affiliations: Imperial College Business School, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Speed of Intervention in Algorithmic Markets: Controlling Collusion and Stability
detail.abstract: Algorithmic pricing is prevalent in online marketplaces, raising concerns that learning algorithms may sustain supracompetitive outcomes. We study two sellers in a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma who delegate decisions to memoryless value-based learning algorithms. A platform steers demand toward sellers choosing the more competitive action. Using a fluid approximation, we characterize how intervention intensity, learning architecture, and implementation speed determine market dynamics. Stronger intervention lowers cooperation levels at the fixed point. Algorithmic responsiveness determines the location of stationary outcomes, while action-dependent learning rates determine their local stability. As intervention intensifies, the fixed point can lose stability through a Hopf bifurcation and its local basin of attraction shrinks as the stability threshold is approached. Consequently, an abrupt intervention may leave inherited Q-values outside the target's local basin of attraction and lead to persistent oscillations, whereas gradual intervention leads to a stable market outcome. We also derive local bounds on implementation speed and rollout time. Our results show that platform regulation of algorithmic collusion may require choosing not only how much to intervene, but also how quickly to implement the intervention relative to the algorithms' learning dynamics.

title: A Structural Equation Modelling Analysis of Gamification's Impact on Purchase Intention
affiliations: , Gulf College and Gulf College

detail.title: A Structural Equation Modelling Analysis of Gamification's Impact on Purchase Intention
detail.abstract: Gamification has become a prevalent approach for appealing users and encouraging desired behaviours in many fields, comprising marketing, education, banking, healthcare, and numerous other fields. This paper explores in what way integrating gamified elements, such as Points, Badges, Rewards, Challenges, Leaderboards, and Interactive Activities, impacts the online shopping experience for buyers. This study investigates the influence of gamification on the buying intention of the buyers adopting online shopping. It examines the role of perceived ease of use, social interaction, perceived utility and perceived enjoyment in impacting buyers’ intention in online buying. The findings of this study intend to provide a valuable insight for e-commerce firms and sellers, aiding them to design and enhance online shopping platforms personalized to the inclinations of consumers. Finally, this study contributes to the wider understanding of consumer behaviour in the digital era and highlights approaches that can enhance the online shopping experience for buyers, nurturing customer engagement, and growth of the business.

title: Enhancing Behavioural Supply Chain Management: A Study of Trust, Culture, And Spirituality Effects
affiliations: and University of Delhi - University of Delhi

detail.title: Enhancing Behavioural Supply Chain Management: A Study of Trust, Culture, And Spirituality Effects
detail.abstract: This research aims to enhance the theoretical framework of behavioural supply chain management by integrating principles from psychology and supply chain management. It examines the influence of trust, culture, and spirituality on supply chain systems through both qualitative and quantitative methods. A literature review established the theoretical foundation, while a survey of 565 Indian professionals provided data analysed using SPSS and SMART PLS. Additionally, expert interviews offered qualitative insights. Findings reveal that trust and culture significantly impact behavioural outcomes and supply chain performance, with spirituality acting as a mediator. Despite its contributions, the study acknowledges limitations, such as a semi-systematic literature review and a narrow focus on selected behavioural factors. Future research should explore additional dimensions for a more holistic understanding. By integrating psychology with supply chain management, this study provides valuable insights for practitioners seeking to enhance effectiveness and sustainability in supply chain operations.

title: Digital Sovereignty and the Future of Business: How Dependence on Foreign Technology Shapes Organizational Resilience

detail.title: Digital Sovereignty and the Future of Business: How Dependence on Foreign Technology Shapes Organizational Resilience

detail.abstract: Organizations across both advanced and emerging economies have become structurally dependent on a small number of foreign-owned technology providers for cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence capability, and critical digital platforms. This paper examines how that dependence shapes organizational resilience, defined as the capacity of a business to withstand disruption, adapt to shocks, and sustain operations under stress. Drawing on current market concentration data, documented large-scale outage events, emerging regulatory responses such as the European Union's cloud sovereignty initiatives, and the literature on organizational resilience and dynamic Digital Sovereignty and Organizational Resilience size can use to assess and manage foreign technology dependence, and closes with implications for firm strategy and public policy.

title: The NeuroImprint™ Model: The Predicted Cost of Action and Dual Executive Safety Archetypes

detail.title: The NeuroImprint™ Model: The Predicted Cost of Action and Dual Executive Safety Archetypes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author, Giselle Baumet, is the owner of Giselle Baumet LLC and founder of NeuroImprint™. The theoretical framework, mathematical modeling, and conceptual analysis presented in this working paper were developed independently by the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper presents a theoretical framework and synthesizes non-identifiable, qualitative observational insights derived from executive consulting practice. No formal human subject clinical trials or interventional experiments were conducted for this working paper, and no identifiable individual data are reported.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external financial funding or grant support. It was independently conducted and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: Executive performance in high-stakes environments is traditionally evaluated through an outcome-driven, binary lens: individuals either execute strategic intent with high discipline or fail due to operational dysfunction and lack of willpower. This conventional model overlooks a critical neurobiological reality: the central nervous system does not evaluate action purely on strategic value, but on predicted metabolic, psychological, and interoceptive cost. Drawing upon predictive processing and active inference frameworks, this paper introduces the NeuroImprint™ Model. We model executive friction not as a failure of grit or habit formation, but as a top-down generative prediction of unsustainable physiological cost.

reference: Vol. 93 Tennessee Law Review 221-228 (2026)
title: Just Prosecution

detail.title: Just Prosecution

declarations.funderStatement: Funding was provided by the University of Akron School of Law.

detail.abstract:
Prosecutors were once envisioned as the heroes of the criminal legal system, wielding immense power to secure justice. Yet their role remained largely untethered to a coherent, principled framework. Without clear guardrails, traditional prosecution contributed to mass incarceration, racial disparities, and punitive excesses. Progressive prosecution sought to redress these deficiencies, but a lack of cohesive theoretical grounding, accompanied by a divestiture of power, left prosecutions weak. Reform was fragmented by electoral pressures but remained subject to abolitionist critiques. This article asks readers to consider the idea of Just Prosecution as a way of reimagining the prosecutor’s role—raising the question of what purposes should form the foundation of prosecution. Just Prosecution challenges us to consider the foundational principles of the prosecutorial system rather than merely stripping away the flaws of traditional prosecution, leaving a weakened framework. Instead, it seeks to engage in a conversation about building a new model that balances public safety with individual liberty. In contrast to the abolitionist theory, which primarily highlights systemic flaws without offering a tangible alternative, Just Prosecution advocates for an individualized approach wherein prosecution is pursued only when a narrowly tailored justification exists.
Just Prosecution suggests a first-principles framework that prioritizes both liberty and safety as coequal imperatives. The article critiques the penological justifications of retribution, deterrence, and rehabilitation, as either exceeding the prosecutor’s proper remit or being inconsistently applied. It suggests that prosecution should be based upon incapacitation and specific deterrence to prevent identifiable safety issues. It reconceptualizes prosecutorial discretion, urging prosecutors to act as problem-solvers who wield power incisively, maximizing safety when appropriate while limiting interference with liberty. Ultimately, Just Prosecution charts a new normative path by challenging existing paradigms and envisioning prosecutors as stewards of trust, agents who harmonize public safety and individual liberty in a mutually reinforcing manner.

title: Identity Alignment: The Narrative Foundation of Leadership Commitment Why People Follow Causes Larger Than Themselves

detail.title: Identity Alignment: The Narrative Foundation of Leadership Commitment Why People Follow Causes Larger Than Themselves

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests, personal relationships, or other conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this working paper. The views expressed are solely those of the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a conceptual theoretical work based on analysis of existing scholarly literature and publicly available organizational examples. It did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or animal subjects. Accordingly, institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Leadership scholarship has long recognized that commitment cannot be explained by formal authority or rational persuasion alone. Existing research demonstrates that social identity, organizational identification, and collective meaning influence follower behavior, yet comparatively less attention has been devoted to the mechanism through which leadership narratives become aligned with followers' self-concepts and generate sustained commitment. This paper examines the relationship between identity, organizational meaning, and leadership influence through a conceptual analysis of scholarship on social identity, organizational culture, and narrative leadership. The analysis identifies a theoretical gap concerning how leaders connect organizational narratives to followers' identities during periods of organizational continuity and change. To address this gap, the paper develops the concept of Identity Alignment, defined as the degree to which a leadership narrative aligns with how followers understand themselves, their values, and their place within a larger collective story. The analysis argues that leadership commitment emerges not solely from agreement with organizational objectives but from the extent to which individuals recognize their identities within the narrative being advanced. By identifying Identity Alignment as a distinct leadership mechanism, this paper extends existing scholarship on identity and organizational leadership while contributing a foundational construct to Narrative Power Leadership Theory (NPLT). The findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding why leaders generate extraordinary commitment when organizational narratives reflect who followers believe they are.

title:
De-Banking in Canada: Institutional Processes, Customer Consequences,
and the Limits of Reconsideration
An Exploratory Essay

detail.title:
De-Banking in Canada: Institutional Processes, Customer Consequences,
and the Limits of Reconsideration
An Exploratory Essay
detail.abstract: De-banking—the involuntary termination of a customer’s banking relationship—has emerged as a significant and understudied phenomenon within Canada’s financial regulatory landscape. Although Canadian banks operate within a robust framework governed by the Bank Act, the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA), and FINTRAC guidance, the increasing reliance on riskbased compliance models has expanded the circumstances under which financial institutions may sever ties with clients. This paper examines the institutional processes that lead to de-banking, including Know-Your-Customer (KYC) obligations, automated transaction monitoring, internal risk scoring, and the structural insulation of compliance departments. It argues that the opacity mandated by anti-tipping-off provisions creates an environment in which customers are often denied meaningful explanations for account closures, even when no wrongdoing has been proven. The study further analyzes the consequences of de-banking for individuals, joint account holders, and small businesses. These consequences extend beyond the immediate loss of access to funds and payment systems, encompassing reputational harm, barriers to financial participation, credit disruptions, and long-term financial exclusion. Particular attention is given to the collateral impact on spouses and partners whose accounts may be terminated solely due to their financial association with the primary subject of inquiry. Comparative insights from the United Kingdom, Australia, and the United States illustrate that Canada’s challenges are part of a broader global trend driven by heightened AML/ATF expectations and institutional risk aversion. The paper also evaluates the avenues available for reconsideration and redress, including internal bank escalation mechanisms, the role of the bank’s internal ombudsman, the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments (OBSI), and limited legal remedies such as judicial review. It concludes that while these mechanisms provide nominal pathways for recourse, structural constraints—particularly the confidentiality of compliance investigations—significantly limit their effectiveness. The final chapter proposes policy reforms aimed at enhancing transparency, procedural fairness, and consumer protection without undermining Canada’s AML/ATF objectives. Overall, this research demonstrates that de-banking in Canada reflects a tension between regulatory compliance and financial inclusion. It highlights the need for clearer procedural safeguards and more balanced oversight to ensure that risk-based banking does not inadvertently produce unjust or disproportionate outcomes for consumers.

title: The Doctrine as Fixed Point: Endogenous Penalty Enforcement, Multiplicity, and the Irreversibility of Capital Shocks in Markets for Expert Services

detail.title: The Doctrine as Fixed Point: Endogenous Penalty Enforcement, Multiplicity, and the Irreversibility of Capital Shocks in Markets for Expert Services
detail.abstract: In markets for expert services under improving AI, separation through an outcome-contingent liability commitment survives only if the commitment that must be posted falls below what can be posted, which yields the condition ξ¯κ ≤ 1 − 1/(Mθ0) with M = min{¯ L/v, m}, where m is the multiple of actual loss that survives review under the penalty doctrine. That literature, including our own, treats m as a legal datum. It is not. Post-Cavendish the enforceable multiple is measured against the legitimate interest the clause protects; where the protected interest is the preservation of human fallback capability, that interest exists only if the commitment separates, which requires a sufficiently large m. We close the loop and study the resulting doctrine map m′ = D(m). Six results follow. First, D is monotone on a complete lattice, so a fixed point exists, and it is unique unless ¯ λ/(4ς) > 1, where ¯ λ is the maximal doctrinal uplift and ς the dispersion of the case-level separation threshold; when multiplicity obtains there are generically three fixed points, of which the outer two are stable. Second, calibrating (c,ς) from the primitives of the companion paper and ¯ λ from primary legal sources yields a taxonomy: the United States (¯ λ = 0) and negotiated German B2B contracting (¯ λ = 24) are determinate regimes, at m∗ = 1.00 and m∗ = 25.0 respectively; England and, since BPL v Morgan Securities (2025), India are multiple regimes with m∗ L = 1.03, watershed mu = 1.95 and m∗ H = 4.00. Third, and against the framing of the companion paper, the two ceilings are not independent: with M = min{ℓ,m} the doctrine map inherits the solvency cap, and the equilibrium ceiling is discontinuous at ℓ = mu, falling by 0.92 at that point. Fourth, the collapse is irreversible: restoring ℓ does not restore m, because the doctrine has crossed into the lower basin. Re-running the companion paper’s regime map under an endogenous doctrine reproduces its published counts exactly when m is held fixed and changes them when it is not — cells surviving ξ = 0.2 after the January 2026 insurance exclusions fall from twelve to six — and it polarises the map: intermediate cells disappear. Fifth, perturbing the adjustment with idiosyncratic noise makes the long-run doctrine unique and delivers a closed-form tipping point: the stochastically selected doctrine maximises a doctrinal potential, selection switches at the Maxwell point c∗ = 1 + ¯ λ/2 — the midpoint of the doctrinal range, independent of the dispersion ς and of any symmetric heterogeneity distribution — and between the Maxwell point and the fold the permissive doctrine survives on borrowed time. Irreversibility becomes metastable rather than absolute: the expected recovery time is Kramers-exponential, 1032 periods at noise σ = 0.05, and the claim is falsified on a thirty-period horizon only if σ > 0.29; the welfare cost of the trap is in any case capped at the drafting cost of primary-obligation substitutes, which escape the doctrine entirely. Sixth, the order-theoretic core of the paper — existence, orbit bounds, watershed invariance, and irreversibility under arbitrary dominated policy paths — is machine-checked in Lean 4; the checker reports that no theorem depends on any axiom.

title: Collective Hedging in the Gulf: The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement (2026), its Design, and its Regional Repercussions

detail.title: Collective Hedging in the Gulf: The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement (2026), its Design, and its Regional Repercussions

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patients, or primary data collection. The analysis relies exclusively on publicly available official statements, news reporting, and published think-tank commentary; no ethics approval was therefore required.

detail.abstract: On 7 August 2026, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement (MJDA), committing that an armed attack against any one signatory shall be regarded as an attack against all three (Saudi Press Agency 2026; Breaking Defense 2026). This article provides an early, theoretically grounded case study of the agreement's need, design, and repercussions, drawing on triangulated open-source reporting and official statements in the absence of the treaty's full text. Building on Kuik's (2008) and Ciorciari's (2010) hedging frameworks, Schweller's (2004) theory of underbalancing, Christensen and Snyder's (1990) work on chain-ganging and buck-passing, and Buzan and Wæver's (2003) regional security complex theory, the article argues that the MJDA is best understood as an instance of collective hedging: a multi-state extension of hedging theory, previously developed mainly to explain individual small-state alignment choices, to a trilateral, formally codified instrument that nonetheless preserves each signatory's prior alignments and withholds the institutional commitments characteristic of a genuine collective-defense revolution. The pact's mutual-defense clause is deliberately elastic; its cooperation provisions and repercussions for the signatories are asymmetric, with Türkiye bearing structurally higher entanglement risk than Saudi Arabia or Pakistan; and its regional effects vary in kind rather than degree across Iran, Israel, India, and the United States. The article operationalizes the hedging-versus-revolution debate with a falsifiable indicator framework and closes with propositions for future empirical testing. The MJDA offers a rare real-time case for refining hedging theory beyond its Southeast Asian origins and for tracking the diffusion of security authority toward middle-power, intra-regional arrangements in a multipolar system.

title: Women with Children Prefer not to Work Exclusively from Home
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU), University of Newcastle and The University of Adelaide

detail.title: Women with Children Prefer not to Work Exclusively from Home

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval and informed consent The study was approved by the University of Newcastle Human Research Ethics Committee on 18 March 2022 (reference H-2021-0382). All participants provided informed consent before completing the anonymous online survey.

detail.abstract: We collect stated-preference data on preferred work location using a three-category choice set: Office, Hybrid and Home. The distinction is particularly informative when examining the interaction between gender and children. Among the four gender-by-children groups, women with children have the lowest predicted probabilities of preferring either home-or office-based work. Instead, women show a particularly strong preference for hybrid work. Their preferences contrast with the more evenly distributed preferences of men and of women without children.

title: Thinking about the Possibilities of a Decolonial Global Local (Glocal) Ethical Resonance Theory: Decolonial Glocal Ethical Resonance Theory

detail.title: Thinking about the Possibilities of a Decolonial Global Local (Glocal) Ethical Resonance Theory: Decolonial Glocal Ethical Resonance Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Penelitian ini bersifat independen dan tidak memiliki hubungan apapun dengan pihak lain

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes the conceptual foundation of the Decolonial Glocal Ethical Resonance Theory (DGERT) as a normative framework for understanding ethical communication in the digital era. The theory responds to the persistent dominance of Western-centric ethical paradigms that frequently overlook the epistemological, cultural, and moral traditions of local communities. Rather than positioning global and local ethics as competing frameworks, DGERT conceptualizes ethics as a dynamic process of resonance in which universal human values interact dialogically with indigenous knowledge systems, producing context-sensitive yet globally relevant ethical practices. Drawing on decolonial thought, glocalization theory, communication ethics, and moral philosophy, the study develops a theoretical synthesis that recognizes plurality, reciprocity, epistemic justice, and cultural dignity as fundamental principles of ethical communication. 
     Using a conceptual and interdisciplinary approach, this paper integrates insights from decolonial scholars, communication ethics, media studies, and local wisdom traditions to formulate the core dimensions of ethical resonance. The proposed theory emphasizes that ethical legitimacy emerges not from the unilateral imposition of universal norms but from continuous negotiation between global standards and locally embedded moral values. In this perspective, ethical communication becomes a relational and adaptive process capable of responding to cultural diversity, technological transformation, and asymmetrical power relations within digital ecosystems. 
     The study argues that DGERT offers an alternative paradigm for journalism, digital media governance, artificial intelligence ethics, and platform accountability by strengthening inclusive, culturally responsive, and socially sustainable communication practices. The theory contributes to the expanding discourse on decolonizing communication scholarship by introducing ethical resonance as a bridging mechanism between global normative principles and local ethical traditions. Ultimately, the proposed framework seeks to enrich contemporary communication theory through a decolonial, pluralistic, and glocal ethical perspective that is applicable to increasingly interconnected societies.

title: Housing Boom and Capital Allocation within the Firm: Evidence from China
affiliations: , East China Normal University (ECNU),  and Peking University - Guanghua School of Management

detail.title: Housing Boom and Capital Allocation within the Firm: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of China's Shantytown Renovation Programs (SRPs)driven housing booms on firms' capital allocation. Using prefecture-level SRP data and firm-level panel data, we identify a within-firm capital allocation channel: SRPs, particularly cash-based resettlement, induce housing price surges, prompting firms to reallocate capital from productive assets to real estate, especially those with lower returns on productive investments. Instrumental variable regressions confirm the causal link, showing 1% additional planned SRP units reduce firms' productive investment by 0.27%. Further, such reallocation increases industry-level TFP dispersion and firm underinvestment, causing resource misallocation. This study complements existing literature by highlighting an underexplored mechanism, differing from credit-based channels (collateral or crowding-out), and extends understanding of housing policies' firm-level effects.

title: Digital Marketing Capabilities and SME Internationalization in Pakistan: A Proposed Framework Linking Digital Marketing Capability to Internationalization Barriers

detail.title: Digital Marketing Capabilities and SME Internationalization in Pakistan: A Proposed Framework Linking Digital Marketing Capability to Internationalization Barriers
detail.abstract: Small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) make up the large majority of Pakistan's business establishments, yet relatively few participate meaningfully in international markets. Reaching foreign customers typically requires firms to build market knowledge, find trustworthy partners, establish credibility abroad, meet cross border compliance requirements, and fund market entry activity, demands that fall hardest on resource constrained SMEs. Digital tools can, in principle, lower some of these costs by making information and communication cheaper and by letting firms reach foreign customers without a physical presence overseas. Whether this actually happens for Pakistani SMEs, and through what mechanism, has not been tested directly. This paper sets out a framework, grounded in the resource based view (RBV) and the Uppsala internationalization model, in which digital marketing capabilities, not digital access in general, but the organizational ability to use digital channels strategically, improve internationalization performance partly by reducing specific market related and informational barriers. A cross sectional survey of Pakistani SMEs engaged in or preparing for international business is proposed, with data to be analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS SEM). The paper's contribution at this stage is the framework and research design themselves, not empirical findings, which would follow from a subsequent data collection phase.
