title: Resolution of Non-performing Loans

detail.title: Resolution of Non-performing Loans
detail.abstract: The aim of the analysis is to determine whether there are differences in the resolution of non performing loans depending on the specificities of the economy, on the one hand, or of the business of the corporate borrower, on the other hand - or whether the processes of NPLs resolution are always the same. This paper is, therefore, divided into two parts: the first, which focuses on the recovery of non performing loans from various corporate borrowers and the other, which focuses on the recovery of non-performing loans in different economies.

title: How Does Pillar Two Affect Tax Revenues in Production Countries and Tax Havens?
affiliations: Senshu University - School of Economics

detail.title: How Does Pillar Two Affect Tax Revenues in Production Countries and Tax Havens?
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework to study the strategic implications of Pillar Two on production countries and tax havens. Using a Stackelberg game framework in which tax havens act as first movers and production countries respond strategically, the paper analyzes the effects of increases in the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) rate on equilibrium tax rates and tax revenues. The analysis shows that higher IIR rates induce production countries to raise their corporate tax rates, thereby increasing their tax revenues. In contrast, tax havens respond by lowering their tax rates to mitigate the erosion of their profit-shifting tax base, which ultimately reduces their tax revenues. The paper also compares this policy with an alternative global initiative that raises the cost of profit shifting through stricter enforcement. Unlike higher IIR rates, stronger anti-profit-shifting measures increase tax revenues in both production countries and tax havens. These findings suggest that strengthening the enforcement of anti-profitshifting rules may be more politically feasible than further increases in the global minimum tax rate as the next stage of Pillar Two.

title: Beyond the Host Nations: Indirect Economic Spillovers of FIFA World Cup 2026 for Non-Host Emerging Economies

detail.title: Beyond the Host Nations: Indirect Economic Spillovers of FIFA World Cup 2026 for Non-Host Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: Research on the economic impact of mega sporting events has focused almost entirely on host countries, leaving non-host economies largely unexamined despite mechanisms in the existing literature, such as leakage and crowding-out, that suggest their economic effects should extend beyond host borders. This paper addresses that gap through a qualitative case study of Pakistan's connection to the 2026 FIFA World Cup, examining three channels: trade and manufacturing, remittances, and broadcasting. Using official trade and financial data alongside industry reporting, the paper finds clear evidence of a manufacturing-driven effect, most notably through Sialkot's role in producing the tournament's official match ball and a measurable rise in football exports. In contrast, remittance data show no clear World Cup-related pattern, while broadcasting shows a smaller, visibility-driven effect. These mixed results suggest that non-host emerging economies are unevenly connected to mega events, largely through channels that have developed passively rather than through deliberate strategy. The paper argues that Pakistan, and countries like it, could capture greater economic benefit from future tournaments through more intentional preparation, and calls for further research examining other non-host economies.

title: The MAAZ Model for Global Industrial and Economic Presence
affiliations: Keiser University

detail.title: The MAAZ Model for Global Industrial and Economic Presence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this conceptual research paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: China’s industrial rise has reshaped global trade and production networks. Its influence is not limited to export volume: it also rests on dense supplier networks, large-scale manufacturing, infrastructure, financing, access to raw materials, and durable commercial relationships. The United States has responded through tariffs, reshoring, nearshoring, friend-shoring, technology controls, investment restrictions, and targeted industrial support. These tools matter, but they do not fully answer a practical question faced by many economies: if dependence on Chinese products or supply chains is to be reduced, what competitive alternative will replace them? This paper proposes the MAAZ Model for Global Industrial and Economic Presence, a conceptual framework for developing a distributed international manufacturing network led by the United States in cooperation with allied economies and host countries. At its center is the MAAZ Factoryfor-Factory Principle (MFFP). The principle does not call for one American factory for every Chinese factory. Instead, it identifies country-product markets where Chinese supply is highly concentrated and tests whether an economically viable alternative manufacturing capability can be established in the most suitable regional location. Participating facilities are described as MAAZ Partnership Plants (MPPs). These plants would operate in host countries while meeting an appropriate U.S.-standard baseline and all applicable host-country and destination-market regulations. The model also links manufacturing to trade finance, possible expansion of U.S. banking operations where legally and commercially feasible, dollar-linked international finance and contracts, commercial intelligence, international technical expertise, local workforce development, regional markets, and potential access to the U.S. market. The paper further proposes a Global Economic Base Network (GEBN) and several analytical measures for future empirical testing, including the Factory-for-Factory Opportunity Score (FFOS), China Price Advantage Gap (CPAG), Chinese Value-Added Exposure (CVAE), and Industrial Knowledge Transfer Index (IKTI). Initial regional cases include Mexico, India, Egypt, Indonesia, Türkiye, and South Africa. Sudan is considered separately as a longer-term agro-industrial and resource-processing case, contingent on adequate security, institutional capacity, infrastructure, and investment conditions.

title: I Can't Predict a 1,000-Year Catastrophe

detail.title: I Can't Predict a 1,000-Year Catastrophe
detail.abstract: Under the Basel regulations, the 0.999 quantile — a central parameter of the financial safety architecture, on the basis of which capital requirements for credit risk, operation-al risk, and numerous Pillar II risks have been determined for years — is interpreted in supervisory documents as an event occurring "once in a thousand years." This interpre-tation, reproduced in academic literature and sectoral practice, is the subject of the pre-sent paper. In contrast to the criticism already established in the literature, which con-cerns the estimation difficulties encountered at distant quantiles, this article poses a dif-ferent question: whether the temporal interpretation itself of the 0.999 quantile as a 1,000-year event has any statistical, regulatory, or even practical justification. The pa-per presents the manner in which the temporal interpretation of the 0.999 quantile was embedded in successive Basel accords (Basel I, II, CRR III), and subsequently dissemi-nated in academic works. It is then demonstrated that this definition derives from a bor-rowed, yet never explicitly acknowledged, conceptual apparatus employed in hydrology — the concept of the return period, used to describe phenomena such as the hundred-year flood. It is likewise shown that transferring this convention to the domain of socio-economic phenomena requires a tacit assumption regarding the indexing of successive risk realizations along a time axis — an assumption that, in this context, lacks the nat-ural justification it possesses in the world of physical phenomena. The analysis further demonstrates that the concept of the 1,000-year event is not directly embedded in the construction of risk models, cannot be verified by means of backtesting, and is rendered redundant by the practice of regular model recalibration. Drawing on the experience of hydrology, where an analogous concept — the "hundred-year flood" — has become the subject of criticism and has led to a revision of how risk is communicated, the paper suggests that an analogous debate should be initiated in the field of finance. Such a de-bate would aim to bring the definitions in use, and their interpretation, closer to reality, thereby helping to reconcile, at the axiological level, the approaches applied in the con-struction of risk models. The paper concludes that the temporal interpretation of the 0.999 quantile is an empty artifact, devoid of cognitive and practical value, and propos-es replacing it with definitions grounded in the actual mechanics of extreme events.

title: Who Writes It Down: Measuring Documentation Selection in Infrastructure Cost-Overrun Evidence
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Who Writes It Down: Measuring Documentation Selection in Infrastructure Cost-Overrun Evidence

keywords: Each Committed Before the Statistics It Governs

detail.abstract: The empirical literature on infrastructure cost overruns rests on datasets assembled from documents-audit reports, completion reports, press coverage-rather than from statistical samples of any defined population. We measure, for the first time we are aware of, the selection process that decides which completed projects become evidence at all. Using the Asian Development Bank's closed-transport portfolio as an enumerable population (325 projects), we draw a seeded probability sample of 90 and follow each drawn project to a logged documentary fate; we then replicate the design on a second, independently enumerated frame-the World Bank's 1,416-project closed-transport portfolio. Three stages of a selection funnel emerge, each now carrying a number. Entry into the official record: 17% of projects closed by 2022 have no completion report at all (11/66). Visibility beyond the institution: 60% of the random draw is invisible in all four external documentary systems searched (national audit, news, academic literature, Wikipedia); only one project in six has any external source stating a cost figure. Outcome-selected attention: in a blind test in which searchers never saw outcomes, an over-budget project was 5.3× more likely to be picked up by a national audit institution than an at-or-under-budget one (27.8% vs 5.3%, bootstrap 95% CI [1.06, 16.89])-to our knowledge the first quantitative estimate of audit-attention selection, in exactly the channel the mechanism predicts. We characterize its evidential weight exactly: concordant across estimators (risk difference [0.006, 0.444]; odds ratio 6.9 [1.2, 40.2]; Fisher exact p = 0.029) and robust in point estimate to project-size adjustment, but NOT significant after Holm correction across the six pre-declared channels (adjusted p = 0.17), with country-cluster inference inconclusive at seven events. A pre-registered single-primary replication on the World Bank frame returned the same direction (9.1% vs 2.7%, RR 3.4) but did not meet its confirmation criterion (Fisher p = 0.55) at 13% achievable power-the frame's audit-capture base rate proved ~3× lower than the design assumed. We then ran the pre-specified confirmatory design-a census of the two frames' 111 India and Philippines projects, where audit-institution visibility is densest (clean instrument; 29% capture base rate among resolved projects; ≥86% power at RR 3)-and it returned a null with no direction: capture 26.7% among over-budget vs 30.0% among at-or-under projects, RR 0.89 [0.34, 2.33], Fisher p = 1.00; effects of RR ≥ 3 are excluded there. That null sharpened the hypothesis-outcome-selection should operate where audit attention is scarce, not where coverage is structural-and a second pre-registered test on a fourth frame confirmed it: on a census of the UK Government Major Projects Portfolio (376 outcome-resolved projects; the National Audit Office publishes selectively), over-baseline projects were captured by NAO reports at 18.2% vs 8.7% (RR 2.09 [1.21, 3.62], Fisher p = 0.009; robust to project-size adjustment, OR 2.10). Audit-attention selection is therefore real and conditional: ~2× outcome-selection where the auditor chooses its targets, none where auditing is mandated-a mechanism confirmed at pre-registered standard across four enumerated frames. The consequences are large: within one provenance-gated pool, over-budget frequency is 79.7% among auditor-documented projects and 23.4% among development-bank-documented ones, while the probability-sampled truth for the ADB frame is 32.1% [21.4, 45.2] with a median cost ratio of 0.955-and an identical probability sample of the World Bank frame replicates it (37.3% [26.1, 50.0], median 0.986; no-completion-report rate 17.4% against ADB's 17%), converting a one-frame finding into a measured property of the development-bank documentary world. The contrast survives holding region fixed (64.1 pp within developing-region strata) and cannot be carried by project attributes: none of nine sanction-time covariates beats a type-only model out of sample (effects larger than ×1.28 excluded at 80% power), while documentary source adds +0.207 incremental R². We close with a reflexive demonstration: admitting the 52 probability-sampled (development-bank-frame) records to our own forecasting pool measurably tilted its calibration on fame-selected holdout cases-the phenomenon acting on the instrument that measures it-and we derive a frame-balanced growth rule for evidence bases in this field. We audit our own harvest with the same tools and report the result against ourselves.

title: Lending Through the Fire: Credit Expansion and Rising Bank Risk after the 2025 California Wildfires
affiliations: Suffolk University - Sawyer School of Management, Suffolk University - Sawyer Business School and Suffolk University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Lending Through the Fire: Credit Expansion and Rising Bank Risk after the 2025 California Wildfires

keywords: Generating response Copilot said: Wildfire Risk

detail.abstract: The 2025 Los Angeles County wildfires destroyed more than 16,000 structures and triggered large disaster-relief and insurance-claim inflows into a geographically concentrated banking market. Using a difference-indifferences design that compares commercial banks headquartered in Los Angeles (LA) County (i.e., treated banks) to a national control sample of banks unaffected by FEMA-declared disasters over 2022Q1-2025Q4, and an entropy-balanced event-study design over a seven-quarter window centered on the 2025Q1 wildfire onset, this study examines how an acute physical climate shock transmits through banks' capital, credit risk, profitability, management efficiency, liquidity, funding, and credit supply. Entropy-balanced covariate diagnostics confirm close pre-treatment (i.e., pre-wildfire) comparability between treated and control banks. Average-treatment-effect-on-the-treated (ATET) estimates show that treated banks experienced a statistically significant deterioration of capital adequacy and management efficiency, an increase in non-performing loans, and a decline in profitability following the wildfires, with the deterioration concentrated among banks with less than $10 billion in assets. Consistent with a liquidity-creation and recovery-lending channel operating alongside credit-risk contagion, treated banks simultaneously expanded core deposits and total lending. These findings document a disaster liquidity paradox: disaster-relief funds and insurance payouts may have sustained bank funding and credit supply during the initial post-wildfire period, even as asset quality and earnings deteriorated.

title: Climate-Linked Bonds
affiliations: Maastricht University, University of Amsterdam and De Nederlandsche Bank

detail.title: Climate-Linked Bonds
detail.abstract: Climate-linked bonds, issued by governments and supranational organizations, are pivotal in advancing towards a net-zero economy. These bonds adjust their payoffs based on climate variables such as average temperature and greenhouse gas emissions, providing investors a hedge against long-term climate risks. They also signal government commitment to climate action and incentivize stronger policies. The price differential between climate-linked bonds and nominal bonds reflects market expectations of climate risks. This paper introduces a model of climate risk hedging and estimates that approximately three percent of government debt in major economies could be converted into climate-linked bonds.

detail.abstract: This study examines the application of the phenomenological approach in qualitative research across the fields of social sciences, education, psychology, and the humanities. A qualitative literature study was conducted by synthesizing works on descriptive and interpretive phenomenological traditions. The discussion covers the philosophical foundations of phenomenology, its research characteristics, research procedures, data collection techniques, data analysis, strategies for ensuring research credibility, and its strengths and limitations. The study affirms that phenomenology is a qualitative approach directed toward revealing the essential meaning of participants' lived experiences through systematic phenomenological reduction and interpretation.

title: Reassessing Regional Authority in Mughal Bengal: A Spatial, Legal, and Historiographical Analysis of the Naldanga Estate within Mahmudshahi Pargana

detail.title: Reassessing Regional Authority in Mughal Bengal: A Spatial, Legal, and Historiographical Analysis of the Naldanga Estate within Mahmudshahi Pargana
detail.abstract:
This study provides a rigorous historiographical and spatial analysis of the Naldanga Estate situated within the Mahmudshahi Pargana of Mughal Bengal. By re-examining existing legal frameworks, archival evidence, and land administration protocols, this research challenges traditional narratives of regional authority during the Mughal era. The paper utilizes spatial modeling to reconstruct administrative boundaries, socio-economic dynamics, and legal hierarchies, offering a nuanced, evidence-based understanding of Mughal land governance and decentralized power structures in South Asia.

title: The Dependence of Articulation on Relation: A Preliminary Discussion of Being, Knowledge, and the Limits of Self-Representation

detail.title: The Dependence of Articulation on Relation: A Preliminary Discussion of Being, Knowledge, and the Limits of Self-Representation
detail.abstract: Generative Relational Being holds that beings are constituted in relation and that knowledge emerges from relational dynamics. Taken together these two commitments generate a difficulty the framework has not addressed. If knowledge emerges from relational dynamics, and a formal system can articulate those dynamics, then a sufficiently powerful formalism appears able to exhaust what it articulates, which contradicts the long-standing position that an understanding of being precedes its logical expression. This paper resolves the difficulty and, in resolving it, states the framework's ontology and epistemology in a form the companion papers of this series presuppose without arguing. Three results are offered. The dependence of articulation on relation is asymmetric and non-temporal, so it is a relation of grounding and never a sequence of stages; a formulation as a chain of layers is shown to contradict the framework's own commitments. The relation between a being and the knowledge of it is neither identity nor separation, and the two failures are distinct errors with distinct consequences; the resulting position is stated as neither-one-nor-different in place of the weaker formula of non-duality. And complete self-representation is unavailable to a system that produces its own means of representation, for a reason internal to the framework in place of borrowed from any limitative theorem. Two consequences are drawn for the companion papers: the defect in a representation is ontological closure and never loss, and a generative event admits no locus among its participants.

title: Moving Targets: Regulatory Uncertainty and Agri-Food Trade. A Structural Gravity Model of EU Pesticide Maximum Residue Limits

detail.title: Moving Targets: Regulatory Uncertainty and Agri-Food Trade. A Structural Gravity Model of EU Pesticide Maximum Residue Limits
detail.abstract: A large literature establishes that the level and crosscountry heterogeneity of food-safety standards reduce agri-food trade. A third channel, the uncertainty generated by how frequently and unpredictably those standards are revised, has received little attention, largely because it is difficult to measure and identify. This paper develops a structural gravity model of this channel and applies it to European Union pesticide maximum residue limits. Three elements make up the approach: a product-by-year index of MRL-revision uncertainty, built by principal-component analysis from the amendment record of Regulation (EC) No 396/2005; a theory-consistent gravity equation motivated by a real-options argument, in which the sunk cost of market entry makes waiting more valuable as regulatory volatility rises; and a control-function instrumental-variables strategy based on the statutory active-substance renewal calendar. The model is estimated on a panel of 36 exporters, the 27 EU member states as importers, 25 agri-food product groups, and the years 2004 to 2020, built on the CEPII gravity database. A one-standard-deviation increase in uncertainty is associated with about a 17.5% reduction in bilateral trade. The estimate is stable when the level and heterogeneity of the same standards are controlled for and across a range of robustness checks, and the response is concentrated on the extensive margin, the entry of product lines, rather than the intensive margin, as the real-options mechanism predicts. The effect is larger for developing exporters and for perishable, testing-intensive products. The results indicate that the predictability of food-safety regulation, and not only its stringency, shapes market access.

title: The Push and Pull of School Funding: How Application-Based School Finance Reproduces Inequality
affiliations: University of Haifa and Hebrew University of Jerusalem

detail.title: The Push and Pull of School Funding: How Application-Based School Finance Reproduces Inequality
detail.abstract: Educational resource inequality persists across education systems worldwide, disadvantaging schools serving marginalized populations. One underexplored mechanism contributing to these disparities is the requirement that schools proactively apply for funding. Drawing on the case of Israeli public high schools, this study examines how funding formulae contingent on school-initiated applications ("pull" mechanisms) undermine equity-oriented policy goals. Israeli high school funding is distributed through a complex formula combining automatic allocations ("push" mechanisms) with application-based components. This study analyzes nationwide allocation data from 2021-2022 regarding a component of the formula designated for supporting disadvantaged students through resource-intensive classrooms. The findings reveal that, despite its explicit mandate, this resource does not reach those most in need: Schools in low-income municipalities access it at lower rates than those in middle-income localities; Arab schools receive it less frequently than Jewish schools within the same socioeconomic deciles; and schools operated by large municipalities or private providers are more successful than those run by smaller entities. These patterns suggest that application-based funding disproportionately benefits institutions with greater administrative capacity and bureaucratic expertise. The study highlights how the design of funding formulae, particularly the use of "pull" mechanisms, can inadvertently reproduce and reinforce systemic educational inequalities.

title: Learning the Propagation of Policy Shocks in Global Food Trade: A Graph Neural Network Disciplined by Spatial Equilibrium

detail.title: Learning the Propagation of Policy Shocks in Global Food Trade: A Graph Neural Network Disciplined by Spatial Equilibrium
detail.abstract: Export restrictions in staple food markets raise prices far beyond the countries that impose them, yet the incidence of that transmission across the trade network, and the welfare it shifts between developing and developed economies, is hard to measure. This study couples a structural spatial-equilibrium model of the food-trade network with a graph neural network trained to emulate its shock-propagation operator. The panel spans eighteen agricultural commodities from 2008 to 2022; the structural core, an Anderson and van Wincoop multilateral-resistance system calibrated to six core staples, maps a restriction at any origin to the price response at every destination. A graph attention network reproduces this operator out of sample, with a mean coefficient of determination of 0.6496. From it the study derives Systemic Food-Trade Transmission Centrality, ranking origins by the welfare-weighted price pressure of their restrictions. Without being given trade volumes, it identifies Russia for wheat, India for rice, Ukraine for maize, Brazil for soybean and sugar, and Indonesia for palm oil. Welfare losses fall more heavily on developing importers, which bear 1.9456 times the incidence of developed importers, rising to 3.1265 times in rice. A 2022 validation confirms that the model predicts supply reallocation away from the restricting bloc.

title: Skills-Based Hiring vs Degree-Based Hiring: Disruption, Adoption, and the Future of Talent Acquisition

detail.title: Skills-Based Hiring vs Degree-Based Hiring: Disruption, Adoption, and the Future of Talent Acquisition

detail.abstract: The traditional reliance on university degrees as a primary ltering mechanism in hiring is undergoing profound disruption. Skills-based hiring-the practice of evaluating candidates on demonstrated competencies rather than formal credentials-has emerged as a transformative alternative, driven by technological change, persistent talent shortages, and growing recognition that degrees are weak predictors of job performance. This research examines the current state, empirical evidence, and implications of the shift from degree-based to skills-based hiring. Through a comprehensive synthesis of scholarly literature, industry data, and policy analyses (2020-2026), the study identi es that skillsbased hiring has gained substantial momentum, with 85% of employers now using it in 2025, up from 73% in 2023. However, a signi cant gap persists between stated adoption and actual implementation: while 70% of companies claim to have moved to skills-based hiring, only 9% have fundamentally changed their hiring practices. The research evaluates three principal drivers of this shift: technological disruption (particularly AI), degree in ation, and the pursuit of diversity and inclusion. Key ndings indicate that skills-based hiring is ve times more predictive of job performance than education requirements and 2.5 times more accurate than experience proxies. Skills-screened cohorts show 34% lower attrition at 18 months compared to degree-screened cohorts, while removing degree requirements expands eligible talent pools by 67% on average. However, signi cant barriers remain: inconsistent implementation, lack of manager training, fragmented skills taxonomies, and cultural resistance. The study concludes with a four-pillar policy and implementation framework for organizations and governments seeking to transition to skills-based hiring at scale.

title: Who Pays When the Data Center Never Comes? Contract Design and Stranded-Cost Risk in U.S. Large-Load Electricity Tariffs
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Who Pays When the Data Center Never Comes? Contract Design and Stranded-Cost Risk in U.S. Large-Load Electricity Tariffs
detail.abstract: Serving a hyperscale data center can require irreversible utility investment before the customer operates. If the project is delayed, downsized, or cancelled, who pays for unused capacity? This paper studies largeload electricity tariffs as public contracts against customer non-arrival and underutilization. The evidence comprises 27 independent U.S. utility-state-docket policy chains, 167 source-level records, and 93 firstcoder-confirmed clause observations from operative documents. Clauses are coded as present, absent only after full-document audit, or not publicly verifiable; missing evidence is not converted into weak protection. A locked model-assisted blind recoding of 40 core-case cells yields 92.5% state agreement, 85.0% exact ordinal agreement, and quadratic-weighted Cohen's κ of 0.508; it is a reproducibility audit, not human inter-coder reliability. The paper develops a five-architecture typology and a duration-sensitive backing measure comparing enforceable customer support with the remaining life of dedicated assets. A two-period model separates pre-investment deterrence from post-signing abandonment, and a two-state benchmark shows how competition for mobile projects can weaken backing below the national zeroexposure boundary. The cases reveal strong but heterogeneous safeguards. An adversarial missing-as-zero exercise is underpowered and cannot establish rank independence, but shows why the current record cannot support a stable national cardinal ranking. Large-load tariffs determine whether speculativeinfrastructure downside remains with the large customer, moves to utility investors, or is socialized across ordinary ratepayers.

title: National AI as Political Attribution: How National Labels Compress Distributed Production in the UAE's Falcon and Jais Programs

detail.title: National AI as Political Attribution: How National Labels Compress Distributed Production in the UAE's Falcon and Jais Programs
detail.abstract: States present foundation models as national achievements even when production spans public bodies and foreign providers. This article calls that move attributional compression: assigning a distributed production arrangement to one national program and visible organizational carrier. It reconstructs the UAE’s Falcon and Jais programs from 2023 to January 2026 using dated technical, corporate, and contractual records. A provider transition leaves Falcon’s attribution stable; a corporate reorganization changes Jais’s carrier while production traces continue. The paired cases support a temporal mechanism: political attribution follows carrier-defining events, while production follows provider, infrastructure, and technical events, making national labels unreliable maps of capability.

title: How Not to Tabulate the 2028 US Democratic Primary
affiliations: Université Paris-Saclay, Université Paris Cité, ENS Paris-Saclay, CNRS, SSA, INSERM, Centre Borelli, F-91190, Gif-sur-Yvette, France

detail.title: How Not to Tabulate the 2028 US Democratic Primary
detail.abstract: The US Democratic Party introduced a novel electoral system in 2020, combining instant runoff voting (IRV) and proportional representation (PR) with a 15% viability threshold. This tabulation system was chosen over more established methods, such as single transferable vote (STV), as a way to incorporate ranked-choice ballots into a PR system with a 15% viability threshold, which is deeply embedded in the party's rules. Ahead of the 2028 presidential nomination process, party leaders have expressed a desire to expand the IRV+PR system. However, the system has received little attention from the mathematics and public choice communities. We introduce new optimal transport metrics to measure the misalignment between the ensemble of ballots cast and the distribution of delegates awarded. These metrics have the advantage of separating the alignment measure from the tabulation process and from treating all ballots uniformly. These metrics do not restrict their attention to the match between individual ballots and the candidates whose tallies they increment during tabulation; rather, they treat each cast ballot as an equal amount of probability mass to be transported optimally (not via tabulation) to the delegate distribution. We compare eight alternative tabulation schemes, including the "fair reflection" winner: a loss-minimizing tabulation per an optimal transport cost (which, while NP-hard to tabulate in general, can be calculated for many elections). We find that this IRV+PR tabulation scheme fails to improve overall delegate alignment with voter preferences in simulated delegate-allocation elections using real cast ballot records of US rankedchoice voting elections. (By contrast, eliminating the viability threshold enables traditional PR-which examines only the first preference on the ballot-to approach the OT-optimal allocation of ranked-choice ballots in these simulated election.) Moreover, the use of ranked-choice ballots introduces paradoxical outcomes, such as the no-show paradox and generalized non-leader outcomes (candidate A wins strictly more delegates than B while most ballots rank B above A). In fact, using the cast-ballot record for the 2022 special election for Alaska's US House seat to simulate a presidential primary, we find that the OT-optimal tabulation-which 15% viability PR and IRV+PR attain-the Condorcet loser wins more delegates than the Condorcet winner. The IRV+PR system is more susceptible to paradoxical outcomes than alternative tabulation systems. Thus, we recommend that the DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee discourage the use of this novel tabulation scheme. If the desire to incorporate ranked-choice ballots for this delegate-allocation task persists, we recommend the use of STV using large statewide delegate pools (or 0% viability threshold PR that ignores the ranked choices expressed, although it is free of those paradoxes only when voters select one candidate) and further mathematical, legal, and logistical study of a mixed-integer program to minimize the optimal transport misalignment cost and interpretable heuristic approximations thereof. We also recommend the party cease awarding delegates by candidate performance within a district and weighting the totals by the strength of the Democratic ticket in past elections. Such an approach violates "one person one vote," masks the signal voters express with quantization noise, and-in the wake of Callais-dilutes minority representation, without advancing the aims of McGovern-Fraser. The signal-to-quantization-noise ratio increases with the square of the pool size; for each tabulation method, awarding all of a state's delegates based on the statewide vote totals for each candidate improves the optimal transport cost.

title: Rationed Emphasis: Why Disclosure Regimes Must Cap What Counts

detail.title: Rationed Emphasis: Why Disclosure Regimes Must Cap What Counts
detail.abstract: Emphasis regimes in audit reporting let the profession select what to examine closely and credit the documented diligence as a legal defense. A companion paper found the institution a failed deterrent but a working lens; every informational result there rested on a constraint inherited silently from practice-one matter is emphasised-that the standards themselves do not impose. title: Assessing the Impact of Trade Integration on Industrial Development in Botswana
affiliations: Regional Integration & Trade Governance Professional

detail.title: Assessing the Impact of Trade Integration on Industrial Development in Botswana
detail.abstract: Trade integration has been acknowledged to significantly impact industrial development by fostering economic growth, enhancing productivity, and creating employment opportunities. However, Botswana's integration into regional economic frameworks like SADC and SACU has not fully realized its expected benefits, particularly in industrial development and economic diversification. The nation is characterized by its unique economic landscape and reliance on natural resource exports. Its transition from an import substitution strategy to an export-led growth model has not yielded uniform benefits across all sectors, and manufacturing contribution to GDP has declined. Botswana's trade balance has deteriorated, and WIPO has highlighted weaknesses in market sophistication. To this end, a structural approach to the impact of trade integration on industrial development in Botswana was considered to be offered by the New Structural Economics theory, the Neo-Functionalism theory, and the theory of Customs Union. This study employed the causal research design, and Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) time series analysis on data from 1999 to 2022 in Botswana was employed. The findings of the study discovered that tariff barriers have an insignificant long-term effect on MVA in Botswana. This finding suggests that changes in tariff levels alone may not significantly influence manufacturing output. Additionally, trade openness positively and significantly impacts SVA in both the short and long terms, as indicated by the ARDL model results. However, the study reveals a complex relationship between FDI and SVA, such that the ARDL results show that immediate FDI changes have a limited impact on sectoral value-added, yet lagged FDI terms exhibit delayed positive effects. As a result, the government of Botswana should enhance industrial infrastructure, tackle non-tariff barriers, promote trade openness, and strengthen regional trade agreements. Furthermore, the study recommends that the government should invest in infrastructure and training programs, review regulations, and foster local industry support to boost manufacturing productivity. Moreover, a stable FDI strategy is crucial, and strengthening regional trade agreements can enhance global competitiveness and capitalize on economies of scale.

title: Asymmetric Information under the Kafala Sponsorship System: Impacts on Foreign Domestic Workers' Income and Employment Status in the GCC Countries
affiliations: and Texas A&M University

detail.title: Asymmetric Information under the Kafala Sponsorship System: Impacts on Foreign Domestic Workers' Income and Employment Status in the GCC Countries
detail.abstract: This paper examines the legal and policy implications of information asymmetry on foreign domestic workers employed under the Kafala sponsorship system in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries. Drawing from ethnographic and field-based observations in large GCC migrant destinations – including Kuwait, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) – we investigate the information flows and market uncertainties between five key stakeholders: labor-receiving governments, labor-sending governments, recruitment agencies (subagents), sponsors (employers), and social networks. Several factors contribute to asymmetric information: the lack of bilateral labor agreements and government policy coordination, programs between and among government entities, the absence of labor law for domestic workers, and the laissez faire approach of the labor-receiving government. These sources of asymmetric information create serious market vulnerabilities for the domestic worker population, often resulting in loss of employment and early deportation. The concluding section further outlines policy implications and areas of methodological research on GCC migration.

title: Conditional Migrant Integration in the United Arab Emirates: Consequences on Foreign Workers' Welfare
affiliations: , Texas A&M University and Texas A&M University

detail.title: Conditional Migrant Integration in the United Arab Emirates: Consequences on Foreign Workers' Welfare
detail.abstract: This paper examines the case of the low-skilled Asian migrant workforce, a particularly large component of the Gulf countries’ workforce, which has been subject to controversial labor and human rights issues in recent years. This model is of particular importance to contemporary migration debates because it illustrates the complex relationship between economic migration and social integration in one of the world’s most challenging regions for migrant destination, not only in terms of the dynamic complexity of the migration process, but also because of the controversy surrounding government policies.  This specific study of the Asian migrant workforce in the Gulf highlights a migration ecosystem which is illustrative of a trend in how many states manage, regulate, and enforce migrant integration policies to protect their national interests, while simultaneously capitalizing on the benefits of access to this human capital and the inter-connectedness it affords to the global economy. This chapter also offers unique perspectives for OECD countries on how to manage and integrate migrant populations at a time when many countries in Europe and the West struggle to deal with integrating far-smaller populations within their borders.

title: Contemporary Indian Labor Migration in the GCC Region: Emerging Challenges and Opportunities
affiliations: Texas A&M University,  and American University of Sharjah - School of Business and Management

detail.title: Contemporary Indian Labor Migration in the GCC Region: Emerging Challenges and Opportunities
detail.abstract: The Indian migration to the Gulf countries is one of the most complex and dynamic flows globally. Marked as the largest and highly diverse migrants populations, India constitutes more than one billion people, providing both critical labor supply to various traditional Western labor-receiving countries (mostly skilled workers), and recently to the Gulf countries (mostly low-skilled) and of the broader Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. In this chapter, we examine the contemporary Indian migration to the Gulf region by analyzing the current economic, social, and political trends affecting Indian migrant population in the region. Relevant challenges and emerging opportunities for Indian migrants in the Gulf region will also be examined in the context of the existing migration debates.

title: Secular Stagnation as a Learning Trap: Endogenous Drift in a New Keynesian Model with Adaptive Learning
affiliations: The Japan Research Institute, Limited

detail.title: Secular Stagnation as a Learning Trap: Endogenous Drift in a New Keynesian Model with Adaptive Learning
detail.abstract:
This paper formulates secular stagnation—the persistence of low growth and low inflation—as an endogenous, dynamic process in which, under adaptive learning, the economy falls below a lower steady state and drifts into low inflation. In a standard New Keynesian model, as long as monetary policy maintains a response sufficiently close to the Taylor principle, the target steady state is learnable (E-stable), and a lower steady state emerges that constitutes the boundary of its basin of attraction. Once the economy falls below this boundary, it can no longer return to the target steady state and drifts into low inflation. Secular stagnation is thus characterized as a state in which "the economy is stranded in a low-inflation region below the boundary of the target steady state’s basin of attraction and cannot return to the target steady state," a state this paper calls a "learning trap." Conversely, when the monetary-policy response is weak and the target becomes E-unstable, neither this boundary nor any stable resting point exists, and the economy diverges away from the target from any starting point (global instability).
The model yields the following policy implications. First, fiscal policy plays the role of pushing the economy out of the lower steady state ("escape") and, beyond that, of "raising" output to potential GDP without waiting for the slow convergence to the target steady state through the learning of inflation expectations. Second, monetary policy plays the role of "anchoring" the economy at the target steady state: by satisfying the Taylor principle it keeps the target learnable (E-stable)—and, in phases where learnability has been lost, restores it.
The contribution of this paper lies not in prescribing a particular policy for rapidly attaining the target inflation rate, but in elucidating the qualitative mechanism that gives rise to this division of roles. In particular, it shows that, under empirically plausible interest-rate responses, convergence following escape is slow and that fiscal policy can complement this slow convergence by raising GDP to potential—precisely because the effective limit on fiscal policy lies not in budget deficits but in real resources.

reference: ECB Occasional Paper No. 2026/398
title: The use of the Eurosystem’s monetary policy instruments and its monetary policy implementation framework in 2024 and 2025
affiliations: , European Central Bank (ECB) and

detail.title: The use of the Eurosystem’s monetary policy instruments and its monetary policy implementation framework in 2024 and 2025
detail.abstract: The Eurosystem implements its monetary policy through a set of monetary policy instruments (MPIs). This report reviews the main changes in the use of MPIs and the associated developments in the Eurosystem’s monetary policy implementation framework over 2024-25. Inflation returned to the ECB’s medium-term target of 2%, supported by the smooth transmission of monetary policy. After completing the hiking cycle of 2022 and 2023, the ECB began reducing its key interest rates in June 2024. This easing phase occurred alongside further balance sheet normalisation. Holdings in the monetary policy bond portfolios continued to run-off, and funds lent under the third series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO III) were fully repaid by December 2024. In March 2024, the ECB announced several changes to its operational framework for implementing monetary policy following a review process. Finally, the collateral framework remained broad, while temporary crisis-related measures were phased out and climate-related considerations were further integrated.

reference: UP-CIDS Discussion Paper Series 2026-42
title: Semiconductor Industry Development in Taiwan and the Philippines: Comparative Insights for the Global South
affiliations: National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies (GRIPS) and University of the Philippines

detail.title: Semiconductor Industry Development in Taiwan and the Philippines: Comparative Insights for the Global South

keywords: Scientific and Technical Human Capital Policies

detail.abstract:
Main argument: We argue that the contrasting fortunes of the Taiwan and Philippine semiconductor industries are best explained by the differences in how their respective states deployed industrial policies and institutions in shaping development outcomes, particularly across four key areas: public R&D institutions, industrial governance and strategy, industrial clustering and state-business-academia relations, and scientific and technical human capital policies.

Policy landscape: Today, semiconductors are the leading exports for these two political economies. Both their industries started at a more or less similar footing, tracing their origins as assembly, testing, and packaging (ATP) hubs back to the late 1960s. Their paths have since diverged: Taiwan was able to build a fully integrated ecosystem that spans design, fabrication, and advanced packaging and testing, while the Philippines remains largely confined to low-value ATP with no domestic fabrication capacity to date. 

Methods: The study compares Taiwan and the Philippines as cases that shared a relatively similar starting point in labor-intensive ATP in the late 1960s but diverged in outcomes. We examine the policies and institutional arrangements each deployed, particularly during the critical period from the 1970s to the 1990s, when the foundations of their respective industries were laid. 

Findings: Taiwan's ascent to global leadership in semiconductor manufacturing was neither haphazard nor simply the outcome of unfettered market forces, but the result of industrial vision combined with strategic orchestration of public R&D (most notably ITRI), industrial clustering in the Hsinchu Science Park, and an educational system tailored to the industry's needs — a purposeful symbiosis of the state, academia, and industry that produced a self-reinforcing ecosystem conducive to industrial upgrading. The Philippines' experience, by contrast, underscores the consequences of fragmented governance, risk-averse public R&D, and an educational system insufficiently oriented towards industrial priorities. 

Policy recommendations: We propose that developing countries (1) rethink the mandate of public R&D institutions to allow calculated risk-taking and a tolerance for failure; (2) have the state co-invest with the private sector in capital-intensive, strategically important segments of the value chain, socializing not only the risks but also the rewards of public investment; (3) strengthen governance arrangements and expert advisory platforms to overcome information asymmetry and coordination failures; (4) place equal emphasis on building firms' absorptive capacities along with frontier R&D; (5) anchor human capital development explicitly in industrial strategy, including TVET reform and the mobilization of diaspora professionals through "brain circulation"; (6) pursue industrial clustering as a deliberate and coordinated strategy rather than a passive by-product of investment promotion; and (7) strategically leverage the evolving geopolitical landscape to extract developmental concessions, such as technology transfer.

Conclusion: For the Philippines and similarly situated economies in the Global South, moving up the technological ladder will require a more proactive approach to industrial policy, institutional reconfiguration, and a fundamental rethinking of how development is understood and pursued.

title: DraftFM: A Foundation Model for Day-Zero Drafting in Magic: The Gathering

detail.title: DraftFM: A Foundation Model for Day-Zero Drafting in Magic: The Gathering
detail.abstract: Drafting a new Magic: The Gathering expansion begins before any pick from it has been observed: the complete card list is public, but the draft logs that supervised pick models train on do not yet exist. We study this day-zero regime directly. DraftFM is a discrete-choice policy that scores exactly the cards available in the current pack, conditioned on the drafted pool and the state of the draft. Every card enters as a frozen 775-dimensional function of its public card record, structured features and a fixed text embedding, with no card identities, set identities, or usage statistics anywhere in the model, so an unseen card is scored by the same machinery as a familiar one. A 1.6-million-parameter network fitted on 149 million human picks from 29 expansions predicts held-out picks in three expansions withheld in their entirety, reaching 50.8%, 60.4%, and 56.7% top-1 agreement, where uniform chance at the opening pick is about 7%. Refitted on all 32 observed expansions, the same architecture produced a card ranking for the then-unreleased set The Hobbit, sealed with its complete cryptographic provenance and published roughly 36 hours before the set became draftable on MTG Arena. The sealed ranking agrees with six independent expert reviewers roughly as much as those reviewers agree with one another. Evaluation against realized outcomes is committed to a follow-on note, whatever it shows.

title: Constitutional AI: Cognitive Infrastructure as a National Imperative Rebuilding Literacy, Executive Function, Workforce Capacity, and Civic Stability in an AI-augmented Nation

detail.title: Constitutional AI: Cognitive Infrastructure as a National Imperative Rebuilding Literacy, Executive Function, Workforce Capacity, and Civic Stability in an AI-augmented Nation

declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
The United States faces a converging structural crisis: collapsing functional literacy, declining executive function, and a widening workforce divide that legacy educational systems cannot address at scale. Millions of Americans cannot read fluently, regulate attention, or navigate the cognitive demands of an AI-augmented economy. Traditional remediation frameworks — schools, workforce programs, and community institutions — are structurally incapable of meeting the scale, severity, and complexity of the crisis.

This paper proposes AI-augmented tutoring as cognitive infrastructure: a coordinated national intervention that delivers individualized, adaptive, and infinitely scalable remediation to structurally excluded learners. Drawing on cognitive science, human-computer interaction, AI governance, and constitutional theory, the paper designs the federal policy architecture required for deployment — national standards, state integration hubs, institutional nodes, home-based access, privacy safeguards, bias-mitigation protocols, and continuous improvement loops.

Economic modeling demonstrates that cognitive reconstruction expands labor-force participation, increases regional productivity, and reduces public dependency. Civic modeling shows that strengthened literacy and executive function improve deliberative participation, institutional navigation, crisis resilience, and democratic accountability. The paper argues that rebuilding foundational cognitive capacity is not an educational aspiration but a national imperative — and that AI-augmented tutoring, deployed as public-utility-scale infrastructure, is the only intervention capable of meeting the challenge.

Cognitive infrastructure becomes civic infrastructure. AI-augmented tutoring is not the future of education; it is the future of national stability.

title: Reproducible Intelligence: A New Class of Economic Assets and the Emergence of the Agentic Economy
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Reproducible Intelligence: A New Class of Economic Assets and the Emergence of the Agentic Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is shifting the technological frontier from digital information flows to artificial intelligence (AI) systems that perform a growing share of intellectual work. Human expertise remains a rival and often critical resource in judgement and decision-making. However, AI, once trained, is reproducible: a cognitive capability that can be deployed repeatedly without a proportional increase in experts. This paper introduces reproducible intelligence as a distinct class of productive assets, reducible neither to human capital nor to freely available nonrival ideas. Its defining operation is replication rather than transferan event that ownership-based accounting cannot record but provenance-based ledgers can. The boundary between human and artificial input is elastic. This elasticity is measurable: a task-cost model shows how the relative effective price of the two inputs and the ease with which they replace each other determine the organisation of work that minimises cost up to near-complete substitution. Where responsibility cannot be delegated, the constraint acquires a price expressed in the units of the cost of production. As the boundary moves, an agentic economy takes shape. Accounting and organisational design standards will need to accommodate replication-based assets before the underlying technology matures.

title: Jurisdiction's Approval Confusion on the Adoption of IFRS S1 and S2 by Malawi's Listed Companies
affiliations: Blantyre International University - Accounting and Finance Department

detail.title: Jurisdiction's Approval Confusion on the Adoption of IFRS S1 and S2 by Malawi's Listed Companies
detail.abstract: Adoption of IFRS S1 and S2 became mandatory on 1st January 2024 and yet only 33 percent of Malawi's listed companies disclosed to have adopted the said new sustainability standards and purported no significant impact on the financial statements without producing the required reports as per the International Sustainability Standards Board. The board of directors of those listed companies which did not adopt IFRS S1 and S2 expressed ignorance and pushed the issue to the external auditors who incorrectly stated that prior approval was required as a jurisdictional matter. Some listed companies produced ESG and Sustainability Reports which to lesser extent mitigate the problem. Remedial actions are needed now.

title: What If AI Learns How You Generate the New? - A Preliminary Discussion of the Normalisation and Political Economy of Generativity

detail.title: What If AI Learns How You Generate the New? - A Preliminary Discussion of the Normalisation and Political Economy of Generativity
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems have been developed for the most part on accumulated human artefacts. Systems that learn from recorded practice take a different object, since a demonstration, a workflow, a tool-use history, or a sequence of decisions records the course of an activity in place of its product. This paper asks what follows for political economy when the activity so recorded is one through which new possibilities are generated, and it develops the question through the case of research practice, where the question under investigation is itself frequently produced during the enquiry. The argument proceeds in five movements. It distinguishes four levels at which a generative practice admits description, namely outcome, representation, trajectory, and generativity, and holds these levels to be distinct, so that a record of a practice stands to the practice as a proxy stands to what it proxies. It treats the case in which a system maintains a representation of a particular other party and adjusts its operation with respect to that representation, and identifies the coupling so formed as an object lying outside that partition and held by whichever party operates the infrastructure sustaining it. It sets out a stage structure through which a situated practice becomes a portable capability: access, capture, legibility, abstraction, transfer, automation, valorisation, and enclosure. It describes the normalisation through which generative capacity comes to be treated as an ordinary economic input, and establishes a condition on any instrument whose application is triggered by a quantity of generativity. It then reads intellectual property doctrine as a diagnostic, holding that positive law has protected generative capacity through the inseparability of such a capacity from its holder, and that recording weakens the condition on which that protection rested. The normative proposal is stated as a constraint over each relation an arrangement touches, and it withholds any regime. Where generativity is relational, its protection runs through the construction and maintenance of domains affording occasions for its exercise, and the conversion of generativity into a further form of property would reproduce the ontology this paper questions.

title: Training by Travel: Medical Education for OB/GYN Residents after Dobbs

detail.title: Training by Travel: Medical Education for OB/GYN Residents after Dobbs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
After Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, the United States Supreme Court decision that overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, OB/GYN residents' access to abortion training, which is required in all accredited programs, has come under pressure. To receive the foundational training doctors in the field need, many residents in ban states travel to out-of-state programs where abortion is legal. But demand is high, travel for multiple weeks is expensive, and the capacity to train at host sites is limited. 

Training by travel could have ripple effects for the quality of patient care. As the number of OB/GYNs continues to decrease, newly-trained providers will have different, and arguably diminished, skills in delivering not just elective but also medically necessary abortion care. And as exceptions for life and health become how legal, procedural terminations take place in one-third of the United States, there is no guarantee that the doctors in those states will feel comfortable providing that care. 

This article explores the residency training provided today, providers' and institutions' navigation of abortion bans, and what changes in residency programs might mean for patient care in the coming years. Part I surveys the landscape of abortion law after Dobbs; even the strictest bans contemplate instances when abortion is medically required and legally permitted. Part II summarizes the pre-and post-Dobbs expectations for abortion training for OB/GYN residents, describing how graduate medical education has changed for residents in ban states. Part III assesses shorter and longer-term effects of a system that relies on travel and simulation (the use of models) or is out of compliance with national accreditation standards. Part IV concludes with potential paths forward that depend on state and national organizations supporting and funding the networks of health care professionals that facilitate training across the country.

title: Some Lessons from Korea's Experience with Digital Platforms Competition Regulation

detail.title: Some Lessons from Korea's Experience with Digital Platforms Competition Regulation
detail.abstract:
This is a manuscript prepared for the author's presentation at the second panel of the pre-ASCOLA conference, 'The Future of Digital Platforms Competition Regulation: A Global Comparative Perspective' (London, June 2026). 
Through the lens of sociological institutionalism, it reviews Korea's repeated attempts to introduce digital platform competition regulation and their failures from 2020 to 2024. Based on this review, the author draws a broader implication from Korea's experience of failure as follows: when a jurisdiction introduces ex ante competition regulation that goes beyond the traditional ex post enforcement regime, the key question is not only 'what' the substantive rules should be; equally important, or even more important, is 'how' those legal and policy measures are pursued. 
Also, an epilogue briefly reviews Korea's more recent developments in digital markets and AI, welcoming that Korea now appears to be taking a more context-sensitive and cautious approach, relying more actively on its existing competition law toolkit and managing domestic actor interactions and meaning-making processes more carefully than before.

title: Building Socially Conscious Readers: Applying Paulo Freire's Critical Pedagogy in English Literature Pedagogy at Colleges

detail.title: Building Socially Conscious Readers: Applying Paulo Freire's Critical Pedagogy in English Literature Pedagogy at Colleges
detail.abstract: This paper examines the revolutionary potential of Paulo Freire's critical pedagogy to develop socially conscious readers and ignite critical awareness in the unique ecosystem of rural colleges. Situated at the intersection of critical educational theory and literary studies, this qualitative study goes beyond the application of theory to a deeper exploration of the mediating effects of dialogical engagement, problem-posing education, and conscientization on students' engagement with complex literary texts. The study, utilizing triangulation of methods including extensive classroom observations, in-depth focus group discussions and detailed textual analysis of student work, suggests a dialectical relationship between pedagogical practice and the rural milieu. The findings suggest that rural colleges, which are often seen negatively because of infrastructural constraints, are fertile grounds for dialogic 2 and emancipatory learning that speak to Freirean principles. This environment promotes not only better understanding, but the development of critical thinking, cultural affirmation, social consciousness, and most importantly the critical consciousness necessary for students to become socially conscious readers and active citizens. When the teachers and students are co-investigators engaged in literary meaning making and social critique, the 'constraints' of the rural environment can be interpreted as specific pedagogical resources.

title:
Regimes, Not Forecasts 
Reassessing Dynamic Nelson-Siegel Term Structure Forecasting, and a Proposed Descriptive Alternative

detail.title:
Regimes, Not Forecasts 
Reassessing Dynamic Nelson-Siegel Term Structure Forecasting, and a Proposed Descriptive Alternative

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have no conflicts to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: I received no funding specific to this project.

detail.abstract: Diebold and Li (2006) showed that a simple autoregressive model of the Nelson-Siegel yield curve factors produces genuinely useful 12-month-ahead forecasts. Replicated on an extended U.S. Treasury sample running through 2026-roughly 26 years beyond their original 1985-2000 window-that result does not hold: the model loses to a naive random-walk forecast on every tenor tested, under both expanding and rolling estimation windows, with degradation frequently exceeding 10%. The mechanism is identifiable and consistent with independent structural work: the zero-lower-bound period introduced a materially different factor dynamic that the forecasting specification could not accommodate. Rather than treat this as a dead end, this paper develops and formally tests an alternative: a small number of recurring, economically interpretable curveshape states-fewer in number than they first appear, once rate level and curve shape are properly separated. Seven falsifiable hypotheses are tested: bootstrap cluster stability, permutation-tested temporal persistence, chi-square correspondence with Fed policy phase and NBER recession dating (with effect sizes reported), a formally BIC-gated comparison showing a unified hidden Markov model outperforms static clustering (robust to leave-one-episode-out testing), and surrogate-tested spectral hypotheses returning informative negative results. Three analytical errors identified and corrected during testing are reported explicitly. The resulting framework is deliberately descriptive rather than predictive, and is extended into an operational monthly monitoring tool built on causal (filtering-based) inference rather than retrospective smoothing. The paper's central claim is narrower than a forecasting model would be: the curve's useful information may lie in its current state rather than its future trajectory.

title: Beyond rescEU: From Disaster Assistance to Collective Environmental Security — A European Environmental Emergency and Ecological Recovery Corps for Compound Wildfire, Drought and Chemical Crises

detail.title: Beyond rescEU: From Disaster Assistance to Collective Environmental Security — A European Environmental Emergency and Ecological Recovery Corps for Compound Wildfire, Drought and Chemical Crises

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This policy perspective did not involve human participants, personal data, animals, or clinical research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Europe already possesses a substantial civil-protection architecture. The Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), its 24/7 Emergency Response Coordination Centre (ERCC), the European Civil Protection Pool, rescEU reserves, Copernicus services, the Seveso industrial-safety regime and specialist agencies together provide a strong basis for solidarity. The European Commission’s 2026 integrated wildfire strategy further connects prevention, preparedness, response and recovery. The policy problem is therefore not the absence of European action. It is the absence of a single operational chain that is permanently prepared to connect anticipatory environmental intelligence, risk-based pre-positioning, multi-hazard field response, mobile environmental science, pollution containment, biodiversity triage and multi-year ecological recovery when several countries face related crises at the same time.

I propose a European Environmental Emergency and Ecological Recovery Corps (EEERC), established as a civilian operational pillar within a strengthened UCPM and the proposed EU Crisis Coordination Hub. The Corps would combine a small EU-commissioned strategic core with certified national and regional modules. Its mandate would cover compound wildfire–drought emergencies, wildfire impacts on hazardous installations, major inland chemical pollution, critical water and soil contamination, ecological stabilisation and recovery monitoring. Objective risk thresholds would trigger readiness and pre-positioning, while deployment would remain subject to the affected state’s consent. In short: automatic readiness, not automatic entry.

The proposal is informed by current European and North American evidence and by more than fifteen years of my field experience in protected-area management, dryland restoration, industrial pollution control and environmental governance. Those professional experiences are used transparently as a source of design principles, not as a substitute for Europe-specific evaluation. The Corps would reinforce, rather than duplicate, existing institutions. Its added value would be continuity across the full crisis cycle, surge capacity during simultaneous events, common operational standards and public accountability for ecological outcomes. A phased 2027–2030 implementation pathway is presented, with measurable indicators for readiness, response, containment, equity and recovery.

AI disclosure: Generative AI assisted with research support, drafting, language editing, structure and formatting. The author supplied the original policy concept and field experience, reviewed the manuscript, and accepts full responsibility for the final content.

title: How Not to Tabulate the 2028 US Democratic Primary
affiliations: Université Paris-Saclay, Université Paris Cité, ENS Paris-Saclay, CNRS, SSA, INSERM, Centre Borelli, F-91190, Gif-sur-Yvette, France

detail.title: How Not to Tabulate the 2028 US Democratic Primary
detail.abstract: The US Democratic Party introduced a novel electoral system in 2020, combining instant runoff voting (IRV) and proportional representation (PR) with a 15% viability threshold. This tabulation system was chosen over more established methods, such as single transferable vote (STV), as a way to incorporate ranked-choice ballots into a PR system with a 15% viability threshold, which is deeply embedded in the party's rules. Ahead of the 2028 presidential nomination process, party leaders have expressed a desire to expand the IRV+PR system. However, the system has received little attention from the mathematics and public choice communities. We introduce new optimal transport metrics to measure the misalignment between the ensemble of ballots cast and the distribution of delegates awarded. These metrics have the advantage of separating the alignment measure from the tabulation process and from treating all ballots uniformly. These metrics do not restrict their attention to the match between individual ballots and the candidates whose tallies they increment during tabulation; rather, they treat each cast ballot as an equal amount of probability mass to be transported optimally (not via tabulation) to the delegate distribution. We compare eight alternative tabulation schemes, including the "fair reflection" winner: a loss-minimizing tabulation per an optimal transport cost (which, while NP-hard to tabulate in general, can be calculated for many elections). We find that this IRV+PR tabulation scheme fails to improve overall delegate alignment with voter preferences in simulated delegate-allocation elections using real cast ballot records of US rankedchoice voting elections. (By contrast, eliminating the viability threshold enables traditional PR-which examines only the first preference on the ballot-to approach the OT-optimal allocation of ranked-choice ballots in these simulated election.) Moreover, the use of ranked-choice ballots introduces paradoxical outcomes, such as the no-show paradox and generalized non-leader outcomes (candidate A wins strictly more delegates than B while most ballots rank B above A). In fact, using the cast-ballot record for the 2022 special election for Alaska's US House seat to simulate a presidential primary, we find that the OT-optimal tabulation-which 15% viability PR and IRV+PR attain-the Condorcet loser wins more delegates than the Condorcet winner. The IRV+PR system is more susceptible to paradoxical outcomes than alternative tabulation systems. Thus, we recommend that the DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee discourage the use of this novel tabulation scheme. If the desire to incorporate ranked-choice ballots for this delegate-allocation task persists, we recommend the use of STV using large statewide delegate pools (or 0% viability threshold PR that ignores the ranked choices expressed, although it is free of those paradoxes only when voters select one candidate) and further mathematical, legal, and logistical study of a mixed-integer program to minimize the optimal transport misalignment cost and interpretable heuristic approximations thereof. We also recommend the party cease awarding delegates by candidate performance within a district and weighting the totals by the strength of the Democratic ticket in past elections. Such an approach violates "one person one vote," masks the signal voters express with quantization noise, and-in the wake of Callais-dilutes minority representation, without advancing the aims of McGovern-Fraser. The signal-to-quantization-noise ratio increases with the square of the pool size; for each tabulation method, awarding all of a state's delegates based on the statewide vote totals for each candidate improves the optimal transport cost.

title: Barriers to Effective MSP Implementation: Evidence from Farmers in Punjab

detail.title: Barriers to Effective MSP Implementation: Evidence from Farmers in Punjab

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there is no conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research reported in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles applicable to research involving human participants. Informed consent was obtained from all participants before data collection. Participants were informed about the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of their participation, and the confidentiality of the information provided.

detail.abstract:
This study was conducted to identify the problems and constraints faced by farmers in Punjab
in the operation of the Minimum Support Price (MSP) scheme, particularly for the principal
crops. The four major crops—wheat, moong, rapeseed & mustard, and cotton were selected
to represent the crop groups of cereals, pulses, oilseeds, and commercial crops. Crop
selection was based on the highest triennial average gross cropped area within each crop
group. A multistage random sampling technique was used to select districts, tehsils, and
villages. A total of 320 farmers (80 per crop) were randomly selected, and the required data
were collected using a pretested interview schedule.
Garrett’s ranking technique was used to analyse the barriers faced by farmers in the MSP
scheme. Eight major barriers were identified, including a lack of awareness about MSP and
market information, a lack of remunerative prices, delays in procurement, delays in payment,
exploitative middlemen, transportation problems, inadequate institutional facilities, and the
absence of grievance redressal mechanisms. Among these, the lack of institutional capacity to
deliver market services, the lack of remunerative prices, and limited awareness of MSP and
market information emerged as the most significant barriers. The results further revealed that
the the lack of institutional capacity to deliver market services was the most prominent barrier
for moong and rapeseed-mustard growers. In contrast, cotton growers reported a lack of
remunerative prices as the major issue, while wheat growers identified a lack of awareness
about MSP and market information as the primary barrier affecting the effectiveness of the
MSP scheme.

title:
Buying Security in Orbit: National Security Space Procurement in the United States and the European Union
A Comparative Analysis, with Italy as the Principal European Illustration
affiliations: LUISS "G. Carli", Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title:
Buying Security in Orbit: National Security Space Procurement in the United States and the European Union
A Comparative Analysis, with Italy as the Principal European Illustration

contentType.other: first draft of a new research paper

detail.abstract: This article compares how the United States and the European Union acquire national security space capabilities, and asks why instruments that succeed in the American system so often disappoint when European policymakers import them. We argue that procurement instruments are downstream of the commercial base, and that the four principal instruments stand in different relations to it. A commercial reserve and competitive procurement presuppose a supplier population. Equity and lending operate without one. Anchor tenancy is the only instrument that creates one, which is why it must come first in any sequence. We then locate the European constraint more precisely than the literature usually does. Europe does not lack space ventures, and its startups are, if anything, more specialised in the new space economy than their American counterparts. What Europe lacks is the growth capital that carries a firm to industrial scale, to the point that no European private investor led a single European scale-up round in 2025. The prescription that follows is public anchor demand paired with a capital instrument, not demand alone. European law constrains the most aggressive ownership route, the special share carrying control disproportionate to the holding, although recent French practice shows that ordinary equity combined with a long-term public purchase commitment achieves much of the same end lawfully. Italy, whose Earth observation programme entered its operational phase on 1 July 2026, offers the clearest available test of whether public demand can manufacture a commercial base.
