detail.abstract: Self-medication is known to have potential harmful consequences. In times of a health shock, like the COVID-19 pandemic, preventive drug intake may imply irresponsible behaviour. To provide insight into this phenomenon, this study explores the preventive behaviour of 4,642 respondents of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) for the period 2020-2022 and 15 European countries. It aims at highlighting relevant drivers and relies on an econometric analysis backed by random-effects panel logistic as well as pooled logistic estimators. The results indicate that being female, more educated, with income, in worse health, or out of work due to COVID-19 relates to higher odds of using preventive drugs for COVID-19 disease. Interaction effects illustrate that those who report symptoms are additionally more likely to take preventive drugs when in poor health, with income, or having hardly any difficulties with making ends meet. Surprisingly, preventive drug intake when reporting symptoms decreases at older ages. No relevant impact is found for relationship status, financial distress, and country of citizenship. Overall, the study identifies important drivers of preventive drug intake informative for policymaking in the context of a health shock like COVID-19.

title: The Impact of Marriage and Cohabitation on Financial Distress: Evidence from SHARE 2015 to 2022 for 16 European Countries

detail.title: The Impact of Marriage and Cohabitation on Financial Distress: Evidence from SHARE 2015 to 2022 for 16 European Countries
detail.abstract: In this article, the relevance of the known economic benefits of marriage and cohabitation is reconfirmed. Based on data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) of the period 2015 to 2022 and 16 European countries, the severity of financial distress is explained by relational, health, financial, as well as general characteristics. The study reveals that singles are less likely to report greater easiness to make financial ends meet. Furthermore, income and employment appear to enable overcoming financial distress, while liabilities and reduced health facilitate financial distress. From all countries, primarily Danes report greater easiness to make ends meet. Econometrically, the study relies on ordered and non-ordered, panel and non-panel logistic estimators, which integrate, if possible, calibrated longitudinal weights. Overall, the study illustrates that partnership relieves financial distress and that the relationship stability does matter.

title: The Mortality Cost of withdrawing Prostate Cancer Screening
affiliations: Montclair State University

detail.title: The Mortality Cost of withdrawing Prostate Cancer Screening

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: In 2012 the US Preventive Services Task Force recommended against prostate-specific antigen screening, judging that testing causes more harms than benefits. Testing fell by a fifth and never recovered. I estimate the recommendation's effect on prostate cancer mortality, comparing the US against other countries and prostate cancer against other cancers. A steady decline in prostate cancer mortality since 1999 ended after the recommendation, and the mix shifted to a higher fraction of metastatic cases. The rise in mortality becomes statistically detectable four years after the recommendation and has since worsened, reaching 34% excess mortality in 2024. The recommendation's benefits (avoided overtreatment and subsequent complications) were realized immediately, while the excess deaths took several years to surface. So, early studies of the recommendation measured the benefits against an incomplete accounting of the costs.

title: The Influence of Health, Marriage and Cohabitation on Physical Inactivity: Evidence from SHARE for 12 European Countries

detail.title: The Influence of Health, Marriage and Cohabitation on Physical Inactivity: Evidence from SHARE for 12 European Countries
detail.abstract: Physical inactivity is a potential cost driver for health insurance as it may trigger undesirable health effects. In this study, the influence of health, marriage and cohabitation on physical inactivity is explored by means of fixedeffects logistic panel, random-effects logistic panel, and pooled logistic estimators. All three rely on data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) of 42,379 respondents aged 50 to 89 years old in 2015 from 12 European countries for the period 2015 to 2022. The analysis supports the positive influence of education and partnership on physical inactivity, as well as the negative one of ageing, illness, unemployment, limitations, and depression. In particular for partnership, the potentially positive influence on physical inactivity of being back single when higher depressed is surprising. Additionally, employed respondents relate to higher odds of reporting physical inactivity relative to retired respondents, suggesting that physical labour may be limited in their jobs. Lastly, Swedes, Danes, and Swiss relate to the lowest physical inactivity levels, and Italians to the highest. In conclusion, this study supports the importance of health and partnership for physical inactivity.

title: Learned Developer Agents for Emergent Urban Form: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Bottom-Up Land-Use Simulation

detail.title: Learned Developer Agents for Emergent Urban Form: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Bottom-Up Land-Use Simulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The antecedent land-use simulation described in Section 3, including its economic rule sets, land-value dynamics, building catalogue and physical testing, was developed as a Design Research Laboratory thesis at the Architectural Association School of Architecture, 2023–24, in Studio Bhooshan, by the author together with Ashwin Rajendran and Sidharth Tayal. The framework specified in Sections 4 to 7 is the sole work of the present author.

detail.abstract: Rule-based urban simulations encode developer behaviour as fixed scripts, producing morphologies that reflect the modeller's assumptions rather than testing them. This paper proposes a reinforcement learning framework in which development strategy is learned rather than specified, and argues that the resulting agents function as a diagnostic instrument on the rule set itself. The framework is developed against an existing multiplayer land-use simulation, previously constructed by the author and collaborators, in which a communal player finances infrastructure while multiple independent developers acquire parcels and construct mixed-use buildings under a shared economic loop of construction cost, maintenance, rental yield and tax transfer, with land value responding dynamically to cumulative built area and population. The paper specifies the components required to replace scripted behaviour with learned policy: state representation capturing parcel value, adjacency and revenue position; an action space spanning acquisition, construction typology and abstention; and a reward structure derived from the existing economic accounting rather than imposed externally. It sets out what convergence would demonstrate-that the encoded economy is sufficient to generate observed patterns of mixed-use density without behavioural scripting and what characteristic failure modes, including speculative parcel hoarding and premature infrastructure dependence, would reveal about the rule set's omissions. The paper concludes by examining the trade-off learned agents introduce, arguing that gains in behavioural realism come at measurable cost to the legibility on which participatory applications of simulation depend.

title: The WIPO Genetic Resources and TK Treaty: Disrupting the Power Imbalance in International Intellectual Property

detail.title: The WIPO Genetic Resources and TK Treaty: Disrupting the Power Imbalance in International Intellectual Property
detail.abstract: The 2024 WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge (GRATK) is a major milestone in interfacing traditional knowledge with intellectual property. It is the first major Development Agenda-inspired treaty, marking a symbolic shift in the historic trajectory of intellectual property treaty-making, hitherto dominated by the world's industrialized countries. This article situates the GRATK Treaty within the chequered regime complex in which traditional knowledge has been buffeted by the globalization of Eurocentric intellectual property. It spotlights the iconoclastic nature of traditional knowledge in disrupting the conventional agenda-setting power blocs driving international intellectual property. It also highlights critical dynamics, including wild cards - unforeseen and circumstantial events - leadership, diplomatic horse-trading, and issue linkage that collectively contributed to making the Treaty happen against the odds. It concludes that modern intellectual property treaty-making may no longer, as a necessity, reflect simplistic binary alignment of interests. What appears to be the currency of the new order, as represented by the Treaty, is a combination of contingency, diplomatic sagacity, deftness in identifying issue-linkages, and pragmatism in respect of horse-trading or issue linkage bargaining in diplomacy.

title: Estimating Structural Breaks and Spatial Effects in Heterogeneous UK Housing Panels with Latent Multi-factors
affiliations: University of Leeds - Faculty of Business and

detail.title: Estimating Structural Breaks and Spatial Effects in Heterogeneous UK Housing Panels with Latent Multi-factors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: This study proposes a novel econometric method for estimation with multiple structural breaks in heterogeneous panel data models, accounting for latent multiple factor structure and spatial dependence. Utilising the CCEX-2SLS technique, our approach achieves consistent and asymptotically valid individual and mean group estimators, offering significant improvements over traditional methods. A key innovation is the method's flexibility in allowing for different cross-sectional breaks, in other words, individual-specific break points in panel data analysis, which is particularly important in contexts where shocks propagate unevenly across spatial units or with time delays. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate the strong finite-sample performance of our proposed method. Through an empirical application on the UK local housing market covering 345 local authority districts across regions, we demonstrate the method's practical relevance. The analysis reveals that major economic events, such as the 2008 financial crisis and the Help to Buy (HtB) schemes, had substantial and regionally differentiated impacts on house prices. Our results highlight the importance of accounting for spatial dependence and heterogeneous structural breaks in panel data analysis. This framework provides new insights for future research into dynamic processes, with potential extensions including formal testing for common versus different cross-sectional break structures.

title: The Price of Adjustment: VAT-driven Inflation and Its Incidence during Greece's Fiscal Consolidation, 2010-2024

detail.title: The Price of Adjustment: VAT-driven Inflation and Its Incidence during Greece's Fiscal Consolidation, 2010-2024

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this article. The author received no funding for this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethical approval is reuired as the Household Budget Survey microdata are public-use files obtained free of charge from the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT) through its standard application procedure for anonymised microdata
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no funding for this research.

detail.abstract: Greece delivered an unusually large share of its fiscal consolidation through valueadded taxation, raising the standard rate from 19 to 24 percent and reclassifying dozens of product categories between 2010 and 2016. This paper measures what that choice cost consumers through the price level, and who bore it. A legally verified statutory rate panel for 108 HICP items at monthly frequency underpins a distributed-lag event study that estimates pass-through: the baseline announcement-dated estimate for increases is 0.76 at two years, with anticipationinclusive and seasonality-adjusted variants bracketing the level; the single pre-2017 cut passed through at roughly a quarter, later cuts at about 0.7, a pattern consistent with an enforcement channel and with no comparable post-2017 increase in pooled EU cut-side pass-through. Aggregating through the estimated dynamic response path, the reforms enacted over 2010-2016 eventually raised the price level by roughly four to five percentage points, about three of which had arrived by the end of 2016; the 2019-2021 reversal returned most of its statutory relief. Household Budget Survey microdata then deliver both sides of the incidence question: basketprice incidence rises modestly with expenditure, because staple foods kept reduced rates, while the burden relative to net income falls steeply across income quintiles, because consumption-to-income ratios fall with income. The regressivity of a VATled consolidation operates through the consumption rate, not through differential basket inflation.

reference: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/iKIET/221; i-KIET Issues & Analysis, No. 221
title: Mind the (Wage) Gap: The Large Firm-SME Divide and Delayed Labor Market Entry for Young Adults in South Korea

detail.title: Mind the (Wage) Gap: The Large Firm-SME Divide and Delayed Labor Market Entry for Young Adults in South Korea

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/iKIET/221
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This study examines the relationship between South Korea’s dual labor market, the divide between large firms and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), and the increasingly delayed entry of young people into the labor market. As the working-age population shrinks and mismatch widens, the inefficient use of available labor has become a long-term social concern. Delayed entry into the workforce gives workers less time to accumulate skills and experience, eroding human capital and, in aggregate, the skill level of the entire workforce.

Drawing on recent administrative data, the analysis shows that large firms have steadily accounted for about 12 percent of all regular wage workers (excluding temporary workers and day laborers), while the SME share now sits around 39 percent. Although on aggregate, the ratio of average SME wages to average wages at large firms has improved over the past ten years, climbing from 0.43 in 2015 to 0.49 in 2024, in nominal terms the monthly wage gap grew from KRW 2.98 million to KRW 3.65 million3), so workers are likely to perceive the gap as having widened, rather than narrowed.

The labor market has also grown more rigid: workers are likely to stay in their current positions, entries and exits have declined, and moving from an SME to a large firm is almost unheard of; at most, just five to six percent of workers in their twenties (the most mobile cohort) do so. Empirical results indicate that the widening of the wage gap between large firms and SMEs is associated with delayed entry into workforce, and that the effect of the rigid, dual structure of the market on the supply of young adults’ labor supply carries a lag. Given the current wage gap, four-year university graduates are estimated to defer graduation by about one month, and labor market entry by about 3.6 months. Because the structure of the labor market appears to be a quasi-permanent feature of the Korean economy, this study argues for the introduction and continuous, permanent operation of support policies that raise the real wages of young SME workers through direct support to individuals, rather than to firms. The author argues that the permanence of such programs would incentivize long-term employing planning by both young workers and firms.

This paper was translated from the original Korean using the Claude Opus 5 large language model (max effort). The text was reviewed by an editor and the author prior to publication.

title: Main Methodological Approaches to Estimating the Economic Impact of Migration

detail.title: Main Methodological Approaches to Estimating the Economic Impact of Migration
detail.abstract: This study provides an overview of the main methodological approaches used to estimate the economic effects of migration on host countries. With particular attention to forced migration and developing-country contexts, it first discusses the principal channels through which migration may affect host economies and then reviews the empirical methods commonly employed to identify these effects. The analysis focuses on three major areas: labour market outcomes, economic growth, and fiscal balances. It discusses the use of ordinary least squares, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, spatial and skill-cell approaches, as well as structural models, highlighting the assumptions and identification challenges associated with each method. The study emphasizes that the estimated economic effects of migration depend strongly on migrant characteristics, host-country conditions, policy frameworks, the geographical and temporal level of analysis, and the empirical strategy adopted. Given these sources of heterogeneity and the potential for endogeneity and omitted-variable bias, no single empirical method is universally appropriate. The paper therefore stresses the importance of carefully selecting identification strategies and, where possible, using complementary methods to assess the robustness of estimated migration effects.

title: Markets Rewritten

detail.title: Markets Rewritten

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced or been perceived to influence this research. This thesis was conducted independently.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this research, as the study does not involve human participants, patient data, or personal data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Tokenisation promises to make illiquid assets liquid, broaden participation, and improve price discovery. Most of that promise is assessed against mature, institutionally deep Western markets. This thesis asks a narrower and, for India, more consequential question: what happens when tokenisation is introduced into a market that is large in aggregate but narrow in function, where liquidity clusters at the top of the equity market, the bond market is shallow, real estate trades through an informal “mandi” culture, and capital enters through a small number of custodial and institutional chokepoints.

Two original measures are developed to make this concrete: the Liquidity Concentration Index (LCI), which quantifies how unevenly trading activity is distributed across listed companies, and the Market Saturation Index (MSI), a composite of five valuation, ownership, and positioning indicators that tracks how close Indian markets sit to a historically estimated saturation ceiling. A Tokenisation Acceleration Model then estimates how much faster full-scale tokenisation would push the market toward that ceiling, finding a roughly 1.5x acceleration that compresses India's structural runway from about nine years to about six.

The thesis then examines four sectors, real estate, government bonds, private credit, and SME receivables, to show how tokenisation would expose sector-specific fragilities and argues that because these sectors are funded through a common, narrow layer of NBFC intermediaries, stress in any one of them can transmit to all of them at token speed rather than balance-sheet speed. It concludes that the central risk is not the technology itself but the unprepared environment it would enter, and proposes a fifteen-law “Clean Sheet” legal and institutional architecture under which tokenisation could be introduced without amplifying the fragilities identified.

title: Depthwise Feature-specific Transformer with Causal TCN Encoder for Multi-region Short-term Electricity Load Forecasting
affiliations: Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University and Wuhan University

detail.title: Depthwise Feature-specific Transformer with Causal TCN Encoder for Multi-region Short-term Electricity Load Forecasting
detail.abstract: Accurate short-term electricity load forecasting (STLF) supports generation scheduling, reserve management, and demand-side responses in modern power systems. Conventional transformer architectures apply a shared linear projection to all input features, conflating load history, thermal covariates, and cyclical encodings into a single representation and obscuring their distinct temporal characteristics. This study presents the FSE-TCN Transformer, a deterministic encoder-decoder model extending the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) through two contributions, a Feature-Specific Embedding (FSE) module that replaces the shared input projection with independent per-feature depthwise pathways and defers cross-feature interaction to a later gated stage, and a Causal Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) encoder that captures short-range structure through dilated causal convolutions. An optional Attention-based Context Pooling (ACP) mechanism adds a load-state conditioning vector, yielding no significant accuracy gain but reducing run-to-run variance in four of five grids. Evaluated on five grids spanning distinct geographical and climatic regimes across three continents, the model achieves symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (sMAPE) ranging from 1.48% to 2.65%, with R² exceeding 0.975 in every region. Furthermore, it outperforms iTransformer, TiDE, Autoformer, and PatchTST by up to 34%, 43%, 55%, and 79% in terms of sMAPE, respectively. Full-factorial ablation with Type-II ANOVA identified FSE (F = 94.06) and TCN (F = 8.48) as the dominant contributors. SHAP attribution showed Fourier and cyclical encodings driving the largest share of predictions, while wind speed produced the widest attribution spread across climate zones.

title: When Less is More: Pretrained Features Render Attention Redundant in Industrial Defect Classification
affiliations: Hebei University of Technology, Hebei University of Technology, 707 Hi-Tech Co.,Ltd,, Hebei University of Technology and Hebei University of Technology

detail.title: When Less is More: Pretrained Features Render Attention Redundant in Industrial Defect Classification
detail.abstract: A measurement framework is proposed for quantifying the independent contri-bution of attention mechanisms relative to pretrained features and multi-scalefusion in industrial defect classification. Controlled component ablation acrossthree architecturally diverse backbones (ResNet-50, ConvNeXt-Tiny, EfficientNet-B3) and three public datasets (RSW-C, NEU-DET, GC10-DET), using over 100training runs with five-seed uncertainty quantification, establishes a clear com-ponent importance hierarchy. Pretrained weights and multi-scale feature fusioneach account for substantial performance contributions, while the measured ef-fect of attention falls within statistical noise (|∆F1| < 0.003). Centered KernelAlignment, employed as a representational similarity measurement tool, yieldsscores exceeding 0.97, confirming that attention modules produce near-identicalrepresentations to non-attention counterparts. We propose EfficientFPN, a min-imal architecture without attention, and Scale-Class Routing, a 21-parameterlearned scale weighting that outperforms standard multi-scale concatenation.EfficientFPN achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer parameters thanattention-augmented alternatives, demonstrating that measurement-driven ar-chitecture evaluation enables simpler designs.

title: Version Migration as a Correlated Shock: Model Updates as an Unmanaged Risk Channel in LLM-Based Financial Systems
affiliations: Independent Researcher, USA. and

detail.title: Version Migration as a Correlated Shock: Model Updates as an Unmanaged Risk Channel in LLM-Based Financial Systems
detail.abstract: Financial institutions increasingly deploy large language models (LLMs) within credit and other decision-support workflows. However, vendor-driven model updates can alter behavior even when an institution holds its prompts, inputs, and downstream processes fixed. We quantify the decision instability associated with two prespecified model-version transitions: an Ope-nAI efficient-model update and a Google Gemini Flash update. Across both transitions, the experiment covers 100 companies, 12 analysis dates, and three replicates per version, producing 14,400 model calls. Identical inputs and matched per-cell seeds hold sampling conditions fixed, and within-version replicate disagreement provides an empirical noise floor. The primary endpoint is the excess cross-version flip rate above this floor. For the OpenAI migration, the cross-version disagreement rate exceeds the within-version noise floor by 11.2 percentage points (95% CI: 7.7-15.0); for the Gemini migration this excess is 38.1 percentage points (95% CI: 30.3-45.8). A prevalence-churn decomposition shows that the OpenAI update primarily reconsiders individual companies and shifts decisions toward greater severity, while the Gemini update produces a broad distributional shift toward the SAFE category. Neither migration shows clear improvement among observations whose labels change; the Gemini successor also shows lower aggregate class-balanced performance. Vendor version migration can therefore create material, directionally unpredictable decision discontinuities within otherwise unchanged LLM pipelines. We propose a pre-migration parallel-run control that measures excess flip rate, label-distribution shift, per-company churn, and directional drift before production cutover. The findings provide controlled evidence of deployment-level migration risk; broader cross-task and cross-institution effects remain for future study.

title: Diffusion Dynamics of Clean Technologies: Patterns, Drivers, and Policy Implications

detail.title: Diffusion Dynamics of Clean Technologies: Patterns, Drivers, and Policy Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the research outcomes.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved secondary data analysis from publicly available sources (IRENA, IEA, World Bank, BloombergNEF). Therefore, no human participants or case studies were included, and ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by H Heuristics Research, with analytical support from internal project resources. No external commercial or governmental funding was received.

detail.abstract: The global transition toward clean energy technologies represents one of the most consequential diffusion processes in modern economic history. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical analysis of clean technology diffusion across solar photovoltaic energy, wind power, electric vehicles, and associated low-carbon innovations, drawing on data from 2000 to 2024. We apply the theoretical frameworks of Rogers (1962), Bass (1969), and subsequent diffusion scholarship to identify the distinctive characteristics that shape clean technology adoption trajectories. Our analysis reveals four key findings. First, clean technologies exhibit S-curve adoption patterns consistent with classical diffusion theory, but with systematically accelerating diffusion speedssolar PV and lithium-ion batteries have diffused 2-3 times faster than earlier energy technology transitions. Second, learning-by-doing effects, captured through Wright's Law, demonstrate consistent cost reduction rates of 20-28% per doubling of cumulative deployment across major clean technologies. Third, policy instruments-particularly feed-in tariffs, renewable portfolio standards, and carbon pricing-function as powerful exogenous accelerants that shift the diffusion curve leftward by 8-15 years compared to market-only counterfactuals. Fourth, we identify a pronounced regional divergence in diffusion rates, with China and Europe leading adoption while developing economies face persistent barriers related to capital access, institutional capacity, and infrastructure lock-in. The paper contributes to the technology diffusion literature by developing an integrated analytical framework that synthesises demand-pull, technology-push, and policy-driven mechanisms into a unified model of clean technology adoption. We conclude with policy recommendations for accelerating diffusion in lagging regions and discuss implications for meeting Paris Agreement targets.

reference: Journal of Peacebuilding & Development. https://doi.org/10.1177/15423166251345046
title: Development for Peace in Colombia: Experiences with PDETs in El Carmen and Cartagena del Chairá
affiliations: University of Denver - Josef Korbel School of International Studies

detail.title: Development for Peace in Colombia: Experiences with PDETs in El Carmen and Cartagena del Chairá
detail.abstract: As part of the 2016 peace agreement with the FARC insurgent group, the Colombian government began implementation of its Programs for Development with a Territorial Focus (Programas de Desarrollo con Enfoque Territorial), or PDETs. What effect has this program had on sustainable peace, development, and confidence in state institutions? This article presents the results of a survey conducted in Colombia in July 2021 to shed light on some of the successes and challenges of the PDETs in the municipalities of El Carmen near the Venezuelan border in the department of Norte de Santander and Cartagena del Chairá in the southeastern department of Caquetá. These regions are routinely neglected by the Colombian state and suffer from ongoing conflict. Surveys indicate high resident participation in planning but less in the project implementation phase, with projects seen as more effective when community participation is combined with responsive municipal governments. While residents remain optimistic about the PDETs and expressed high confidence in the church and community organizations, they had less confidence in government actors and saw socio-political conditions as hindering program implementation.

title: Green ETF Returns across the Conditional Distribution: Tail Asymmetry, Low-Frequency Market Stress, and Dynamic Dependence

detail.title: Green ETF Returns across the Conditional Distribution: Tail Asymmetry, Low-Frequency Market Stress, and Dynamic Dependence
detail.abstract: We revisit return-distribution and volatility differences between a broad U.S. ESG ETF and the market, and between clean-and fossil-energy ETFs, using a fully reproducible daily sample from January 2017 through July 2026. The design separates two economically different spreads: ESGU minus SPY and ICLN minus XLE. Conditional quantile regressions show near-zero median spreads but substantial dispersion in both tails. Importantly, negative lower-tail estimates denote relative underperformance, not downside protection. A custom GARCH-MIDAS model with twelve strictly lagged monthly VIX observations yields positive long-run market-stress loadings for all four ETFs; all solutions are internal, although ICLN is comparatively ill-conditioned. Formal dynamic-correlation tests around 24 February 2022 show opposite shifts: ESGU-SPY dependence rises, whereas ICLN-XLE dependence falls. These findings reject a single, universal "green premium" narrative. Broad ESG tilting behaves differently from thematic clean-energy exposure, and conditional-distribution evidence cannot by itself identify an ESGpricing mechanism. The paper also documents how sign errors, unavailable ESG-score histories, and boundary solutions can generate misleading interpretations in small-sample sustainable-finance applications.

title: Utility Maximization with Consumption Inaction under Borrowing Constraints
affiliations: Kyung Hee University - Department of Applied Mathematics

detail.title: Utility Maximization with Consumption Inaction under Borrowing Constraints
detail.abstract: We study an infinite-horizon consumption-investment problem with costly upward and downward consumption adjustment, constant labor income, and a nonnegative-financial-wealth constraint. The consumption friction can be reinterpreted as intertemporal loss aversion: households dislike reversing prior consumption decisions, so past consumption acts as a reference point. Mathematically, the model is a two-dimensional state-constrained singular-control problem with two intervention directions and portfolio choice. A Legendre-Fenchel transform removes the portfolio nonlinearity but exposes three competing first-order restrictions: two consumption gradient constraints and a borrowing-induced contact condition that becomes an endogenous boundary of the effective dual domain. We solve the resulting free-boundary system under CRRA preferences. Verification is nonstandard: we construct an obliquely reflected two-dimensional dual diffusion on a nonsmooth endogenous domain, recover primal wealth from the dual derivative, and show that the borrowing regulator and the two consumption regulators vanish through distinct contact identities. Economically, the borrowing constraint shifts adjustment thresholds before it binds, replaces downward adjustment by the zero-wealth boundary at intermediate consumption, and truncates the low-wealth arm of the risky-share profile. In our calibration, stronger intertemporal loss aversion widens the zero-wealth inaction interval.

title: An Audited Contract Boundary for COS Caplet Pricing

detail.title: An Audited Contract Boundary for COS Caplet Pricing
detail.abstract:
We present a bounded verification case study for COS caplet pricing. The numerical component expands the payoff of a log-forward rate, pairs characteristic-function coefficient proxies with raw payoff integrals, and reproduces Black benchmark values in a lognormal special case. Ten Rust test functions pass. Three comparison tests cover five caplet cases, a ten-caplet semiannual cap, and four swaptions against Black/reference calculations; the remaining tests check narrower numerical properties.

The accompanying formal artifact contains 55 theorem declarations and 13 explicit inputs. A declaration-level audit classifies 7 results as substantive conditional algebra, 30 as arithmetic or definitional checks, 16 as imported aliases, and 2 as tautologies. The artifact replays successfully with zero sorry or admitted proof holes in those declarations, conditional on the 13 explicit inputs. It does not formalize the finite COS series, a model-specific characteristic function, exponential coefficient decay, Jamshidian decomposition, analytical differentiation, or the Rust implementation. We therefore make one main claim: the combined artifact provides a reproducible numerical benchmark and a manually audited boundary around selected machine-checked scalar consequences. This is smaller than a verified pricing engine, but it is precise, testable, and suitable as a foundation for stronger future formalization.

title: Corporate Governance Scandals in India's Banking and Financial Services Sector
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Faculty of Law and  National University of Singapore (NUS), Faculty of Law

detail.title: Corporate Governance Scandals in India's Banking and Financial Services Sector
detail.abstract:
In this chapter, we adopt a sector-specific approach to corporate scandals in one jurisdiction, namely India, to examine how corporate governance factors contributed to the scandals on the one hand and how the scandals have either resulted in governance reforms or merit further legal or regulatory transformations on the other. In doing so, we train our sights on the banking and financial services (BFS) in India.

 

After highlighting the specific attributes in governance for BFS companies, including in the Indian context, we outline our aims for the chapter and briefly set out its roadmap. We explore three research questions. First, we consider whether and how poor corporate governance norms and practices contributed to the BFS scandals in India over the last decade. This is essentially the contribution question. Second, we explore the reforms, if any, that were introduced to the laws and regulations relating to corporate governance in the aftermath of these scandals. This covers the reformation question. Finally, we deliberate on reforms that are still required to be carried out based on the learnings from these governance scandals in BFS companies: the normative question. In examining our research questions, while we focus on the governance scandals in BFS companies in India, we seek to make comparisons to international examples to the extent necessary.

 

We structure our chapter essentially along the lines of three broad contributive factors that have led to scandals in BFS companies in India, and highlight the reformative and normative factors relating to each of them. For each, we select one case study involving a recent governance scandal in a BFS company in India within the last decade. The YES Bank episode (2020) illustrates the risks of star-promoter control, excessive risk-taking and wealth tunnelling. The IndusInd Bank accounting scandal (2025) highlights the failure of internal and external gatekeepers, particularly the board and auditors. The IL&FS crisis (2018) demonstrates how regulatory fragmentation, regulatory arbitrage and inter-regulatory turf wars can contribute to systemic failure. Taken together, the cases demonstrate that these governance failures require more than piecemeal responses, calling instead for a wholesale reconsideration of the corporate governance framework applicable to BFS companies.

title: Economic Feasibility of Green Building Certification in India: A Payback Period and Life-Cycle Cost Analysis
affiliations: and

detail.title: Economic Feasibility of Green Building Certification in India: A Payback Period and Life-Cycle Cost Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it did not involve human participants, patients, animal subjects, or collection of personal data. The study was based on publicly available secondary data and published case studies.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: India's construction sector accounts for nearly one-third of national electricity consumption and a rapidly growing share of embodied carbon, making green building certification a policy priority under the National Mission on Sustainable Habitat. Despite the proliferation of rating systems such as the Indian Green Building Council (IGBC), Green Rating for Integrated Habitat Assessment (GRIHA), and Excellence in Design for Greater Efficiencies (EDGE), developers and institutional owners continue to cite uncertain economic returns as the principal barrier to adoption. This paper develops an integrated payback-period and life-cycle cost (LCC) framework calibrated to Indian construction economics, energy tariffs, and discount rates, and applies it to a comparative dataset spanning IGBC-, GRIHA-, and LEED-India-certified commercial, institutional, and residential buildings. Using a 25-year analysis horizon, net present value, savings-to-investment ratio (SIR), and discounted payback period are computed for representative building typologies across three Indian climatic zones (composite, hot-dry, warm-humid). Results indicate incremental capital costs of 3-8% for Silver/Gold-equivalent ratings and up to 15-20% for pioneering Platinum-level demonstration projects, with discounted payback periods ranging from 4 to 11 years depending on typology, tariff structure, and incentive availability. Sensitivity analysis shows that electricity tariff escalation and access to state-level fiscal incentives (additional floor area ratio, property tax rebates, expedited approvals) are the dominant determinants of financial feasibility. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for standardizing LCC disclosure in green building certification and for calibrating incentive design to occupancy-stage rather than construction-stage benefits.

title: The Effect of Mortgage Rates on Neighborhood Housing Costs
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and University of Virginia

detail.title: The Effect of Mortgage Rates on Neighborhood Housing Costs
detail.abstract: We estimate zip-level "housing cost sensitivities" (HCS)-the percent change in local home prices or rents per 1% increase in national home prices caused by Ben-David et al. (2024) mortgage-rate shocks. Using Zillow home-value and rent indices for over 13,000 zip codes, we find wide heterogeneity. Across the interquartile range, local home prices rise between 0.3% to 2.0%, while rents range from-1.5% to 1.1%. We find the HCS are strongly regressive: lower-income zips exhibit substantially larger responses for both prices and rents. Zip-level home-price HCS are highly correlated with the city-level inverse supply elasticity of Guren et al. (2021), yet meaningful unexplained variation remains. Beyond supply constraints, we find that demand amplification (natural amenities), land-cost pass-through, and housing-market liquidity all shape HCS. Our results quantify where mortgage-rate movements most strongly transmit into local housing costs and clarify the mechanisms underlying that heterogeneity.

title: Leaning Against Vulnerability, Cleaning After Stress: Monetary Policy and Financial Instability
affiliations: Korea University and Korea University

detail.title: Leaning Against Vulnerability, Cleaning After Stress: Monetary Policy and Financial Instability
detail.abstract: This paper examines how monetary policy internalizes financial stability considerations when macroprudential tools are institutionally constrained, and whether responses differ across distinct forms of financial instability. Using Korea as an empirical setting-where the Bank of Korea (BOK) controls the policy rate while macroprudential authority is institutionally separated-we construct meeting-level text-based measures of financial stability sentiment (BOK-FSS) from Monetary Policy Board (MPB) minutes and meeting-day news coverage (1999-2024). A fine-tuned Korean RoBERTa classifier distinguishes between financial stress and the build-up of vulnerabilities, capturing policymakers' perceived risks rather than observable financial conditions alone. We embed these indices in a GMM-estimated augmented Taylor rule and uncover a systematic asymmetry: the BOK eases in response to acute financial stress ("cleaning") but tightens in response to rising vulnerability sentiment ("leaning against the wind"). Exploiting the 2011 amendment to the Bank of Korea Act-which strengthened the financial stability mandate while leaving institutional separation intact-we show that the tightening response to vulnerability sentiment is statistically insignificant before 2011 but emerges as economically and statistically significant thereafter, while the easing response to stress remains broadly unchanged. These findings suggest that, when macroprudential tools are constrained, monetary policy increasingly acts as a partial substitute-internalizing vulnerability risks that prudential instruments cannot fully address. Text-augmented Taylor rules further improve out-of-sample prediction accuracy relative to standard rules, and the text-based measures retain significance after controlling for conventional financial indicators, indicating that policymakers' perceived risks contain policy-relevant information beyond observable financial conditions.

title: The Emerging Agentic AI Ecosystem : Towards an interdisciplinary understanding of misuse and migration

detail.title: The Emerging Agentic AI Ecosystem : Towards an interdisciplinary understanding of misuse and migration
detail.abstract: Agentic AI raises completely new challenges that are difficult to identify and measure. In this report, we propose a holistic framework to help identify and contextualise such emerging issues. This work aims to help a broad range of stakeholders comprehend the space and appreciate prevalent approaches to identifying and conceptualising these issues. We intend for our work to demonstrate the value of more holistic interdisciplinary approaches to opening up this discussion. This work conceptualises the scope and character of a range of emergent areas where Agentic AI might be misused to cause harm. Furthermore, we provide an initial conceptual approach to mapping and understanding emergent concerns in this issue area. We align this mapping exercise with the goals of more traditional approaches to systemic risk assessment, which have emerged since the early 2000's, as well as more recent multi-level approaches to socio-technical change. In this report, we have adopted ecological vulnerability as a central metaphor to shift our analytical focus away from classical risk frameworks that treat artificial intelligence hazards as discrete, external threats. Instead, our approach allows us to map the endogenous structural fragility of interconnected socio-technical systems. By viewing agentic misuse through an ecological lens, we can better illustrate how emergent micro-level capabilities do not act in isolation, but rather piggyback on legitimate meso-level infrastructure to generate cascading systemic shocks across the sector. Our initial work has involved the iterative development of this analytical framework through ongoing collaboration between an interdisciplinary research team, as well as early-stage open-source data collection and analysis-through a combination of human and LLM-enabled work. As a result, the framework we present here provides an emergent and demonstrable conceptual coherence and richness. Such concepts provide real utility by allowing the translation of unstructured observations, of a technical and political nature, into a more contextually informed analysis. This ecological approach renders complex socio-technical vulnerabilities legible to policymakers and non-technical stakeholders. It does not in itself evaluate or prioritise risks, but does provide a deeper, more open, and forward-looking framework upon which to identify, develop and evaluate technical and policy interventions. p.1

title: The Ghost In The Draft: Copyright Authorship And The Human Editor Of Llm Outputs: A Comparative Analysis
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Law School

detail.title: The Ghost In The Draft: Copyright Authorship And The Human Editor Of Llm Outputs: A Comparative Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted by Columbia Journal of Law & the Arts

publicationDetails.journalName: Vanderbilt University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Today, millions of humans write with big language models, modifying machine drafts into polished writing. How should we decide whether they own the outcome under copyright law? This Article contends that the question is not new: the law of collaborative writing has long defined when a contribution to a shared document becomes its maker an author of the whole. The Article presents a criterion of collaborative writing: the person who edits an LLM draft owns the final work when her editing displaces the machine’s expressive choices so fully that the work is the product of her authorial mind. The standard is operationalized by three diagnostic criteria: structural displacement, voice and expressive specificity. The Article draws on American joint authorship doctrine, the CJEU's originality case law thru Mio, and English and continental co-authorship traditions. It explains why the standard is doctrinally based on both sides of the Atlantic, and what is left, a thin copyright in the revisions, when the standard is not met. The Article also reverses the analysis and applies to a situation where a human draft is edited by the machine.

title: The Bitcoin Polar Pricing Model: Cycles, Prices, and Predictability
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Bitcoin Polar Pricing Model: Cycles, Prices, and Predictability
detail.abstract: We develop a Bitcoin Polar Pricing Model that transforms Bitcoin prices into polar coordinates to identify, price, and forecast cyclical dynamics. Rather than imposing the four-year halving cycle, we estimate it endogenously: three independent methods converge on 3.86 years, and Bitcoin sits closer to the 1,461-day halving benchmark than Ethereum or the S&P 500 placebos under every method. The model explains 94% of Bitcoin's log-price variation, with significant within-cycle Fourier structure. Apparent predictability rises with horizon, a pattern we interpret cautiously given known overlappingwindow biases. Collectively, the polar pricing model offers a legitimate, economically grounded framework for pricing Bitcoin.

title: A Cold Start: Labor-Market Entry and the Composition of Household Saving

detail.title: A Cold Start: Labor-Market Entry and the Composition of Household Saving
detail.abstract: Do labor-market conditions at school leaving shape how households allocate saving decades later? I link 4,120 women in Japan’s JPSC to job-openings ratios at predicted graduation. Better entry conditions raise regular first employment and raise the later share of saving designated for the spouses—most precisely for the wife—rather than for family-common, child, or other purposes; the wife–husband split is unchanged, and the husband’s conditions carry no detectable effect. Wife-designated flows predict growth in her individually held assets, though treatment effects on those stocks are not established. National-cohort estimates are stable in sign but sensitive to persistent-process inference; within-year prefecture variation is directionally consistent and imprecise.

detail.abstract:
Background: Cross-national thyroid-cancer incidence varies far more than mortality, but ecological associations with health-system capacity can reflect generic development, cancer-data quality or unmeasured confounding. We tested whether incidence–mortality decoupling shows a thyroid-specific diagnostic signature rather than a non-specific feature of national cancer statistics.

Methods: We analysed GLOBOCAN 2024 age-standardised incidence and mortality rates for thyroid cancer and seven comparator cancers in 186 countries and areas. The primary outcome was log incidence–mortality decoupling, ln[(incidence ASR+0.05)/(mortality ASR+0.05)]. Health expenditure per capita was the primary capacity indicator. Oesophageal, liver and pancreatic cancers were prespecified lethal negative-control outcomes. The thyroid-specific estimand subtracted each country's mean negative-control decoupling from thyroid decoupling. We used HC3-robust regression, 5,000 country bootstrap samples, permutation falsification, region fixed effects, alternative negative-control sets, capacity triangulation and residual capacity after nonlinear adjustment for Human Development Index (HDI). An exploratory longitudinal validation linked CI5plus incidence with WHO mortality and health expenditure for 2003–2017.

Results: The primary complete-case analysis included 176 countries. The health-capacity slope was 0.571 for thyroid-cancer decoupling and 0.050 on average for the three lethal controls. Their calibrated contrast was 0.522 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.442–0.600; permutation P<0.001). The estimate remained positive with region fixed effects (β=0.309, 95% CI 0.178–0.441) and across alternative controls and zero offsets. The thyroid signal arose from incidence (β=0.594) rather than mortality (β=0.023, 95% CI −0.057–0.102). UHC coverage and physician density produced concordant calibrated associations. However, capacity residualised on HDI and region was null (β=0.014, 95% CI -0.109–0.137). In 661 registry-year observations from 48 registries in 16 countries, the within-registry estimate was directionally positive but imprecise (β=0.292, 95% CI −0.189–0.772).

Interpretation: National diagnostic ecosystems show a cancer-specific incidence–mortality signature concentrated in thyroid and other detection-sensitive cancers. The pattern is difficult to explain as a uniform inflation of all cancer statistics, but its attenuation beyond HDI and imprecise longitudinal validation preclude an independent causal attribution to health expenditure. The findings support surveillance of diagnostic appropriateness, not a direct estimate of overdiagnosis prevention globally.

title: Where Americans Work Shapes Whether They Vote: Evidence From 30 Million U.S. Workers
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business, Harvard Kennedy School of Government,  and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Management

detail.title: Where Americans Work Shapes Whether They Vote: Evidence From 30 Million U.S. Workers
detail.abstract: Where you work affects whether you vote. Using linked employment and voter records for 30 million U.S. workers across 377K employers, we estimate "Employer Turnout Effects" (ETEs)-organization-specific effects on voter turnout derived from a movers design that accounts for worker self-selection. ETEs have a bias-corrected interquartile range of 5.6 percentage points, comparable to the largest single-contact interventions in the voter mobilization literature. When workers change jobs, their turnout shifts in the direction predicted by the new employer's ETE, with asymmetric effects suggesting that turnout gains may persist after subsequent job changes. ETEs vary across industries (accommodation and food service show the lowest; white-collar sectors the highest), though withinindustry variation far exceeds between-industry differences. Companies that publicly commit to providing time to vote have significantly higher ETEs. These findings identify the workplace as an overlooked but powerful lever for democratic participation.

title: Masculinity Around the World
affiliations: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, University of Melbourne,  and UNSW Business School, School of Economics

detail.title: Masculinity Around the World
detail.abstract: We examine how masculinity norms—the social expectations about how men should behave—predict economic, health, and political outcomes. We field the Global Masculinity Survey, covering 125,000 individuals across 70 countries, to measure adherence to core masculinity norms. Economically, men who adhere more strongly to these norms supply more labor, earn more, and sort into traditionally masculine occupations. However, they take greater health risks and report poorer mental health. Politically, they express stronger support for strongman authoritarianism and military rule. Adherence to masculinity norms is stronger among men exposed to war or economic recession during their impressionable years.

title: Private Credit's Private Conflicts
affiliations: and Washington and Lee University School of Law

detail.title: Private Credit's Private Conflicts
detail.abstract: Many of the largest alternative asset managers simultaneously operate private equity funds, private credit funds, direct lending vehicles, Business Development Companies, insurance subsidiaries, and affiliated financing platforms under common ownership and management structures. These overlapping arrangements increasingly blur traditional distinctions between lender, owner, sponsor, and fiduciary. In this Article, we examine the issues that arise when the lender and owner are the same firm, managed by the same people, answering to different investors, with dissimilar and often conflicting interests. We argue that the existing legal framework, built for a financial system in which lending and ownership were separate functions performed by separate institutions, was never designed to answer that question. The result is a growing category of conflicts that fall through the gaps between fiduciary duties, securities regulation, and contract law.

detail.abstract:
Background: Early-life adverse experiences have been associated with adverse reproductive and menopausal health outcomes, but their associations with premature or early natural menopause remain unclear. We examined whether sexual and physical abuse during childhood and adolescence were associated with these outcomes.

Methods: We included 63,252 premenopausal women in the Nurses’ Health Study II (1989–2021) who completed a violence victimization questionnaire and repeatedly reported menopause status. Multivariable Cox proportional-hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for natural menopause before ages 40 and 45 years. Mediation analyses assessed adulthood lifestyle and psychological factors.

Findings: Over 32 years, 207 premature and 1,644 early natural menopause cases were documented. Risks increased with greater severity and chronicity of sexual and physical abuse (p for trend=0.022 and 0.031, respectively). Compared with women without abuse, women exposed to severe-chronic or multiple types of abuse had HRs of 1.95 (95% CI 1.14–3.35) for premature natural menopause and 1.26 (95% CI 1.01–1.58) for early natural menopause. Smoking and depression explained 31.7% (95% CI 7.8–71.9%) and 13·8% (95% CI 2.8–46.6%), respectively, of the association with early natural menopause.I

nterpretation: Exposure to early-life sexual and physical abuse was associated with higher risks of premature and early natural menopause. Severe early-life abuse may indicate increased susceptibility to early cessation of ovarian function, with smoking and depression representing potentially modifiable pathways.

title: From Business Plan to Adoption Readiness: Trust, Intentions, and Feature Preferences for an AI-Enabled Local Booking Platform in Belfast (HnB Working Paper 2)

detail.abstract:
Independent hair and beauty businesses in the United Kingdom increasingly face pressure to improve digital discovery, reduce no-shows, and convert fragmented booking behaviour into more reliable appointment demand (Smith, 2022; Salons Direct, 2025). Building on the HnB platform concept introduced in Working Paper v1.0 (Pandey, 2026a), this paper examines the conditions under which customers and small providers in Belfast are likely to adopt an AI-enabled booking platform combining style try-on, transparent service discovery, and appointment management.

The paper shifts the emphasis from business planning to adoption analysis. It develops a focused theoretical frame around trust, perceived usefulness, perceived risk, and local social endorsement, while retaining the two-sided market context that makes HnB commercially and strategically distinct (Rochet and Tirole, 2003; Armstrong, 2006; Parker, Van Alstyne and Choudary, 2016). The analysis uses the Belfast survey evidence already collected for the project, with particular attention to customer openness to AI try-on, provider interest in digital booking tools, expected pricing norms, and the role of social proof and local endorsement in reducing adoption friction (Pandey, 2026a; Pandey, 2026b).

The paper argues that early adoption of HnB depends less on novelty than on trust, transparency, and immediate operational value. Customers appear willing to engage with AI try-on when it helps them visualise outcomes and reduce uncertainty, while providers are most responsive when the platform improves calendar control, reminders, visibility, and no-show management without imposing high upfront costs (Salons Direct, 2025; London Loves Business, 2025). The findings support a supply-side-first launch strategy and suggest that the most effective early product positioning is not as a generic booking tool, but as a local trust-building discovery and booking layer for Belfast’s independent personal service market (Moore, 2014; Bichler, 2025).

Working Paper v1.0 established the commercial feasibility, pricing model, and market entry strategy for HnB as a two-sided platform in Belfast, using the same provider and customer survey base (Pandey, 2026a). This second paper uses that evidence to examine whether early providers and customers are actually willing to adopt the platform, and which features and trust signals matter most at the point of decision. Together, the two papers move the project from a viable business plan on paper to an empirically grounded adoption and launch strategy for the Belfast beachhead (Pandey, 2026a; Pandey, 2026b).

This working paper has not undergone formal peer review and does not constitute financial, legal, or investment advice.

title: Real-World Cost-Effectiveness Evaluation of Intravitreal Conbercept Combined With Vitrectomy for Vitreous Hemorrhage from Diabetic Retinopathy: Evidence from Societal and Medical Insurance Perspectives

detail.abstract:
Background: Vitrectomy combined with anti-VEGF agents has been demonstrated an effective regimen for patients with vitreous hemorrhage from diabetic retinopathy, and a comparative cost-effectiveness evaluation of vitrectomy combined with intravitreal conbercept (IVC) before or during surgery compared to vitrectomy in real-world practice from both societal and medical insurance perspectives is necessary to support value-based clinical and reimbursement decisions.

Methods: The Markov model was constructed to simulate progression of vitreous hemorrhage from PDR over a 10-year horizon. Health states were defined based on best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) referred to observational study. Patients with vitreous hemorrhage from PDR received vitrectomy, vitrectomy combined with preoperative IVC (1~10days prior to vitrectomy), and vitrectomy combined with intraoperative IVC (at the end of completion of vitrectomy) from the Tianjin medical insurance system (2022–2024) were analyzed. Model inputs included real-world costs of therapy, intravitreal injection frequencies, drug prices, utility values, and transition probabilities derived from clinical trials. Costs of therapy, indirect costs and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) were calculated separately under both the societal and medical insurance perspectives. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were computed, with sensitivity analyses (one-way, two-way and probabilistic) conducted to assess result robustness.

Results: From both the societal and medical insurance perspectives, the Preoperative strategy (Strategy A) was more cost-effective than the Intraoperative strategy (Strategy B, used as the reference), with ICERs as 93,746.246 RMB/quality-adjusted life years (RMB/QALY) under the societal perspective and 98,510.985 RMB/QALY under the medical insurance perspective, respectively. In contrast, the No Medication strategy (Strategy C) was less cost-effective than Strategy B, with ICERs as -2,097,038.917 RMB/QALY under the societal perspective and -2,041,873.934 RMB/QALY under the medical insurance perspective, respectively. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings.

Conclusion: In our Markov model, preoperative intravitreal conbercept combined with vitrectomy is a highly cost-effective preference for vitreous hemorrhage from PRD compared to vitrectomy alone or with intraoperative IVC from societal and medical insurance perspectives. These findings provide economic evidence to support adjuvant IVC prior to vitrectomy for patients with VH from PDR.

detail.abstract: Existing literature on post-pandemic luxury realignments frequently misdiagnoses conglomerate exposure to the United States as overexpansion into a volatile market. This paper refutes that premise using data through mid-2026. The U.S. luxury ecosystem-anchored by resilient, equity-wealth-driven demand and a historically strong rate of new billionaire creation-remains structurally robust. The strategic error of leading luxury conglomerates, principally LVMH, lies instead in geographic homogenization: treating the U.S. consumer's transaction-driven buying model as an exportable template, rather than recognizing it as one persona among several with structurally different origins. Extending the Wealth Foundation Theory, this paper argues that the deeper variable beneath the US/Europe divergence is wealth vintage rather than geography-a rotation, since the 2008 financial crisis, of the luxury market's central fracture from "the West vs. the era's nouveau-riche" toward a fracture inside the West itself, between European Old Money and an American nouveau-riche built on speculative and technological wealth. Drawing on the brand authenticity framework of Morhart et al. (2015)-engaged across all four dimensions-and on Grayson and Martinec's (2004) indexical/iconic authenticity distinction, this paper contrasts LVMH's expansionist "Napoleonic" strategy with Hermès's defensive "Wellington" strategy through data extending to H1 2026, demonstrating that neglecting domestic cultural roots and relationship-based clienteling for transactional speed measurably erodes symbolic capital, brand authenticity, and, ultimately, financial resilience.

title: Global Stress without Global Shape: Volatility Synchronization and Distributional Fragmentation across Financial Markets
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Global Stress without Global Shape: Volatility Synchronization and Distributional Fragmentation across Financial Markets
detail.abstract: Financial crises are commonly described as episodes in which markets move together, but common volatility need not imply a common return distribution. We separate stress intensity, scale synchronization and distributional-shape synchronization using rolling empirical distributions for the S&P 500, FTSE 100, Nikkei 225 and Hang Seng from 2000 to 2026. Global scale measures average log realized volatility; scale gaps measure cross-market differences in volatility; raw Wasserstein distance measures total distributional separation; and Wasserstein distance between within-window standardized distributions measures shape divergence. The results reject a universal crisis pattern. At 252 days, the GFC is associated with lower shape divergence, whereas COVID is associated with substantially higher shape divergence despite a lower raw distance than in calm periods, driven by a narrower cross-market scale gap. Horizon-matched Newey-West inference confirms a positive COVID shape effect at 252 days (0.0447; 95% CI 0.0339-0.0555). Common-calendar reconstruction yields the same ordering. Markets can therefore share the intensity of stress while differing in asymmetry and tail structure.

title: Moving On From Movement: Sedentism Provides a Key Pathway to Food Security for Hadza Hunter-Gatherers
affiliations: Baylor University, Independent,  and Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine - Department of International Public Health

detail.abstract: Extensive discussion attends to the disadvantages of shifting from mobile hunter-gatherer subsistence  to sedentary living. Fewer studies have investigated the upsides of subsistence transition. In this study, among a sample of 101 Hadza adults in villages and bush-camps, we investigate the influence of multiple measures of subsistence transition on self-reported food security, using an adapted 9-question Household Food Insecurity Access Scale. Our analysis explores seven pathways to food security: Lower residential movement; higher annual cash incomes; engagement in horticulture; and animal husbandry; shop-use; receipt of government assistance; and permanent house-ownership. Of these, decreasing residential movement, shop-use and house-ownership outperformed other predictors in a leave-one-out model-selection. The centrality of decreasing residential movement in fostering food security, especially, corroborates extensive theoretical modelling from the anthropological/archaeological sciences placing sedentism — and the resource security it provides — at the heart of forager substance transitions. We further show that villages had greater food security, lower residential mobility, and greater inequality than bush camps.

title: The Firm: Rent, Structure, and Time

detail.title: The Firm: Rent, Structure, and Time
detail.abstract: Under perfect competition profit is zero and, with it, the entrepreneurial function disappears: the neoclassical model is the one case in which its own object does not exist. This paper proposes an axiomatic apparatus — four primitives, six axioms, six propositions — from which the competitive case, the market configurations that generate rent, and the pathological organizational regimes all follow as special cases. Profit decomposes into four gaps, one per market. Three of them close against a market rate; the labour gap does not, and it is the only internal one. Sustained organizational waste is shown to require a rent that finances it, so that the duration of a pathology is a lower bound on that rent. Over the internal structure a fuzzy membership space is defined in which the transmission power of a position and its achrony turn out to be the same object. An appendix sets out the testing strategy piece by piece and separates what already has external evidence from what remains untested.

detail.abstract: Canada has built strong but compartmentalized protections against discrimination, criminal hatred and unjustified state censorship. Those protections do not yet meet where modern institutional conflict occurs. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms constrains government; human-rights statutes govern specified relationships and enumerated grounds; employment and labour law regulate cause, contract and procedure; professional statutes protect public trust; criminal law reserves punishment for high-threshold conduct. A person whose lawful political conviction triggers dismissal can fall between those regimes, particularly when the employer is private, and the applicable human-rights law does not expressly protect political belief. 1 This paper asks how Canada can close that gap without weakening protection against antisemitism, anti-Palestinian racism, anti-Indigenous racism, anti-Black racism, Islamophobia, anti-Asian racism, misogyny, homophobia, transphobia, ableism or any other form of discriminatory harm. Its governing principle is direct: hate for none; equal protection for all. The objects of legal protection are the person and the community, not the state, government, national movement, or ideology. Political belief is protected as a feature of citizenship; independently wrongful conduct remains subject to regulation. The paper uses the controversy over Zionism and anti-Zionism as its principal legal stress test because it exposes the hardest classification questions. Jewish identity and safety cannot be reduced to a political position on Israel. Palestinian identity and safety cannot be reduced to a political position on Hamas or a constitutional settlement. Zionism and anti-Zionism may be religious, ethical, historical, or political commitments for different people, but neither label supplies a conclusive answer about discrimination. Context must determine whether disputed language criticizes an ideology or state, operates as a proxy for a protected people, threatens or harasses an identifiable person, or affects professional service. 2 The analysis combines constitutional doctrine, criminal law, human-rights legislation in all fourteen Canadian jurisdictions, labour and employment principles, professional-regulation statutes, hospital and nonprofit governance, official discrimination data, and comparative precedents from the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and Europe.
