detail.abstract:
Background: Preoperative prediction of distant metastasis (M1) in differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC) remains challenging, although it is critical for staging, risk stratification, and treatment planning. We aimed to develop and externally validate a preoperative CT-based deep-learning model for predicting M1 status in DTC.

Methods: In this retrospective two-center study, patients with DTC treated between January 2013 and May 2023 who underwent preoperative contrast-enhanced neck CT were included. Center 1 was used for model development and internal cross-validation (n=881; M1, n=119), and Center 2 was used for independent external validation (n=145; M1, n=15). ThyroidFusionNet evaluated candidate configurations integrating CT images with clinicopathological variables, radiomics, and tumor-habitat features through systematic ablation analysis. Exploratory post-hoc interpretability analyses included CT attribution, radiomics attribution, and WSI-based pathology anchoring.

Findings: Among prespecified configurations, the CT+radiomics model achieved the best overall performance. It achieved an internal AUC of 0.889 (95% CI 0.860–0.917) and an external AUC of 0.952 (95% CI 0.910–0.983). At the predefined threshold, external sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV were 0.933, 0.846, 0.412, and 0.991, respectively. More complex multimodal fusion strategies did not improve external validation performance. Interpretability analyses suggested that model predictions were associated with suspicious lymph-node regions, distributed radiomics features, and exploratory histomorphologic prototypes.

Interpretation: A preoperative CT+radiomics deep-learning model demonstrated strong discrimination for predicting distant metastasis status in DTC using routinely acquired CT data. The model may serve as a risk-stratification tool to predict patients who require more intensive metastatic evaluation. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted before clinical implementation.

title: Synthetic Biology for Climate Resilience & National Biosecurity in Pakistan (2028-2038)

detail.title: Synthetic Biology for Climate Resilience & National Biosecurity in Pakistan (2028-2038)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships with any individuals, organizations, or institutions that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on analysis of publicly available data, policy documents, and secondary literature. It does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental interventions. Therefore, no ethical approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Pakistan's economic and security vulnerabilities, stemming from climate instability, agricultural degradation, and biomedical dependence, demand transformative policy intervention. Synthetic biology, which integrates molecular engineering with computational design, offers scalable and cost effective solutions to these interconnected crises. This paper outlines a national strategy for integrating synthetic biology into Pakistan's policy and industrial frameworks over the period 2028-2038.

The proposed framework advocates the establishment of a National Synthetic Biology Council under the Ministry of Science and Technology to coordinate governance, investment, and risk oversight. Five policy pillars structure the strategy: governance and coordination, education and workforce development, research and development infrastructure, industry and private sector engagement, and safety, ethics, and public trust.

The framework recommends a distributed network of twelve synthetic biology sandboxes embedded within existing universities as low cost innovation centres. Flagship programmes target climate resilient crops, microbial water remediation, methane mitigation in livestock, and modular vaccine platforms. Financial modelling suggests that a five-year investment of US$20-35 million, structured through public private blended finance, can catalyse a bioeconomy contributing US$20-25 billion to GDP by 2038, while substantially reducing Pakistan's biomedical import dependence.

Comparative analysis of the United States, European Union, China, India, and Rwanda demonstrates that synthetic biology has become a strategic national asset in countries that acted early. Pakistan's delay in establishing a coherent national framework has already resulted in measurable opportunity costs. The proposed roadmap provides an actionable, fiscally grounded, and institutionally realistic pathway for Pakistan to enter this space before the window closes.

title: An Enhanced Benders Decomposition Framework for health Care Scheduling Problems: A case study of Covid-19
affiliations: K. N. Toosi University of Technology, K. N. Toosi University of Technology and Iran University of Science and Technology

detail.title: An Enhanced Benders Decomposition Framework for health Care Scheduling Problems: A case study of Covid-19
detail.abstract: During pandemic situations, hospitals experiencing shortages of ICU beds and medical staff require coherent and effective control systems. Insufficient medical personnel increases workload pressure, which may negatively affect patient recovery rates. Although societal restriction protocols can temporarily reduce patient inflow during peak periods, such measures are unsustainable in the long term, making subsequent infection waves inevitable. This study proposes a fair and accessible resource allocation framework to mitigate patient overload and reduce burnout among medical staff, while simultaneously considering optimal capacity expansion through the establishment of temporary healthcare centers. The resulting large-scale optimization problem is solved using a developed Benders Decomposition Algorithm (BDA). To improve computational efficiency, a novel theoretical enhancement is introduced to accelerate convergence, drawing on classical Operations Research concepts, including duality properties and the Complementary Slackness Theorem (CST). The performance of the proposed enhancement is evaluated against the Pareto-optimal cut. Uncertainty in patient demand, as a defining feature of pandemic conditions, is modeled using Fuzzy Scenario-based Programming (FSP). Several approaches are employed to prioritize fairness and accessibility in resource allocation as wait-and-see decisions. A real-world case study of hospitals in northeastern Tehran is conducted under six scenario-generation cases. By applying the capacity shortage ratio, it becomes possible to allocate ICU bed capacity in each period to non–COVID-19 patients. In the worst-case scenario, there is a capacity shortage in all periods, even for the admission of COVID-19 patients, whereas in the best scenario, at least 50% of the capacity can be allocated to non–COVID-19 emergency patients. The findings indicate that, in the worst case, a 20% increase in hospital capacity results in a 74% reduction in the shortage.

title: Medical Malpractice, Artificial Intelligence and Physician Liability: Who Is Responsible for AI-Assisted Medical Errors?

detail.title: Medical Malpractice, Artificial Intelligence and Physician Liability: Who Is Responsible for AI-Assisted Medical Errors?
detail.abstract: Clinical artificial intelligence has moved from pilot deployment to routine use in radiology, pathology, triage, and diagnostic support, yet malpractice doctrine still asks a single question designed for a single actor: did the treating physician breach the standard of care of a reasonably prudent practitioner? This article argues that the persistence of that question, unmodified, produces a structural liability gap whenever an AI system contributes to a diagnostic or treatment error. Drawing on doctrinal, comparative, and institutional analysis across the United States, the European Union, Germany, the United Kingdom, Japan, and Brazil, the article shows that four candidate defendants-the treating physician, the healthcare institution, the device manufacturer, and the AI developer-each escape meaningful accountability under existing frameworks for a different reason: physicians are protected by deference doctrines calibrated to human colleagues, institutions diffuse responsibility through credentialing and procurement layers, manufacturers invoke learned-intermediary and software exclusions from product liability, and developers rely on continuous post-market model drift to sever the causal chain between design and harm. The article's original contribution is the Clinical Algorithmic Liability Attribution Standard (CALAS), an institutional framework that reallocates the burden of causal proof according to a system's autonomy tier and mandates a shared, apportioned liability pool financed jointly by developers and institutional deployers rather than litigated de novo in each malpractice claim. The analysis proceeds through comparative doctrinal review, an institutional and empirical account of AI-enabled device authorization and clinical uptake, and jurisprudential analysis of the human-oversight standards that have emerged from adjacent algorithmic-accountability litigation. The article concludes that without a dedicated attribution standard, the liability gap will not close through incremental judicial adaptation of existing malpractice and product liability doctrine, because those doctrines were built on an assumption-a single, identifiable, professionally licensed decision-maker-that AI-assisted medicine no longer satisfies.

title: A Closer Look at Generation Z: Financial Knowledge and Financial Anxiety During the Economic Shock
affiliations: Incheon National University, University of Alabama and Seoul National University

detail.title: A Closer Look at Generation Z: Financial Knowledge and Financial Anxiety During the Economic Shock
detail.abstract: This study examined financial anxiety, financial knowledge, and the impact of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) shocks on Generation Z, comparing them with Millennials, Generation X, and Baby Boomers. Using the 2021 U.S. National Financial Capability Study (NFCS, N = 21,734), we estimated ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions to identify generational differences. We tested the moderating role of financial knowledge through interaction analyses and post-estimation Wald-type tests of coefficient equality across generations. Generation Z exhibited the highest level of financial anxiety (M = 5.27) and the lowest level of objective financial knowledge (M = 2.33) among all the cohorts, and also reported the greatest exposure to COVID-19-related health and labor shocks. COVID-19 shocks were positively associated with financial anxiety, whereas both objective and subjective financial knowledge were negatively associated, suggesting a protective role for financial literacy. Wald tests confirmed that these associations differed significantly across generations. Interaction analyses revealed asymmetric moderating patterns: objective financial knowledge was associated with reduced anxiety differentials in response to combined health and labor shocks, whereas subjective financial knowledge was associated with amplified anxiety differentials among respondents experiencing labor-related shocks. These findings highlight the distinctive role of objective financial knowledge in fostering resilience during economic disruptions and the need for generation-specific financial education programs.

title: The Perils of Urban Redevelopment for Black Business Districts The Perils of Urban Redevelopment for Black Business Districts
affiliations: University of Oregon - School of Law

detail.title: The Perils of Urban Redevelopment for Black Business Districts The Perils of Urban Redevelopment for Black Business Districts
detail.abstract:
From Tulsa, Oklahoma to Portland, Oregon, Black business districts—also known as "Black Wall Streets"—have long been targets for racial terrorism, destruction, and displacement. While nothing is particularly conspicuous about Black-owned restaurants, barbershops, and grocery stores, the values they represent—economic advancement and self-determination—entangle them within the web of institutional and systemic oppression. Although acts of physical destruction might seem less imminent today than in the past, Black business districts still confront a structural force that similarly threatens their viability: urban redevelopment. 

Urban redevelopment comprises a comprehensive set of policies, measures, and initiatives aimed at revitalizing historically divested neighborhoods. However, for many Black business districts, urban redevelopment is just the latest iteration of state-sponsored practices that disrupt Black entrepreneurship and fracture collective spatial identities. Balancing fragile economic gains against encroaching gentrification, Black business districts face a practical dilemma as redevelopment goals routinely converge and diverge among different interest groups. While state agents purport that urban redevelopment promotes economic stimulation and poverty deconcentration, critics contend that urban redevelopment processes can disenfranchise the very communities that Black business districts seek to empower. 

From Reconstruction to the present, Black business districts have confronted—and resisted—a plethora of discriminatory policies aimed at undermining their economic development and discouraging collective social action. Part I examines the legacies of violence and disenfranchisement that have historically plagued Black business communities, from vigilante attacks such as the Tulsa Race Massacre, to formal laws suppressing Black economic activity. Part II explores the parallel outcomes of urban renewal and urban redevelopment, situating the phenomena within the context of exclusionary state and federal policies. Part III calls on municipalities to adopt proactive, community-building frameworks that preserve the integrity of Black business districts and encourages renewed economic attention to historically divested neighborhoods.

title: Unified Theory of Digital Authenticity A Field-Level Formulation for Identity, Provenance, and Lifecycle Authenticity

detail.title: Unified Theory of Digital Authenticity A Field-Level Formulation for Identity, Provenance, and Lifecycle Authenticity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The research was conducted within the Ark Institute — Research Division.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This volume presents the Unified Theory of Digital Authenticity, a field‑level formulation that integrates the primitives of the Special Theory and the algebraic substrate of the General Theory into a single geometric and dynamical structure. The theory models authenticity as a field phenomenon governing identity, provenance, and lifecycle behavior across distributed, autonomous, and multi‑system environments.

The Unified Theory defines the Authenticity Field, its operators, invariants, and conservation laws, and establishes the admissible transitions and dynamics that determine how authenticity is preserved, transformed, or lost under interaction. It formalizes drift, entropy, collapse, and reconciliation as field effects, providing a coherent mathematical and conceptual framework for analyzing authenticity across time, transformation, and system boundaries.

The formulation demonstrates that failures of trust in digital systems—fraud, impersonation, corruption, systemic collapse—are not isolated phenomena but predictable consequences of missing or violated field structure. By unifying the primitives and algebra into a single field, this work provides a foundation for rigorous analysis, cross‑domain evaluation, and the design of systems capable of maintaining authenticity at scale.

For the first time, these principles are programmable and executable as a real‑time calculation layer for the digital universe, capable of measuring identity, continuity, provenance, and truth as they unfold. This volume completes the Authenticity Trilogy and establishes the field framework upon which future research, applications, and implementations may be built.

title: Franklin Writes a Law Review Article on the Intellectual Property Implications of Rage Bait
affiliations: St. Thomas University - School of Law

detail.title: Franklin Writes a Law Review Article on the Intellectual Property Implications of Rage Bait
detail.abstract:
Rage bait poses emerging challenges for intellectual property law that are not adequately captured by conventional fair use analysis. Although many rage bait works are defended as parody, satire, or other expressive uses, some such uses are directed neither principally toward criticism nor artistic commentary, but toward the deliberate exploitation of another's intellectual property to generate emotional reactions, attention, and algorithmic amplification. Prominent examples include the political and cultural reappropriation of Franklin the Turtle, Pepe the Frog, Success Kid, Dr. Seuss characters, and Disney properties, where familiar works are placed into inflammatory, violent, or controversial settings not principally to criticize the originals, but to maximize engagement through outrage.

This Article argues that existing copyright doctrine insufficiently addresses the reputational and market harms that can arise when outrage-driven reinterpretations reshape public perception of expressive works, while trademark law cannot be expanded to remedy those harms without risking the creation of “mutant species of copyright.” Rather than replacing fair use doctrine, this Article proposes a five-factor “deliberate exploitation test” that operates within the first fair use factor by providing a more structured method for evaluating whether a secondary user's asserted transformative purpose instead reflects the deliberate exploitation of a copyrighted work's goodwill, cultural reputation, or anticipated controversy. The analysis may also inform the fourth factor where such exploitation produces cognizable effects upon existing or reasonably likely markets. This approach seeks to preserve robust protection for parody, commentary, and future creative borrowing while giving meaningful effect to an author's right to exclude and avoiding the doctrinal expansion of copyright through trademark or moral-rights principles.

title: Natural Resources and Growth: From General Curse to Conditional Risk

detail.title: Natural Resources and Growth: From General Curse to Conditional Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: No applicable
declarations.funderStatement: No applicable

detail.abstract: Why do some resource-rich economies prosper while others stagnate? This paper offers a structured interpretive review of influential contributions from Dutch disease to critical minerals. A purposive sample tracks whether leading scholars changed position over time. The evidence does not show a simple reversal. It shows a movement from broad crosscountry claims towards conditional, mechanism-specific arguments attentive to endogeneity, institutions and state capacity. Resource rents become hazardous when they are large, concentrated, volatile and weakly governed. Norway, Botswana, Chile and Indonesia illustrate partial escape. Natural resources are therefore neither curse nor blessing by themselves.

title: Healthcare Utilisation After Positive Faecal Occult Blood Screening Despite No Colorectal Cancer: A Quasi-Experimental Cohort Study ​
affiliations: Karolinska Institutet, Karolinska Institutet, Karolinska Institutet, Karolinska Institutet and Karolinska Institutet

detail.title: Healthcare Utilisation After Positive Faecal Occult Blood Screening Despite No Colorectal Cancer: A Quasi-Experimental Cohort Study ​

declarations.declarationOfInterest: EN declares other funding from the Einar Belvén foundation, unpaid board membership of Swedish Society of Family Medicine research council and the European Commission on lung cancer working group. HD declares honoraria for lectures organized by the Swedish Society of Gastroenterology.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The Swedish Ethical Review Board approved the use of individual proprietary registry data (#2020-06757, #2023- 05985-02, #2024-03205-02).
declarations.funderStatement: The study was financed by The Swedish Cancer Society grant 24 3564 Pj (Blom) and grant 25 4029 FE (Dubois), The Swedish Research Council grant 2024-02679 (Blom) and grant 2025-07712 (Nemlander), and Region Stockholm, Sweden, grant FoUI-999619 (Blom).

detail.abstract:
Background: As organised colorectal cancer (CRC) screening programmes expand across Europe, little is known about their downstream effects on healthcare utilisation beyond the screening pathway. This study aimed to compare changes in healthcare utilisation among individuals with positive screening results without diagnosed CRC and participants with negative screening results..

Methods: We conducted a longitudinal cohort study within a Swedish population-based CRC screening programme using faecal occult blood tests (FOBT), among individuals aged 60–69 years. Individual-level registry data linked across multiple national and regional databases were analysed using a difference-in-differences design with Poisson regression. Screening participants between 2008 and 2021 were included, whereas individuals with diagnosed CRC were excluded. Four outcomes were pre-specified: outpatient visits in primary and specialist care for gastrointestinal diseases or psychiatric health disorders, all-cause primary care visits, gastroscopy procedures, and dispensed prescription drugs.

Findings: The sample consisted of 13,400 individuals with positive FOBT results and 204,591 individuals with negative FOBT results. There was a statistically significant relative increase of 11·13% (95% CI 4·51–18·66%) in outpatient visits for the selected diagnoses among individuals with positive FOBT results compared with those with negative results in the post-screening period. This increase was driven primarily by specialist outpatient visits in gastrointestinal care (86·42% [95% CI 61·36–120·69%]), and gastroscopy procedures (36·68% [95% CI 13·39–71·99%]). Notably, the analysis did not show changes in primary care utilisation for diagnoses of gastrointestinal diseases or psychiatric health disorders, nor for dispensed prescription drugs.

Interpretation: The findings of this study suggest that the consequences of organised CRC screening extend beyond the intended screening pathway. False positive CRC screening results appear to generate downstream healthcare utilisation concentrated within specialist gastrointestinal care, without evidence of spillover to primary care or increased prescription drug use.

title: Culturally Adapted Collaborative Care for Asian Americans with Type 2 Diabetes: Cardiometabolic Outcomes, Effect Modification, and Return on Investment
affiliations: Harvard University - Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard University - Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard University - Joslin Diabetes Center, South Cove Community Health Center, Inc., Harvard University - Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard University - Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard University - Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard University - Joslin Diabetes Center and Harvard University - Joslin Diabetes Center

detail.title: Culturally Adapted Collaborative Care for Asian Americans with Type 2 Diabetes: Cardiometabolic Outcomes, Effect Modification, and Return on Investment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: KHKL is a member of the board of directors of the Association of Diabetes Care & Education Specialists. All other authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study protocol was approved by the Committee on Human Studies at Joslin Diabetes Center (Protocol #STUDY00000104). The approval covered analysis of South Cove Community Health Center data. The requirement for informed consent was waived given the retrospective observational design using routinely collected clinical data.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (grant NU58DP007393), the Beatson 50-Year Medalist Fund, and the AADI Fund of Joslin Diabetes Center.

detail.abstract:
Background: Asian Americans bear a disproportionate burden of type 2 diabetes at lower body-mass index and face language barriers, yet evidence for culturally adapted management is limited. We evaluated the Asian American Diabetes Initiative (AADI).

Methods: In this retrospective cohort study (January 2023 to July 2025) we evaluated Asian American adults with type 2 diabetes receiving AADI collaborative care (endocrinology-led management, bilingual DSMES, Asian-pattern nutrition therapy, bicultural coordination, microvascular screening). The primary analysis was within-patient, comparing each participant’s pre- and post-referral trajectory, benchmarked against concurrent standard diabetes care at a community health center (SCCHC) and other cohorts. The primary outcome was composite ABC goal attainment at 24 months (HbA1c <7%, BP <130/80 mmHg, LDL-C <100 mg/dL).

Findings: Among 330 AADI and 2,868 standard-care participants, composite ABC attainment rose from 10% at referral to 29% at 24 months in the primary within-patient analysis (+19·1 percentage points, 95% CI 14·2–24·0). Attainment was 29% versus 20% in standard diabetes care (difference 9 percentage points, 95% CI 4–14). A restricted analysis of the 125 SCCHC-referred participants was directionally consistent (8 percentage points, 95% CI 0·7–16·5). Differences also favored AADI for HbA1c, LDL-C, and systolic BP, with a DSMES dose-response and attenuated limited-English-proficiency disparity.

Interpretation: Culturally and linguistically adapted collaborative care was associated with improved cardiometabolic outcomes, with a higher-risk population reaching attainment comparable to majority cohorts, reframing diabetes equity from disparity reduction toward parity. Pragmatic randomized trials are needed.

title: Vision and Language Models for Classifying Maxillary Sinus Disease on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: A Transparent Multimodal Benchmark
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London, King Abdulaziz University and Queen Mary University of London

detail.title: Vision and Language Models for Classifying Maxillary Sinus Disease on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: A Transparent Multimodal Benchmark

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a secondary analysis of the publicly available, fully de-identified MMDental dataset. Original data collection, informed consent, and anonymisation were approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Lishui University (approval identification number: 2022YR014), in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and the committee separately approved open publication of the anonymised dataset under a Creative Commons Attribution (CC-BY) licence. No additional institutional ethics approval was required for this secondary analysis, as no identifiable patient information was accessed at any stage.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Background: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) frequently captures the maxillary sinuses incidentally, and reliable automated detection of sinus abnormality is clinically relevant. Unlike most vision–language benchmarks in medical imaging, which pair images with pre-existing, human-authored clinical reports, findings text can also be generated directly by a large language model from the image itself—raising the question of how much diagnostic value such AI-derived text carries, and whether that value depends on independent verification. Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) benchmarks risk overstating performance if the provenance of each input—image, raw AI-generated text, or radiologist-verified text—is not clearly separated and reported.

Methods: We used 300 mid-sagittal CBCT slices from the MMDental dataset. ChatGPT generated findings text and a provisional normal/abnormal label for every slice (majority vote, three independent readings from the image alone); primary classification performance was assessed on this full, unfiltered set (n=300). A radiologist then independently reviewed each case’s image together with ChatGPT’s description, producing their own diagnosis; three cases were excluded as insufficient, yielding 297 confirmed cases. On this subset, every model was retrained and re-evaluated under identical 10-fold cross-validation on both the provisional ChatGPT-only labels (“pre”) and the radiologist-confirmed labels (“post”), isolating the effect of label provenance from image or architecture. Eight vision architectures, seven language classifiers, and five VLMs were evaluated throughout; three generative models performed exploratory note-drafting.

Findings: Raw ChatGPT-generated text produced the highest performance of any modality or condition: language models reached near-ceiling AUC (0·992 to 1·000, n=300), exceeding every vision model (AUC 0·799 to 0·880) and every VLM image-only probe (AUC 0·63 to 0·69). On the 297-case pre/post analysis, this advantage depended heavily on label source: language and text-derived VLM performance fell substantially from ChatGPT-only to radiologist-confirmed labels (e.g. BERT-base AUC 0·999 to 0·837), while vision-model performance was stable or modestly improved (e.g. DenseNet-121 0·867 to 0·891). The radiologist reclassified 62 of 297 cases (21%) relative to ChatGPT’s provisional read, and a meaningful proportion of raw ChatGPT text was clinically uninterpretable or unsupported by the imaging.

Interpretation: As shown here for the first time, raw, image-derived AI-generated text yields the highest apparent classification performance in this benchmark, but this reflects the text’s alignment with its own self-generated labels rather than verified diagnostic content, and a substantial share of that text is not clinically explainable. Radiologist-confirmed text and labels give a lower but trustworthy estimate of true performance, on which convolutional neural network (CNN) vision models remain a stable, comparatively inexpensive baseline. Multimodal dental AI should report performance separately by modality and label provenance rather than pooling headline metrics.

title: Sex Differences in Early Social Attention Behaviors in Autism
affiliations: University of Western Ontario and University of Western Ontario

detail.title: Sex Differences in Early Social Attention Behaviors in Autism
detail.abstract: Autism is diagnosed more frequently in males than females, although evidence suggests that autistic females may present with a behavioral phenotype and are often under-recognized. Social attention (SA) behaviors, including attention to stimuli and engagement in social interactions, are considered a core feature of autism. However, SA behaviors may differ between autistic females and males, potentially limiting the sensitivity of approaches identifying autistic girls. We examined sex differences in SA behaviors at 2 years of age in children with an increased familial likelihood of autism. Behavioral data from the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales-II (VABS-II) were obtained from 415 children enrolled in the Infant Brain Imaging Study (IBIS) Network who did and did not later receive an autism classification. Nineteen VABS-II items related to SA were identified through a keyword-based selection process and examined using binomial logistic regression analyses. Six SA-related items significantly differentiated biological sex within the autistic group only. Autistic girls were more likely to demonstrate behaviors related to social engagement and interaction, whereas autistic boys showed greater scores on behaviors related to attention to commands and non-specific bids for attention. These findings suggest that sex differences in SA behaviors emerge as early as the second year of life.

title: PRACT: Patient-specific Pareto-balanced robust electrode implantation planning for deep brain stimulation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing Medical University - Nanjing Brain Hospital, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing Medical University - Nanjing Brain Hospital and Nanjing Medical University - Nanjing Brain Hospital

detail.title: PRACT: Patient-specific Pareto-balanced robust electrode implantation planning for deep brain stimulation
detail.abstract: Preoperative trajectory planning for deep brain stimulation (DBS) is essential for surgical safety and effective stimulation. Existing automated methods often combine multiple anatomical criteria into a single aggregate cost, which may conceal an insufficient safety distance to an individual risk structure when vessels, sulci, and ventricles are evaluated simultaneously. Uncertainties in anatomical modeling and spatial localization may further alter the distances between candidate trajectories and adjacent critical structures, reducing trajectory stability. To address these issues, we propose PRACT, a patient-specific Pareto-balanced robust trajectory planning framework for DBS electrode implantation. PRACT integrates the stimulation target, clinically feasible entry regions, and three major risk structures within a patient-specific planning space, and constructs structure-specific safety distance fields for quantitative evaluation. Spatial perturbations are introduced to identify trajectories that remain feasible under plausible anatomical and localization variations. Robust candidates are then ranked using a Pareto-balanced strategy that accounts for trade-offs among vascular, sulcal, and ventricular safety distances. PRACT was evaluated on a 20-case NBH-STN-DBS cohort and the public Lead-Tutor dataset. Compared with clinical trajectories, PRACT increased the median safety distances to vessels, sulci, and ventricles by 1.23, 0.90, and 1.55 mm, respectively, in the clinical cohort. In the external dataset, the median increases in sulcal and ventricular safety distances were 1.33 and 1.29 mm. These results support PRACT as a quantitative, interpretable, and clinically reviewable framework for patient-specific DBS trajectory planning.

title: The Effect of Mutual Eye Contact Salience on Cooperation and Coordination in Virtual Teams
affiliations: , , Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

detail.title: The Effect of Mutual Eye Contact Salience on Cooperation and Coordination in Virtual Teams
detail.abstract: Initial interactions are crucial for establishing collaboration in virtual teams; however, virtual environments often lack the non-verbal cues necessary to mitigate strategic uncertainty. We examine whether making mutual eye contact salient and observable during an initial video meeting can improve subsequent coordination and cooperation in three-person virtual teams. Using state-of-the-art eye-tracking technology and a novel gaze-adaptive video meeting system, we conduct a preregistered lab experiment where teams engage in non-game-related pre-play communication before a Weakest-Link Game. Eye-tracking data reveal that the amount of mutual gaze exchanged in treatments with or without the gaze-adaptive technology did not differ. Thus, making eye contact salient did not alter gaze patterns. However, salience significantly increased minimum effort in the first round, which is a measure of cooperation in the sense of selecting a more Pareto-efficient equilibrium, before any performance feedback is available. The treatment did not significantly influence wasted effort, our measure of the team's coordination. The treatment's effect on cooperation weakened as rounds progressed, and participants began responding to realized performance rather than initial social signals. Exploratory mediation analyses (2SLS, SEM) are consistent with the treatment operating through increased interpersonal trust and higher beliefs about teammates' contributions. Our findings suggest that a low-cost, non-verbal salience cue can help newly formed virtual teams avoid low-effort coordination traps at the outset of collaboration.

reference: CESifo Working Paper No. 12907
title: Longevity Beliefs and Retirement Planning: Evidence from an Information Experiment and Expert Forecasts
affiliations: Free University of Bolzano-Bozen, Faculty of Economics and Management, , Free University of Bolzano, University of Trento and Free University of Bozen-Bolzano

detail.title: Longevity Beliefs and Retirement Planning: Evidence from an Information Experiment and Expert Forecasts
detail.abstract: Using original survey data from working-age individuals in Northern Italy, we study longevity beliefs and other key knowledge components relevant for retirement decisions. We find substantial dispersion in population longevity beliefs, with 40% of individuals misestimating life expectancy by more than five years, and highly fragmented knowledge across domains. Providing actuarial life expectancy information – tailored by age, gender, and county of residence – does not affect beliefs about individuals’ own longevity or retirement plans, reflecting a disconnect between beliefs about one’s own longevity and that of others. We compare our results with forecasts provided by 262 academic experts. On average, experts accurately anticipate the levels and correlations of longevity literacy with other knowledge components, but they mispredict a strong updating response of own longevity expectations to the provision of population information that deviates markedly from what we observe in the data.

title: Does Equitable Education Financing Improve Educational Quality? Evidence from Indonesia's Secondary Education Sector
affiliations: Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, Universitas Padjadjaran Bandung and Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia

detail.title: Does Equitable Education Financing Improve Educational Quality? Evidence from Indonesia's Secondary Education Sector
detail.abstract: A key priority for improving secondary education standards in Indonesia and reducing disparities in education services across schools is the equitable distribution of education funding. Equitable funding is seen as a tactical tool for increasing access and raising education standards. However, there is a lack of empirical data demonstrating how equitable education funding can lead to high-quality education services. Most previous studies have focused on fund allocation, with little attention paid to the function of financing efficiency as a mechanism explaining the relationship between equitable funding and quality education. This study examines the impact of budget allocation effectiveness, equitable education funding, and stakeholder collaboration on the quality of education services at the secondary education level in Indonesia. The study combines a mixed methods approach with a sequential explanatory design. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling was used for quantitative analysis, which was further refined through in-depth interviews and thematic analysis using NVivo. Quantitative findings indicate that education service quality and funding efficiency positively influence stakeholder collaboration, equitable education funding, and budget allocation. Qualitative results reveal that stakeholder participation in education governance, transparency, accountability, school institutional capacity, and equitable funding distribution are important factors in improving education quality. By indicating that financing efficiency is a crucial mechanism linking equitable education financing to the quality of education services, this study adds to the literature on education financing. These results confirm that equitable funding distribution, effective education governance, and efficient resource management are essential for improving the standards of secondary education in Indonesia.

detail.title: Consumer Perception of Corporate Value Endorsement
detail.abstract: Do consumers naively reward corporate value endorsement? In an online market experiment, U.S. consumers reason about and buy from sellers who endorse values with varying strategic incentives and costs. Consumers reward value-endorsing sellers but discount strategically motivated endorsements; surprisingly, costly endorsements do not outperform cheap ones. Consumers' beliefs appear sophisticated: they anticipate pandering, understand selection, but also expect a larger strategic response when endorsement is costly. A rational-inference benchmark approximates observed willingness-to-pay for strategic sellers, indicating that consumers reward a calibrated probability of genuine alignment. Open-ended narratives reveal consumers' sophistication outside the experiment, where profit and genuine motives are both recognized. These findings help explain why cheap value appeals persist and suggest that the main friction is not consumer credulity, but limited responsiveness to the intensity of costly commitment.
